infons.kwd: Multi-omics Extracellular vesicles Cancer Biomarkers

passages.text: Unlocking the power of extracellular vesicles: multi-omics integration for cancer biomarker discovery

The search for reliable cancer biomarkers is increasingly driven by the need for non-invasive tools that can monitor tumor dynamics in real time. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are a heterogeneous family of nanoparticles secreted by almost all cell types under physiological and pathological conditions. By carrying proteins, nucleic acids, lipids and metabolites that reflect the molecular state of their cells of origin, EVs act as dynamic messengers of tumor biology. Their stability and abundance in easily accessible body fluids make them ideal candidates for liquid biopsy, offering a unique opportunity to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying cancer initiation, progression and therapy resistance. Advances in high-throughput omics technologies, including proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics and transcriptomics, have enabled comprehensive profiling of EV cargo. These approaches have already identified promising biomarkers now entering clinical application, creating opportunities for earlier detection and more personalized interventions. However, relying on a single omics layer captures only a fraction of the molecular complexity underlying malignant disease. Integrative multi-omics strategies might uncover the regulatory networks and signaling pathways that drive tumor heterogeneity and evolution. Bioinformatics multi-omics integration focuses on developing tools that combine data from multiple omics experiments, revealing how their components interact and how these interactions change in disease. This review summarizes recent advances in EV-based multi-omics research for cancer diagnosis and clinical management, emphasizing how integrative approaches not only enhance biomarker discovery but also provide a systems-level understanding of disease mechanisms, paving the way toward precision and personalized medicine.
Background

Biomarker discovery is increasingly shaping the direction of biomedical research, focusing on the identification of novel biomarkers capable of not only accelerating the diagnostic process but also guiding therapeutic decision-making. Biomarkers are commonly defined as "objectively measurable indicators of normal biological processes, pathogenic processes or pharmacological responses to a therapeutic intervention". Although, in cancer research, tissue biopsies have traditionally represented the gold standard for diagnosis and clinical management, the rise of non-invasive biomarkers is reshaping the field. These non-invasive indicators may include a diverse range of molecular entities such as proteins, small molecules or fragments of RNA and DNA that can be detected in easily accessible biological fluids, offering the potential for early diagnosis and specific therapy. These molecules may be released freely because of pathological processes associated with cancer or other related metabolic diseases. Beyond their free circulation, such molecules can also be encapsulated within extracellular vesicles (EVs), phospholipid bilayer structures known to play a pivotal role in cell-to-cell communication under both physiological and pathological conditions. EVs can act locally, at the immediate proximity of the releasing cells or mediate signaling at distant sites from their release. EVs have been identified in a wide range of biological fluids where they transport lipids, proteins, metabolites, DNA and RNA, thus representing an ideal source for biomarker discovery through multi-omics approaches. Omics technologies including proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics and transcriptomics enable comprehensive profiling of EV cargo, shedding light on their role in disease development and progression, as well as their potential diagnostic applications. The high-throughput nature of these technologies, however, generates large and complex datasets, making robust post-acquisition data analysis a crucial step. Within the framework of systems biomedicine, the integration of multi-omics data is essential to achieve a systemic and coherent understanding of underlying biological processes. Several bioinformatic tools have been developed to facilitate such integration, both at the level of single biomarkers and pathway analysis. Moreover, the growing application of artificial intelligence offers powerful opportunities to design predictive algorithms that combine multi-omics data and clinical parameters.

In this review, we comprehensively describe the potential of extracellular vesicles as a promising source of biomarkers for cancer diagnosis and clinical management. We will introduce the fundamentals of EV biogenesis and their role in intercellular communication, followed by an overview of the major omics technologies that enable in-depth characterization of their molecular cargo. More importantly, we will highlight the emerging chances offered by integrative multi-omics approaches, which not only enhance biomarker discovery but also provide a system-level understanding of disease mechanisms, paving the way toward precision and personalized medicine. We will present state-of-the-art strategies for multi-omics data integration, how important the level of integration of the different omics data is and how a hybrid approach can combine elements from multiple integration strategies, revealing that integration is not a one-size-fits-all solution but a key methodological decision. We will highlight the principal features of each tool (type of analysis, input data, interface and output) in order to help reader to choose the best integration method, considering the characteristics of the EV dataset, the study design and the type of biological or clinical question.
Extracellular vesicles: from their origin to their potential in biomarker discovery

Extracellular vesicles are a heterogenous family of nanoparticles secreted by almost all cell types under physiological and pathological conditions. When first discovered, EVs were only considered "waste carriers" responsible for removing unwanted molecular components from the cells to maintain normal tissue homeostasis. However, it is now well established that cells can package signaling molecules in EVs, to protect them from rapid degradation, contributing to local and long-distance intercellular communication. EVs have also been found to contribute to pathological diseases such as heart disease, neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. Therefore, given their nature, EVs are a rich source of potential biomarkers in several biomedicine fields.
Extracellular vesicle classification and biogenesis

Extracellular vesicles biogenesis: Schematic representation of the main classes of extracellular vesicles, illustrating their relative sizes and biogenetic pathways. Exosomes (30-150 nm) originate from the endosomal system and are released upon fusion of multivesicular bodies with the plasma membrane; microvesicles (100-1000 nm) are generated by outward budding of the plasma membrane; apoptotic bodies (1000-5000 nm) released during programmed cell death as membrane-bound fragments containing cytoplasmic and nuclear components

Conventionally, extracellular vesicles (EVs) are classified according to their size: with small EVs typically < 200 nm and large EVs >= 200 nm. However, these size ranges overlap considerably, making biogenesis pathways a more reliable criterion for categorization. The Minimal Information for Studies of Extracellular Vesicles (MISEV 2023) guidelines describe three main EV subtypes: exosomes (30-150 nm), microvesicles (100-1000 nm) and apoptotic bodies (1000-5000 nm) (Fig. 1). Apoptotic EVs are released as fragments of cells undergoing programmed cell death and include large apoptotic bodies and small apoptotic vesicles. Their formation is associated with outward blebbing of the plasma membrane, accompanied by externalization of phosphatidylserine, which serves as an "eat-me" signal for clearance by phagocytes. Exosomes and microvesicles share the common feature of membrane trafficking processes, but their biogenesis is distinct. Microvesicles form directly at the plasma membrane. Their budding is driven by a combination of several factors that starts with the redistribution of phosphatidylserine to the outer leaflet and cytoskeletal remodeling with action-myosin contraction, which disrupts membrane symmetry and promotes outward vesicle formation. In contrast, exosomes are small EVs of endosomal origin, formed through inward budding of the late endosomal membrane to generate intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) within multivesicular bodies (MVBs). Fusion of MVBs with the plasma membrane results in the release of these vesicles, which carry signaling competent proteins, lipids and nucleic acids that mediate intercellular communication. In vitro, exosome biogenesis has been shown to be orchestrated by the endosomal sorting complex required for transport (ESCRT), a machinery of ~ 30 proteins organized into five functional subcomplexes. ESCRT-0 captures ubiquitinated cargo, ESCRT-I and -II drive ILV budding, ESCRT-III mediates vesicle scission and the Vps4 complex ensures final membrane separation and ESCRT recycling. In addition to the ESCRT-dependent route, lipids such as ceramides and other proteins such as tetraspanins (e.g., CD9, CD63) contribute to ILV formation and exosome release. Small GTPases, notably Rab27a/b and Rab11, regulate vesicle trafficking and membrane fusion, while accessory proteins such as ALIX and syntenin modulate cargo selection. In recent years, advances in high-resolution imaging, proteomics and nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) have revealed additional subtypes, such as large oncosomes, migrasomes and nanoscale non-vesicular particles like exomeres and supermeres. While the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles (ISEV) recommends the umbrella term "EVs" unless origin is definitively demonstrated, functional and molecular distinctions between subtypes remain important. Among these subtypes, exosomes remain the most extensively studied due to their functional roles in physiological and pathological processes.
Molecular composition of EVs

Extracellular vesicles composition: Schematic representation of extracellular vesicles illustrating their structural organization and molecular composition. EVs enclose a diverse cargo of metabolites, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids, reflecting their cellular origin and functional roles. The vesicle surface is coated by a biomolecular corona formed by adsorbed biomolecules that influence EV stability, biodistribution and biological interactions

Lipids and proteins form the primary structural backbone of EVs (Fig. 2). The lipid bilayer contributes to maintain membrane integrity with EV content protected from proteases and nucleases present in the extracellular space. EV lipidic bilayer also displays a distinct composition that does not always reflect the plasma membrane of the parent cell. Indeed, lipidomic analyses have shown that sphingomyelin, cholesterol, phosphatidylserine and ceramide are the main classes of lipids represented in EVs, while phosphatidylcholine and diacyl-glicerol are decreased compared to the original cell membrane. Moreover, EV subtypes display unique enrichment patterns: small EVs (exosomes) contain two- to three-fold higher levels of cholesterol and sphingomyelin relative to their cells of origin, whereas larger EVs such as microvesicles are characterized by increased exposure of phosphatidylserines on their outer surface. Such lipid asymmetry is critical not only for membrane curvature and vesicle release but also for modulating interactions with target cells, immune evasion and circulation half-life. Proteins constitute the second major class of structural components, decorating the vesicle surface and contributing to EV identity (Fig. 2). Canonical membrane-associated proteins include tetraspanins (CD9, CD63, CD81 etc.), integrins, MHC molecules, transporters and receptors, which mediate selective recognition and uptake by target cells (Fig. 2). Proteins involved in EVs biogenesis are also abundant, particularly those derived from the endosomal pathway, such as ESCRT components (ALIX, TSG101) and small GTPases (RAB27A, RAB11B, ARF6) that regulate vesicle formation and release. In addition to canonical proteins, EVs also display distinctive surfaceome proteins that are highly relevant for diagnostics and therapeutic applications. These include cell type or disease-specific surface markers, such as tumor-associated proteins, which can be exploited for selective isolation and detection of EV subpopulations. Beyond their diagnostic value, these surface proteins influence EV function by modulating interactions with recipient cells, affecting uptake, signaling and tissue targeting. Characterizing these unique surfaceome components is therefore critical for understanding the functional heterogeneity of EVs and for developing their clinical applications in disease monitoring and targeted therapies. However, the proteins carried by exosomes are not limited to structural or surface functions. Many are packed as cargo, including signaling proteins, metabolic enzymes, transcription factors as well as membrane receptors that can translocate to the nucleus, such as EGFR, Notch and Wnt. In addition to proteins, EVs carry a diverse repertoire of nucleic acids and small metabolites as cargo (Fig. 2). Although DNA is detected only in limited cases, including fragments of genomic and mitochondrial DNA, EVs are consistently enriched in RNA species, especially small RNAs like microRNAs, ribosomal RNA fragments (18S, 28S) and tRNAs, highlighting their potential as vehicles for horizontal transfer of genetic information and as biomarkers for disease. Metabolomic studies have also revealed the presence of small bioactive molecules such as sugars, vitamins, aromatic compounds and amino acids (Fig. 2). These metabolites, together with proteins and RNAs, are not merely passive components, they can modulate signaling pathways, influence gene expression, reshape metabolic networks and alter cellular behavior in recipient tissues. Collectively, this rich and diverse cargo provides a systems-level insight into the physiological and pathological roles of EVs and underscores their potential as biomarkers and therapeutic mediators. Given the high potential of EVs, different studies have focused on characterizing their content. Publicly accessible data repositories, such as Exocarta and Vesiclepedia, have collected the results of these studies, storing information about protein, nucleic acid, metabolite and lipid content. Moreover, the use of advanced techniques, such as super-resolution microscopy, has enabled the analysis of individual EVs. This has revealed that various biomolecules including proteins, lipids and nucleic acids, can adhere to the surface of EVs upon their release into biological fluids, forming what is known as the biomolecular corona (BC) (Fig. 2). This phenomenon can influence EV properties by changing the aspect of their superficial layer and their ability to reach specific tissues and interact with them. Together, the EV structural and cargo components not only reflect their cell of origin but also create a distinct "molecular fingerprint", enabling the differentiation of EV subtypes and the identification of specific disease states.
Physiological roles of EVs

Extracellular vesicle's role in physiology vs cancer: Schematic overview illustrating the dual roles of EVs. In physiology (green), EVs contribute to cell-cell communication and signaling pathways, tissue repair and regeneration, immune system functions, reproduction and neonatal development and aging. In cancer (red), EVs promote angiogenesis, immune modulation, therapy resistance, pre-metastatic niche formation and distant organ communication, highlighting their role in tumor progression and metastasis

Beyond their early portrayal as waste, EVs are now recognized as biologically active particles, as cells preserve homeostasis through the balance between synthesis and autophagy processes such as degradation and recycling of bioactive molecules. Different studies have demonstrated that the secretion of EVs can prevent the intracellular accumulation of potentially cytotoxic material. On the other hand, the fate of those EVs harboring potentially unneeded biomolecules once outside the cell is still not clear. Beyond their role as carriers of molecular cargo, EVs have emerged as essential mediators of physiological intercellular communication (Fig. 3). Indeed, cell-to-cell communication can be mediated by direct interaction through cellular junction but also by the secretion of biomolecules either free or packed within EVs. Given their structural properties, EVs can transport biomolecules across short and long distances, even to difficult-to-reach organs such as the brain, by crossing the blood-brain barrier. Extracellular vesicles regulate critical signaling pathways including Wnt, Hedgehog and Notch during development and tissue homeostasis and their cargo can adapt in response to physiological conditions such as exercise or metabolic stress (Fig. 3). In the immune system, EVs exert dual function. While they act as key players promoting the maturation of immune cells as well as the activation of immune response, EVs can also be promoters of anti-inflammatory responses. EVs are also potent mediators of tissue repair and angiogenesis, transferring pro-regenerative RNAs, proteins and lipids to damaged cells and enhancing vascular remodeling through factors such as VEGF and matrix metalloproteinases (Fig. 3). During pregnancy, placental and trophoblast-derived EVs support embryo implantation, immune tolerance and maternal-fetal communication, while breast milk EVs contribute to neonatal gut and immune development (Fig. 3). Finally, EVs are increasingly linked to aging, as their abundance and cargo composition shift with age, influencing cellular senescence, neurotrophic support and systemic inflammatory status (Fig. 3). Collectively, EVs are not merely passive byproducts of cellular activity but functional and dynamic mediators in a wide range of physiological processes. Their composition and abundance are highly responsive to environmental and physiological cues, including exercise, hypoxia, temperature fluctuations and therapeutic interventions. These features underscore their potential as sensitive indicators of health and disease. At the same time, the context-dependent variability of EV content presents a significant challenge for accurately interpreting their molecular signatures in biomarker discovery and clinical applications.
EVs in cancer

In cancer biology, EVs have emerged as central players in tumor progression, metastasis and therapy resistance. Tumor-derived EVs (TDEVs) actively remodel the tumor microenvironment by delivering oncogenic proteins, nucleic acids and metabolites that promote angiogenesis, stromal activation and immune evasion (Fig. 3). Various cancers exploit EVs to communicate with distant skeletal muscles and adipose tissue, promoting lipolysis and muscle wasting, which contributes to the development of cancer-associated cachexia. The organotropism of TDEVs often involves the recognition of surface markers present on EVs by the target recipient cells. This interaction depends on integrins present on the surface of EVs to mediate the selective uptake. EVs contribute to the formation of pre-metastatic niches by conditioning distant tissues through the delivery of extracellular matrix remodelers and vascular permeability factors. Immune escape is facilitated by the transport of immune checkpoint molecules, such as PD-L1, which inhibit T cell activity, as well as by immunosuppressive cytokines and miRNAs (Fig. 3). A growing body of evidence also indicates that TDEVs mediate drug resistance by transferring resistance-associated molecules, such as specific microRNAs, between tumor cells, thereby disseminating adaptive traits across the tumor population (Fig. 3). Moreover, TDEVs carry fragments of tumor DNA, oncogenic receptors such as EGFR or HER2 and distinct RNA signatures that can be detected in patient biofluids. Their heterogeneity mirrors that of the tumor, with specific EV proteomic and transcriptomic profiles correlating with cancer subtypes, disease stage and prognosis. As such, EVs represent not only functional mediators of malignancy but also a promising source of minimally invasive biomarkers for cancer detection, patients' stratification and treatment monitoring.
EVs as source of biomarkers

Extracellular vesicles in biofluids as a source of biomarkers: EVs can be isolated from blood, urine, saliva, cerebrospinal fluid, breast milk and other body fluids, offering a minimally invasive alternative to tissue biopsies

The finding that EVs are present in nearly all biological fluids has generated significant interest in their potential as biomarkers. EVs can be readily isolated from blood, urine, saliva, cerebrospinal fluid, breast milk and other body fluids, offering a minimally invasive alternative to tissue biopsies (Fig. 4). Their lipid bilayer ensures stability to encapsulated molecules, protecting nucleic acids and proteins from enzymatic degradation. Moreover, since EV cargo mirrors the molecular makeup of the originating cell, they carry a tissue-specific molecular fingerprint that can be accessed through liquid biopsy. Unlike conventional biopsies, which require surgical procedures and may capture only a limited region of a tumor, liquid biopsy allows for the repeated, non-invasive sampling of biological fluids, enabling real-time monitoring of disease progression, treatment response and early detection of pathological changes. This approach holds promise not only for diagnostics but also for patient stratification and personalized therapeutic decision-making. The concept of precision medicine has evolved over recent decades from early stratified treatment approaches based only on clinical and histopathological features to a data-driven paradigm integrating clinical with genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic information. Decision-making process in precision medicine is largely driven by biomarkers, which serve as indicators of disease presence, progression or specific physiological states. In this framework, liquid biopsy-based strategies, including EV profiling, represent a natural extension of precision medicine by enabling dynamic, longitudinal and minimally invasive assessment of patient-specific disease biology. Several studies have demonstrated the diagnostic and prognostic value of EV-derived miRNAs, proteins and DNA fragments in diverse malignancies, including breast, lung, liver and prostate cancers. Even salivary EVs are gaining popularity as the choice for identifying potential biomarkers of diseases of the oral cavity such as squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). Their application for early-stage diagnosis is associated with a five-year survival rate of 20% for half of the patients. Recently the field's capacity to derive EVs from extracellular space within an organ has been shown, including heart, kidney, muscles, lungs, liver and various cancer tissues (breast cancer, renal cell carcinoma, colon cancer and ovarian cancer). In this context, the proteomic analysis of EVs derived from colon mucosal tissues reveals a distinct protein profile between EVs secreted in the tumor microenvironment and those present in non-tumor mucosa. Even frozen tissues can be a potential source of EVs. In a recent work Artuyants et al., developed a pipeline for EVs extraction directly from nine frozen bio banked endometrial cancers samples. Proteomics profiling identified EV markers associated with the main endometrial cancer subtypes. Nevertheless, significant challenges remain. The pronounced heterogeneity of EVs complicates their use as biomarkers, affecting all steps of the workflow, from sample handling to quality control of isolated particles. The study of EVs requires a comprehensive description of the source material, including donor characteristics for human or animal samples such as age, biological sex, health status and exposure to medications or other substances. The quantity and quality of the starting material, together with all sample collection procedures, must be clearly documented. Sample pre-processing should be performed as early as possible to remove cells and minimize artefacts arising from cell activation or death. Storage conditions before and after EV isolation must be fully reported, including temperature, storage duration, container type, use of preservatives or cryoprotectants and the number of freeze-thaw cycles, as these factors can significantly affect EV integrity and composition. Commonly employed isolation methods, such as ultracentrifugation, size-exclusion chromatography, immunoaffinity capture and microfluidics, differ in yield and purity and often result in the co-isolation of contaminants, including lipoproteins, protein aggregates and cell-free nucleic acids. Considering these challenges, standardization of isolation protocols and adherence to the MISEV2023 guidelines are critical for fully harnessing the biomarker potential of EVs. The guidelines classify EV protein content using a five-category framework to assess EV preparations: Categories 1-2 confirm EV identity, Category 3 evaluates the presence of common contaminants and Categories 4-5 provide contextual information on intracellular origin or co-isolated components. Comparing the abundance of EV-associated proteins with that of non-EV proteins enables an assessment of sample purity. This distinction is essential for biomarker discovery, as it ensures that identified molecular signals reflect bona fide EV cargo rather than contaminants, thereby enhancing the reliability and translational potential of EV-based biomarkers. Quality control measures should be implemented throughout sample collection, pre-processing and EV isolation. In EV biomarker studies, results should also be compared with non-enriched materials such as whole biofluids. Finally, researchers are encouraged to follow the relevant ISEV Task Force recommendations specific to their EV source. Rigorous standardization improves reproducibility and comparability across studies, reducing technical variability that can obscure biologically meaningful EV-associated signals. By minimizing pre-analytical and analytical biases, these guidelines enhance the reliability of EV cargo profiling and facilitate the identification of robust, disease-specific biomarkers. Well-characterized and consistently processed EV samples support the integration of EV-based biomarkers into clinical workflows, enabling more accurate patient stratification, disease monitoring and therapeutic response prediction, ultimately strengthening the translational impact of EV research and their implementation in precision medicine.

Over the past decade, rapid progress in high-throughput technologies has transformed biomedical research by enabling simultaneous analysis of thousands of molecular features in a single experiment. Genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics, supported by next-generation sequencing, mass spectrometry and advanced imaging, can generate extensive datasets that capture the molecular complexity of health and disease. These technologies make it possible to compare molecular patterns that define cellular states and pathological processes, offering valuable insights into disease mechanisms. When combined with powerful computational and bioinformatics tools, omics-driven approaches provide a proficient way to identify novel biomarkers and to advance diagnostics, prognostics and therapeutic strategies, especially in oncologic research (Table 1). Omics analyses can be successfully applied to EVs to characterize their molecular cargo and identify potential biomarkers for disease diagnosis and prognosis. This ongoing "omics revolution" has therefore become a cornerstone in uncovering molecular pathways and accelerating the development of precision medicine.
Genomics and transcriptomics analysis of EVs

Genomics and transcriptomics are among the most mature "omics" technologies. Together, they provide complementary insights into the molecular basis of biology, since alterations in DNA sequences lead to substantial changes in RNA transcripts. The technological evolution of sequencing has been a key driver in advancing these approaches. High-throughput platforms now allow genome and transcriptome wide interrogation at single-nucleotide resolution. Two main processes are thought to be the major sources of EV-DNA. The first is cell death: during apoptosis and necrosis, DNA fragments are passively incorporated within EVs. EV-DNA can secondly originate from an active mechanism of secretion that employs EVs to maintain cellular homeostasis under physiological conditions but can contribute to disease progression in pathological states. EV-DNA biomarkers have been consistently reported to mirror the genetic status of tumor cells, carrying both nuclear and mitochondrial sequences. For instance, BRAF mutations have been detected in exosomal DNA from melanoma cell lines, while amplified c-Myc sequences were identified in isolated serum vesicles from mice bearing medulloblastoma. These findings validate that EV-derived DNA can preserve driver mutations and reflect the genetic landscape of the parental tumor. Beyond mutations, EV-DNA carries copy number variations (CNVs) and epigenetic modifications such as methylation patterns that reflect the cell of origin. Deep sequencing and targeted methylation profiling of EV-DNA have demonstrated tumor-specific methylation patterns. Tn5-assisted Enzymatic Methyl-sequencing with Post conversion Tailing (TEMPT) approach, designed by Lin et al., applied to EV-DNA can robustly distinguish gastric cancer patients from controls and even differentiate between early and advanced gastric cancer stages with relatively high performance in both discovery and validation cohorts (AUC = 0.8). The study statistical power remains limited by the modest cohort size, making difficult to explore relationships between EV-DNA signatures and clinical features (e.g., age, stage, treatment response). Compared to DNA, RNA represents the predominant nucleic acid species in EVs. Numerous studies have reported the presence of mRNAs, miRNAs and lncRNAs within exosomes and microvesicles. Advanced high-throughput RNA sequencing has further revealed a wide variety of RNA subtypes across EV subpopulations isolated from biological fluids. By capturing the dynamic landscape of coding and non-coding RNAs, transcriptomics provides insight into how cells respond to physiological and pathological changes, even by the release of RNA packed in EVs. Importantly, the protective encapsulation of RNA within EVs distinguishes them from other circulating nucleic acids. Direct profiling of tumor-derived transcripts from plasma cell-free RNA (cfRNA) has often shown poor success due to RNA degradation in circulation. In contrast, EVs shield their RNA cargo from enzymatic degradation, enabling reliable detection even in challenging clinical samples. Recent studies have demonstrated the potential of EV-RNA cargo for cancer diagnostics, although the clinical maturity of these biomarkers can vary considerably. Breast cancer (BCa) derived-EV transcriptomics revealed dynamic changes in EV-RNA content at the time of diagnosis and 7-days after breast surgery. While several individual biomarkers exhibited high specificity but only moderate-to-low sensitivity, limiting their standalone diagnostic value, a combined model of eight RNAs (three lncRNAs, three snoRNAs, one miRNA and one piRNA) achieved high diagnostic performance with AUC of 0.90 upon Leave One Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV). In addition, several of these RNAs also correlated with estrogen receptor (ER) and HER2 status, supporting the use of EV transcriptomics for both diagnosis and patient stratification. However, the lack of validation in an independent cohort raises the possibility of overfitting and thus the clinical applicability of the signature remains preliminary. Similarly, in prostate cancer (PC), transcriptomic analysis of EVs isolated from plasma and urine EVs identified 69 RNA biomarker candidates, including protein-coding genes, lncRNAs and piRNAs that decreased after prostatectomy. Messenger RNAs such as FOXA1, MAZ and LCP1, previously linked to PC progression and poor prognosis, were detected in urinary EVs, underscoring their translational relevance. Importantly, a subset of candidates, such as miR-375-3p, piR-28004 and AMD1, were validated in an independent cohort of 20 patients via RT-ddPCR, showing significant reductions in urinary EVs after surgery, whereas others (GLO1, MAZ, NKX3-1) trended similarly but did not reach significance. Although this validation cohort was relatively small, it provides early external support for these markers, positioning them at a more clinically mature stage. Established RNA-derived markers such as the lncRNA PCA3 are already incorporated into the FDA-approved ExoDx Prostate test, a non-invasive urine exosome gene expression assay, further highlight the clinical utility of EV-based approaches. Collectively, genomic and transcriptomic profiling of EVs offer a minimally invasive means to identify disease-specific molecular signatures, opening new avenues for biomarker discovery and clinical application. While technical challenges remain, the accumulated evidence strongly supports EV nucleic acids as a promising source of liquid biopsy biomarkers.
Proteomics in EVs

Proteins are among the key constituents of EVs, forming both membrane components and internal cargo. They are central to vesicle biogenesis, uptake and intercellular communication. Protein expression levels, post-translational modifications (PTMs), interactions and localization are critical determinants of biological activity, making comprehensive proteomic characterization essential for understanding EV roles in physiology and disease. Because EVs are typically isolated in small quantities, high analytical sensitivity is required. Liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) is the most widely used and versatile method for EV proteomics, enabling detection, identification, characterization and quantification of thousands of proteins. Recent huge advances have facilitated the discovery of EV-associated protein biomarkers with significant potential for diagnostics, prognostics and therapeutic monitoring across various diseases. Melanoma-derived EVs (MTEX) exhibit a characteristic eight-protein signature capable of distinguishing patients with progressive disease (PD) from those with non-evident or stable disease (NED/SD). All identified proteins contribute to melanoma progression and metastasis, suggesting that MTEX proteomic profiles hold prognostic relevance. Similarly, comparative analysis of plasma-derived EV proteomes from healthy individuals, patients with benign breast tumors and those with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) revealed distinct molecular signatures. Healthy controls exhibited the highest number of unique EV proteins, while only two (ZG16B and APOC2) and one (HISTH2B) were unique to the benign and TNBC groups, respectively. These findings underscore the value of EV proteins as surveillance markers for early detection and disease risk assessment. Despite encouraging findings, the clinical relevance of both studies is constrained by small cohort sizes and the absence of validation of the identified biomarkers in an independent sample set, which is necessary to demonstrate robustness. Proteomic analysis also allows characterization of PTMs within EV proteins, opening new opportunities for biomarker discovery. PTMs such as phosphorylation, glycosylation, ubiquitination, acetylation and methylation finely regulate protein structure, stability and activity. Aberrant PTM patterns often reflect disease-specific signalling events. In non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), quantitative phosphoproteomic analysis of EVs isolated from tumor and adjacent normal tissues identified over 2,000 phosphorylation sites on approximately 1,500 proteins, including 152 kinases, of which 25 were differentially expressed. Taken together, proteomic and PTM profiling of EVs provide a powerful platform for uncovering disease-associated signatures and identifying novel diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers.
Metabolomics in EVs

Beyond proteins and nucleic acids, EVs also carry small molecules that play active roles in intercellular communication by modulating metabolic pathways and cellular responses. Metabolomic analyses of EVs, particularly using high-resolution mass spectrometry platforms, are therefore crucial for identifying early biomarkers and elucidating disease progression. During their biogenesis, EVs can incorporate metabolites such as carbohydrates, amino acids, nucleotides and enzymatic cofactors. Increasing evidence suggests that EVs act as autonomous metabolic units, capable of influencing metabolism in recipient cells. In lung cancer, metabolomic analysis of 102 urinary EV samples identified diverse classes of metabolites, including organic acids, lipids, heterocyclic compounds and benzenoids. Using a random forest model, a diagnostic panel achieved AUC up to 1 and 0.96 in the training and testing set, respectively. 84% accuracy was reached in the validation cohort, highlighting urinary EV metabolomic signatures as promising non-invasive biomarkers for disease early detection. Recent studies have also examined faecal EVs, which mediate interactions between the host and the gut microbiome. In a controlled study comparing patients with solid tumors and healthy controls, LC-MS-based profiling revealed significant differences in metabolite abundance. Metabolite set enrichment analysis linked these changes to key pathways such as arginine biosynthesis and branched-chain amino acid metabolism. Based on ROC analysis, glutamic acid emerged as an effective discriminator between individuals with solid tumors and healthy subjects. Moreover, Puhka et al. examined metabolic alterations in EVs isolated from urine samples of prostate cancer (PC) patients and compared them to EVs from healthy individuals. Notably they demonstrated that metabolic alterations, such as changes in ribose 5-phosphate, glucuronate and isobutyl-L-carnitine, were detectable in EVs from the urine of PC patients but not in the urine itself. This exploratory study, even lacking relevant diagnostics metrics evaluation highlight EVs as a sensitive source for non-invasive biomarker discovery. Collectively, these findings underscore the emerging role of EV metabolomics as a powerful approach to detect disease-associated metabolic alterations.
Lipidomics in EVs

Lipids are fundamental constituents of EV membranes, conferring structural integrity, driving vesicle biogenesis and modulating interactions with recipient cells. Given their pivotal structural and signalling roles, investigating the lipid composition of EVs is essential for understanding their biological and pathological functions. The lipidomic landscape of EVs provides critical insights into the biochemical alterations accompanying cancer progression. Specific lipid classes, such as sphingolipids, are differentially expressed in cancer-derived EVs compared with those from normal cells, highlighting their potential as malignancy indicators. Notably, several studies have reported a significant enrichment of lipid subclasses, particularly ceramides and phospholipids, in EVs derived from cancer cells, suggesting their association with tumor aggressiveness. Untargeted lipidomic profiling of breast cancer-derived EVs and their parental mammary epithelial cells revealed an enrichment of sphingolipids and glycerophospholipids in cancer EVs. Because the lipid profile reflects the metabolic state of tumors, lipidomic profiling of EVs offers a non-invasive means to capture tumor-specific molecular signatures from biofluids such as plasma or urine. Nevertheless, it is crucial to underline that the lipid composition of EVs exhibits marked variability among different cancer types, for instance, between breast cancer and renal cell carcinoma, offering a diverse landscape of potential diagnostic markers and therapeutic targets. Liu et.al applied LASSO regression analysis, on 11 EV-associated lipids in 126 breast cancer (BC) cases, identified a three-lipid panel for BC screening. Using 10-fold cross-validation repeated 25 times, the panel demonstrate robustness achieving AUCs of 0.76 (training set), 0.74 (internal validation set) and 0.80 (external test cohort), with specificity reaching 1 in the external set. Independent lipidomic analyses across two cohorts further support the potential of EV-lipid profiling for BC screening. In other breast cancer studies, lipidomic profiles differ significantly between metastatic and non-metastatic tumors, revealing mechanisms through which EVs may contribute to tumor progression and dissemination. Specific lipids, including phosphatidylcholines and sphingomyelins, display altered distributions in EVs from breast cancer cells, correlating with disease severity. Furthermore, lipid mediators derived from EVs are increasingly recognized for their roles in shaping the tumor microenvironment, thereby influencing therapeutic responses and patient outcomes. The cellular origin of EVs is a key variable in lipidomic interpretation, as vesicles derived from distinct cell types within a tumor exhibit unique lipid signatures. Although this heterogeneity adds complexity, it also provides deeper insights into intercellular communication within the tumor microenvironment. For example, comparative lipidomic analyses of EVs from tumor-associated macrophages and those from tumor cells can elucidate pathways of immune evasion and tumor promotion. External factors such as diet, lifestyle and environmental exposures also influence EV lipid composition, opening new avenues for personalized medicine. Cancer patients may exhibit distinct EV lipidomic profiles shaped by these factors, supporting the development of individualised therapeutic strategies. Integrating EV-based lipidomics into clinical oncology thus holds promise not only for improving diagnostic accuracy but also for guiding precision treatment approaches based on each patient's unique lipidomic signature. Dysregulated lipid metabolism is a hallmark of cancer, reflecting altered cellular signalling. In clinical studies, isolated blood plasma EVs from women with primary or metastatic breast cancer and healthy controls were classified with about 90% accuracy, upon LOOCV, based on EV lipid composition, highlighting once again the potential of EV-associated lipids as powerful non-invasive biomarkers. The use of advanced analytical platforms such as LC-MS/MS and robust bioinformatic tools, which are rapidly evolving, is reshaping cancer detection and management. Together, metabolomic and lipidomic analyses of EVs complement proteomic and transcriptomic approaches, providing a more comprehensive understanding of EV-mediated communication and their potential as diagnostic, prognostic and therapeutic biomarkers. However, most findings are still at an exploratory stage, with limited validation across large and clinically representative cohorts. The lack of independent verification remains a major bottleneck and future studies will require larger, well-characterized patient populations to establish the robustness, reproducibility and true clinical utility of EV-based signatures.
Single-omics data analysis applied to EVs

Single-omics approaches provide a focused perspective on the molecular composition of extracellular vesicles, enabling detailed characterization of their cargo, identification of functional signatures and discovery of potential biomarkers. Despite this, the functional interpretation of large-scale omics datasets remains challenging due to their complexity and high dimensionality. The increasing accessibility of omics technologies has, however, catalyzed the development of user-friendly, web-based tools that facilitate data processing and functional analysis, making such insights more accessible to researchers with limited computational expertise. These platforms allow exploration of pathways, networks and biological processes in a reproducible and systematic manner, supporting rapid hypothesis generation and functional annotation. For RNA-based analyses, tools such as ExpressAnalyst provide web-based pipelines for high-throughput RNA-sequencing data, integrating robust statistical methods with advanced visualization capabilities to identify differentially expressed genes and interpret functional pathways. In the field of metabolomics, MetaboAnalyst offers comprehensive support for both targeted and untargeted studies, encompassing data processing, normalization, statistical analyses and metabolic network visualization. Proteomics research has benefited from platforms such as STRING, Cytoscape and DAVID, which facilitate exploration of protein-protein interactions, functional modules and pathway enrichment. Lipids, as major components of EV membranes, play critical roles in vesicle formation, stability and uptake. Nevertheless, in the lipidomic field, the structural complexity and functional diversity of lipids present significant analytical challenges. LipidSig 2.0 has emerged as the first web-based platform providing integrated and comprehensive analysis for efficient mining of lipidomic datasets. This tool allows to automatically identify lipid species, assigning 29 comprehensive characteristics and supporting 24 data processing methods, thereby enabling researchers to decipher complex lipid profiles and link them to specific biological contexts. Its automated workflows encompass data preprocessing, lipid identification, differential expression analysis, enrichment and network analysis. While these general-purpose tools can be adapted for EV studies, dedicated workflows and pipelines specifically optimized for EV data remain limited, highlighting an ongoing need for EV-focused solutions. Curated repositories such as ExoCarta, EVpedia and Vesiclepedia have been fundamental in advancing EV research by providing comprehensive listings of EV-associated proteins, RNAs and lipids, thereby supporting annotation, cross-study comparisons and knowledge discovery. Vesiclepedia is integrated into functional analysis tools such as FunRich, functional enrichment analysis tool, enabling more context-specific and accurate interpretation of EV molecular cargo. Among EV-specific tools, EVscope represents a particularly advanced pipeline for the analysis of EV RNA-seq datasets. It employs an optimized genome-wide expectation-maximization algorithm to improve multi-mapping read assignment at single-base resolution, addressing the challenges posed by fragmented and low-abundance EV RNAs. EVscope also incorporates a broad annotation covering 19 RNA biotypes, including protein-coding genes, lncRNAs, miRNAs, piRNAs, retrotransposons and other non-coding RNAs and offers downstream modules to infer tissue or cellular origins of EV RNAs using bulk and single-cell RNA-seq reference datasets. While EVscope delivers highly detailed and EV-specific analyses, its use requires more computational expertise than web-based platforms. Together, these developments illustrate the complementary roles of general-purpose and EV-specific tools in elucidating the molecular landscape of extracellular vesicles. Web-based platforms enhance accessibility and facilitate rapid functional interpretation, whereas specialized pipelines like EVscope provide high-resolution, context-specific insights that are essential for fully understanding the biological complexity of EV cargo.
Multi-omics for biomarker discovery

Analysis of individual omics layers has greatly advanced the field of cancer diagnosis, despite these strides, relying on a single-omics platform provides only a limited view of the intricate molecular interplay involved in tumor development and progression. Consequently, integrating data from multiple omics sources has become essential for a more comprehensive understanding of oncogenic processes. Extracellular vesicles are especially well-suited for multi-omics integration due to the pronounced heterogeneity in their cargo, encompassing a variety of biomolecules reflective of their parent cells. Unlike cells, EVs content is highly tissue-specific, making EVs a uniquely valuable and non-invasive source for the discovery of biomarkers representative of the tissue of origin. Given the vast and heterogeneous nature of the data produced by these platforms, computational analysis becomes an essential component, enabling meaningful integration and interpretation across multiple layers of biological information. Together, the combined experimental and computational framework maximizes the power of multi-omics to reveal clinically relevant insights for biomarker discovery.
Multi-omics integration strategies

Overview of single-omics profiling and multi-omics integration strategies: The top panel shows distinct feature matrices generated independently from genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and lipidomics for downstream analysis. The bottom panel highlights the multi-omics integration strategies: early integration, which concatenates features from different omics into a single dataset; intermediate integration, which uses statistical or machine learning models to learn joint representations or networks across layers; and late integration, which analyzes each omic separately and fuses results at a meta level

The advent of omics technologies has opened new frontiers in cancer research, providing powerful tools to examine tumors across multiple biological layers. Cancer is not driven by isolated molecular events but by intricate regulatory networks. Consequently, the integrative analysis of multi-omics data has gained increasing attention in recent years. Multi-omics integration serves as an umbrella term encompassing diverse approaches tailored to different experimental designs and study contexts. This field within bioinformatics focuses on creating tools that integrate data collected from separate experiments, connecting different omes to reveal how their components interact and how those interactions may change. Performing multi-omics analysis typically requires that all molecular layers derive from the same biological sample, ensuring direct comparability across datasets. However, this is often challenging, as extraction procedures must be optimized for different classes of biomolecules. Consequently, it can be difficult to achieve optimal recovery for each molecular fraction from a single sample. Researchers must therefore balance the benefits of sample-level integration against the technical limitations of parallel extractions or alternatively rely on biological replicates to mitigate the variability introduced when separate samples are used for each omic layer. Recent progress in high-throughput technologies now enables the simultaneous profiling of multiple omics layers with exceptional sensitivity and resolution. As the time and cost required to generate these datasets continue to decrease, integrating omics data is becoming both a compelling opportunity as well as a considerable challenge for biologists, computational scientists and biostatisticians. While these innovations allow an unprecedented level of insight into tumor biology, they also produce vast and heterogeneous datasets, underscoring the pressing need for specialized computational methods for effective integration and analysis. Multi-omics integration can be broadly classified as either knowledge-driven or data-driven. Knowledge-driven approaches typically analyze each omics layer independently to identify relevant molecular features, which are then mapped onto curated biological databases, including pathways, ontologies, or interaction networks. These methods offer interpretability and a strong biological rationale but rely heavily on the completeness and accuracy of existing knowledgebases. In contrast, data-driven integration approaches adopt a hypothesis-free, exploratory strategy, allowing the de novo discovery of shared patterns and correlations across multiple omics layers. To navigate this complexity, three main integration strategies have been proposed: early integration, which combines features from multiple omics into a single dataset; late integration, which analyzes each omics layer separately before merging results and intermediate integration, which employs statistical or machine learning models to jointly extract patterns across data layers (Fig. 5). However, not all developed tools fall strictly within one of these categories, as many employ a hybrid approach that combines elements from multiple integration strategies. The rapid growth of multi-omics datasets, especially in cancer research, has also driven the increasing use of artificial intelligence, where machine learning and deep learning approaches are proving highly effective at detecting meaningful signals, revealing hidden interactions and generating translational insights that advance precision medicine.

Beyond their biological impact, omics platforms generate high-dimensional and complex datasets, with computational integration often representing the rate-limiting step in multi-omics studies. To address this challenge, a wide range of integrative analysis tools have been developed to combine information across different modalities, enabling molecular data to be explored in a system-wide manner (Tables 2-3). These strategies can be applied not only to capture coordinated variation across regulatory layers and uncover crosstalk among pathways but also to enhance the identification of robust biomarkers by linking molecular signatures across multiple omics levels. Importantly, the choice of integration method depends on data characteristics, study design and the specific biological question, emphasizing that integration is not a one-size-fits-all solution but a key methodological decision. Data preprocessing is a critical foundation for effective multiomics integration. Preprocessing steps typically include rigorous quality control, normalization to adjust for platformspecific effects and batch variation, imputation or handling of missing values and feature filtering to remove lowvariance or noisedominated variables that can otherwise overwhelm integrative models and obscure biological signal. Scaling and transformation (e.g., logtransform) are essential to bring disparate omics measurements onto comparable scales before integration. Clear reporting and justification of these preprocessing decisions not only improve analytical robustness but also enhance reproducibility and biological interpretability of integrated results. Biochemical pathways are a central focus in systems biology, providing a framework to interpret molecular changes across different omics layers. Several computational tools have been developed for joint pathway analysis, enabling researchers to integrate multi-omics datasets and interpret results in the context of biological networks (Table 2). Integrated Molecular Pathway-Level Analysis (IMPaLA) is one of the earlier tools designed for the combined analysis of multi-omics data based on a collection of pathway resources aggregated from 11 public databases, including Reactome, KEGG and WikiPathways. IMPaLA supports multiple identifier formats and allows two types of enrichment analysis: over-representation analysis (ORA) performed in the restricted list of statistically significant features and Wilcoxon enrichment analysis (WEA), which instead requires the complete features list associated to fold change levels. IMPaLA, however, is limited to human pathways and can support the simultaneous analysis of only two types of input omics layers at a time. Conversely, the multiGSEA R package implements a multi-layer gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)-based approach across up to eight pathway databases, with the possibility to integrate transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic layers simultaneously. In contrast to IMPaLA, multiGSEA supports 11 organisms and provides extensive ID mapping resources. Both approaches provide table form output with ranked pathways, overlap with the input dataset and statistical p-values, for single omics level as well as multi-omics combined p-values thus delivering a robust measure of pathway activity across different molecular layers. On the other hand, those tools do not provide visualization strategies of the obtained results. For a more interactive and visual approach, PaintOmics 4 has been designed for web-based pathway integration and visualization. It incorporates KEGG, Reactome and MapMan databases, allowing applicability to both animals and plants. Beyond conventional pathway enrichment, PaintOmics introduces new modules for metabolite-centered analysis, such as metabolite hub analysis, which identifies compounds potentially regulated by surrounding gene expression changes and metabolite class activity analysis, which assesses whether specific metabolic classes exhibit disproportionate regulation. Another complementary platform is OmicsNet, a highly interactive web-based application for multi-omics network construction that allows sophisticated 2D and 3D visualization. Users can upload lists of relevant genes, proteins and metabolites, which are then mapped onto molecular interaction databases to generate networks highlighting biologically relevant associations. Together with the webtool programmers have also released the OmicsNetR package which can be used to locally recreate or further customize networks before moving to OmicsNet for interactive visual exploration. PaintOmics and OmicsNet focus more on interactive network exploration rather than purely providing only enrichment-based outputs. Similarly, specialized tools have been developed to reduce the complexity of multi-omics data, each offering complementary strategies enabling the extraction of key features from omic-layers for the identification of disease-associated patterns and patient stratification (Table 3). MixOmics is a widely used R package for omics data supporting different frameworks: single-omics analysis (pca, spca, plsda, splsda), two-omics (pls, spls) and multiple-omics analysis (P-integration and N-integration). By reducing dimensionality while retaining major sources of variation, mixOmics enables informative visualizations and interpretation of biological systems, overcoming one of the main limitations of omics datasets: the curse of dimensionality. MixOmics supervised frameworks are particularly relevant for biomarker discovery. For example, the DIABLO method integrates multiple omics datasets measured on the same samples (N-integration) to identify correlated omics variables across datasets which are predictive of phenotypic groups. In parallel, the MINT framework in mixOmics enables the integration of independent studies measured on the same variables (P-integration), thereby supporting reproducible biomarker identification across cohorts. In contrast, the Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA) adopts an unsupervised approach. This statistical method can define hidden factors that capture the major sources of variability and provide a low-dimensional representation of the multi-omics space that facilitates subgroup discovery, detection of continuous molecular gradients and outlier identification. More recently, playOmics has emerged as another open-source R package focused on workflows for biomarker discovery. It combines data management, visualization and statistical modeling with automated feature selection and predictive model construction. Using cross-validated ranking strategies and iterative logistic regression, playOmics identifies combinations of prognostic markers with high predictive performance. Finally, OmicsAnalyst offers a web-based platform designed for interactive multi-omics integration, allowing users to start from data harmonization and then explore multiple approaches for visualization and downstream analysis. Unlike R-based packages, it emphasizes accessibility by combining more than a dozen established analytical methods into three main visual analysis tracks: correlation network analysis (2D or 3D networks), cluster heatmap and dimension reduction track. This latter provides a range of multivariate approaches to explore global data structures, including the DIABLO method taken from the mixOmics R package. Together with a variety of integration methods, OmicsAnalyst also provides interactive visualization strategies both in 2D and 3D. Taken together, the variety of available tools highlights that there is no universal solution for multi-omics integration. Therefore, the choice of method should be guided by the characteristics of the dataset, the study design and the type of biological or clinical output that is sought. Careful alignment between analytical strategy and research objectives is essential to fully exploit the potential of multi-omics data in systems biology and translational applications. To facilitate the selection of the most appropriate tool for multi-omics integration based on specific needs and the characteristics of the omics dataset, we have summarized the key aspects of commonly used multi-omics integration tools, including their strengths, limitations and best use cases for EV data (Table 4).
EV multi-omics studies

Building on the structural and functional properties of extracellular vesicles, together with the power of high-throughput omics technologies, multi-omics integration has demonstrated tangible potential in translating EV cargo into actionable cancer biomarkers. In a pilot study by Yu et al., researchers profiled serum and urine metabolome, together with gut microbiome and isolated serum EV proteome in 15 patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC) versus 11 patients with non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). This integrated approach revealed 159 molecular features distinguishing MIBC from NMIBC, among them in particular 18 serum-EV proteins, together with 26 metabolites identified in serum and urine and 2 gut microbes, were specifically associated with cancer progression. Despite the preliminary nature of this study and the limited patient cohort, significant alterations highlight the potential of integrating metabolomics- and proteomics-derived biomarkers across multiple biological fluids, including circulating EVs, for staging bladder cancer progression. In another study, proteomic, metabolomic and lipidomic analyses were performed on EVs isolated from serum samples of 11 CRC patients and 8 healthy individuals, as well as on conditioned media derived EVs from CRC cellular models (FHC vs. HT-29 cell lines). Joint-pathway analysis revealed shared metabolic routes between patient samples and cellular models, including aminoacyl-tRNA biosynthesis and fatty-acid-related metabolic processes. Analyzing these components could provide insights into CRC molecular mechanisms and support the development of targeted therapies. Overall, this study provides exploratory yet valuable proof-of-concept findings on how EV content could contribute to non-invasive and clinically practical approaches for CRC diagnosis. Likewise, Luo et al. employed a multi-omics approach combining transcriptomics and proteomics to characterise the exosomal cargo of lung adenocarcinoma stem-like cells (LSLCs). These vesicles, in comparison with lung adeno carcinoma bulk cells (LBCs) isolated EVs, were shown to be enriched with 218 markers across RNAs and proteins engaged in extracellular matrix (ECM) organization, ion transport, cell adhesion and migration, all fundamental pathways in tumor development. To assess the clinical relevance of such markers, experimental validation was performed on patient-derived LSLCs (PLSLCs) isolated from lung adenocarcinoma tissues, which is a key aspect of this study. Proteomic analysis validated 53 LSLC markers as upregulated in PLSLCs versus primary tumor cells, with ALDH3A1, ALDH1A1 and ALDH5A1 ranking among the top 10 most altered proteins. In melanoma research, EV-based multi-omics strategies have also delivered promising results. Plasma-derived EVs were isolated and analyzed for proteomic and metabolomic profiling. Single-omics analyses of plasma-EVs from showed limited classification power when compared to healthy controls. The proteomic approach identified PRG4, APOC4 and HPR as potential discriminating proteins, but even the best-performing combination of PRG4 and APOC4 reached only 73.4% accuracy. Similarly, the metabolomic based classification, driven mainly by PC 34:3 and LPC 18:2, achieved 82.98% accuracy. When proteomic and metabolomic datasets were integrated, a focused two-feature multi-omics signature composed of PRG4 and PC 34:3 achieved 85.11% accuracy, outperforming the single-omic classification benchmarks. Similarly, in studies of brain metastases from lung cancer, investigators combined small RNA sequencing with LC-MS/MS proteomics in serum-derived exosomes from a lung cancer mouse model which develops brain metastasis. This approach identified miR-206-3p and vinculin (VCL) protein as promising biomarkers. To validate those results RT-qPCR was performed on serum-derived EVs, showing miR-206-3p marked upregulation in metastatic mouse model. Immunoblotting showed marked increase in VCL protein levels in metastatic versus control group. Collectively, these studies demonstrate that EV-based multi-omics integration provides a powerful and versatile platform for cancer biomarker discovery. By leveraging complementary molecular layers such as proteomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics and lipidomics, researchers can achieve a more systemic understanding of EV biology and tumor complexity. This integrative strategy not only enhances biomarker sensitivity and specificity but also yields mechanistic insights into the pathways driving cancer progression. Despite this potential, limitations persist due to small cohorts, which constrain statistical power and generalizability. These studies remain substantially preliminary without rigorous external validation on independent cohorts.
Future trends in multi-omics integration: the use of artificial intelligence

To handle the massive volume and complexity of data generated by modern omics platforms, AI has emerged as a powerful approach capable of managing high-dimensional datasets and enhancing their integration for biomarker discovery. By uncovering patterns often invisible to traditional analytical methods, AI enables the fusion of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic information to support early cancer detection, patient stratification, and therapy response prediction. The choice of AI methodology depends strongly on the characteristics of the data and the intended clinical goals. Classical machine learning models, such as Random Forests and Support Vector Machines, are particularly effective in settings with smaller sample sizes and curated feature sets, offering interpretability and computational efficiency. Deep learning approaches, in contrast, excel in large-scale multi-omics environments where manual feature extraction is infeasible, facilitating automated discovery of molecular patterns across multiple omics layers. Recently, building on classical and deep learning frameworks, prompt-based multi-omics data integration has emerged as a promising approach for the combined analysis of diverse biological omics layers. The PromptBio platform exemplifies AI progress by utilizing a multi-agent architecture that automates various essential processes in bioinformatics data analysis. It incorporates specialized agents, such as DataAgent and OmicsAgent, which support automation in tasks like data loading, pipeline execution and statistical analysis. The platform's capability of dynamic code generation empowers researchers to tailor analyses to their specific scientific queries, pushing beyond the limitations of standardized workflows, overcoming their common limitations, and enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of datasets interpretations. Such AI-driven approaches hold great promise for innovation in the field of extracellular vesicle research, pushing to the next level the comprehensive integration of omics layers as a powerful source of novel biomarkers and mechanistic insights. As AI technologies continue to evolve, they may enable the development of more sophisticated predictive models capable of simulating complex biological interactions based on omics data. For instance, advancements in machine learning algorithms could uncover hidden relationships among varying omics layers, potentially identifying previously unrecognized biological pathways and processes. These insights could pave the way for enhanced personalized medicine, where diagnostic and treatment strategies align closely with an individual's unique molecular profile. Despite encouraging progress, the application of artificial intelligence to EV multi-omics workflows continues to face well-recognized constraints. EV omics is affected by heterogeneous pre-analytical variables (biofluid type, isolation method, purity), block-wise missingness across omics layers, batch effects and annotation biases in pathway databases, all of which can undermine the generalizability of AI models. Moreover, given the frequent combination of small cohorts and high-dimensional datasets, overfitting remains a persistent challenge. As widely discussed, these limitations necessitate rigorous regularization, careful validation strategies and explainability analyses to ensure the biological credibility of results. This remains an evolving field and formal clinical practice guidelines for AI-assisted EV biomarker discovery are not yet established. Although MISEV2023 defines rigorous research standards for EV isolation, characterization, and reporting, it does not constitute clinical practice guidelines for the deployment of AI-integrated EV multi-omics biomarkers within care pathways. Similarly, inter-society initiatives are advancing standardization efforts and the development of reference materials, but formal guidance on clinical validation, regulatory-grade performance, post-deployment monitoring and model governance is still emerging. High-quality standardized metadata, reproducible computational practices, federated or controlled data-sharing frameworks and sustained domain-expert oversight are essential, yet not universally adopted. Until such foundations become routine, AI-assisted EV biomarker findings should be considered exploratory and supported by robust external validation and explainability analyses.
Conclusions e Future directions

The integration of multi-omics approaches in extracellular vesicle research holds immense promise for advancing biomarker discovery and precision medicine in the oncologic field and beyond. In biological systems, omics layers are highly interconnected: genomic alterations can lead to changes in transcriptomes, which may in turn influence epigenetic modifications and protein expression. In turn, variations in protein abundance or activity can drive shifts in metabolite levels and alter lipid composition, reflecting the metabolic state of cells. Treating these layers independently can produce incomplete or biologically superficial insights. By combining insights from different omics layers researchers can achieve a comprehensive understanding of cancer pathophysiology, thereby improving diagnostic accuracy, patient stratification and therapeutic monitoring. However, the translational potential of multi-omics-based EV biomarkers is contingent upon the establishment of standardized methodologies. The International Society for Extracellular Vesicles (ISEV) has made significant strides in addressing these challenges through the development of reference materials, guidelines and task forces focused on rigor and standardization. A notable recent initiative is the ISEV-ELBS Intersociety Working Group, founded in 2023 through collaboration between ISEV and the European Liquid Biopsy Society (ELBS). Continuous optimization of extraction protocols is required to maximize the simultaneous recovery of different biomolecules. Likewise, bioinformatic workflows must be tailored to specific research objectives. Achieving an optimal balance between standardization and flexibility from EV isolation to downstream data analysis, appears essential to fully unlock the potential of multi-omics approaches. Meanwhile, the rapid evolution of high-throughput analytical platforms is accelerating the shift from bulk-EV (Bu-EV) to single-EV analyses (Si-EV), providing unprecedented resolution and revealing diagnostic features inaccessible through bulk studies. In this context, this review provides a detailed description of the available tools and a transparent guide to researchers to choose the best integration strategy for EV multi-omics datasets, also in consideration of the experimental study and the characteristics of the multi-omics data, since there is no single strategy suitable for all types of studies. In the next future by combining multi-omics EV profiles with artificial intelligence among which machine learning algorithms, it will become easier to identify complex molecular patterns, predict disease progression and tailor therapeutic strategies with unprecedented precision. When coupled with comprehensive clinical datasets, this integrative approach can enable truly personalized cancer diagnosis, prognosis and treatment monitoring. Together, these strategies promise to transform EV multi-omics research from a promising experimental paradigm into a clinically actionable framework that delivers precision oncology at the patient level.

passages.text: Advances on drug therapy for KRASG12C-mutant non-small-cell lung cancer
Highlights
This article highlights the research progress and clinical trial results of KRASG12C targeted inhibitors.
The resistance mechanism and research progress of KRASG12C targeted inhibitors are described.
Combination treatment strategies and novel therapies for KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC.

Lung cancer has an extremely high mortality rate among malignant tumors, posing a significant threat to human health Among all lung cancer cases, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for a significant proportion and has become a hot topic in clinical research and treatment. The Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS) is one of the most common oncogenic drivers in NSCLC, closely associated with tumor initiation, treatment response, and prognosis. However, due to the relatively smooth surface of the KRAS protein and the lack of drug-binding pockets, it has long been regarded as an "undrugable target". With further research, recently, targeted drugs targeting the KRASG12C gene mutation have achieved significant breakthroughs in clinical trials, especially the application of KRASG12C-specific inhibitors adagrasib and sotorasib, which has changed the treatment landscape for NSCLC patients. To address challenges such as tumor heterogeneity, the complexity of the tumor microenvironment, interpatient variability, and acquired drug resistance mechanisms, combination therapy strategies involving KRASG12C inhibitors have emerged sequentially. This article systematically reviews the progress of targeted therapy for KRASG12C-mutant NSCLC and the results of related clinical trials, while exploring novel therapeutic strategies for patients with KRASG12C mutations, aiming to provide a reference for the selection of clinical treatment regimens.
