passages.text: The efficacy of intra-operative injection of [99mTc] labelled colloidal nanoparticles for sentinel lymph nodes identification in breast cancer
Background

Sentinel lymph node (SLN) biopsy is a critical component of axillary staging in breast cancer management. Traditionally, Technetium-99m (Tc-99m) labelled colloidal nanoparticles is injected preoperatively in the nuclear medicine suite, followed by imaging, while blue dye is injected intraoperatively. Despite the use of topical anesthetics, preoperative radio-tracer injections can be painful, time-intensive, and resource-demanding. To address these limitations, we implemented intraoperative radio-tracer injection under anesthesia, instead of the traditional procedure at the nuclear imaging suite. This study evaluates whether intraoperative Tc-99m labelled colloidal nanoparticles administration affects SLN identification rates.
Materials and methods

A retrospective analysis of breast cancer patients who underwent surgery at Rambam Health Care Campus (2020-2023). Unfiltered Tc-99m sulphur colloid and blue dye were injected intraoperatively, and SLN detection rates were assessed.
Results

Among 350 patients (352 procedures), radioactive SLNs were successfully identified using Tc-99m in 89.5 % of cases. When both Tc-99m labelled colloidal nanoparticles and blue dye were used, the identification rate increased to 93.2 %. SLN detection was higher in upfront surgery compared to neoadjuvant therapy cases (radio-tracer alone: 92.2 % vs. 85.1 %, p = 0.048; dual tracer: 95.9 % vs. 88.8 %, p = 0.015). Advanced T-stage (OR 5.1, 95 %CI 2.3, 11.3; p < 0.001) and N-stage (OR 3.7, 95 %CI 1.8, 7.3; p < 0.001) were associated with lower SLN detection rates.
Conclusions

Intraoperative Tc-99m labelled colloidal nanoparticles injection is an effective alternative to preoperative injection, achieving comparable SLN detection rates while eliminating patient discomfort, reducing procedural complexity, and optimizing surgical workflow.
Highlights
Intraoperative radiocolloid injection efficiently detects sentinel lymph nodes.
Intraoperative injection avoids the pain associated with preoperative injection.
Intraoperative injection offers financial as well as logistical advantages.
Introduction

Sentinel lymph node (SLN) biopsy plays a crucial role in the management of breast cancer allowing for appropriate staging and tailoring of the treatment plan. Compared to axillary lymph node dissection (ALND), SLN biopsy is a less invasive procedure which results in faster recovery and reduces the risk of complications such as lymphedema, nerve damage, and shoulder mobility issues, contributing to a better long-term quality of life for patients undergoing breast cancer treatment.

The identification rates for SLN with dual tracer (radiocolloid and blue dye) are over 90 %, with low false negative rates and favorable recurrence rates. Unlike blue dye, which is injected intraoperatively under anesthesia, Tc-99m labelled colloidal nanoparticles is typically administered preoperatively in the nuclear medicine suite, often causing significant pain and unnecessary stress.

Approval to inject radio-tracers within the operating room was obtained in our institution at 2019 allowing the surgeons to inject the radioactive tracer to the breast while the patient is under anesthesia, inattentive to the injection pain, similar to the standard practice with dye injection. This method has been described in a relatively few studies from individual centers. Although these studies report good results in hundreds of patients, most medical centers still administer the radio-tracer prior to surgery at the nuclear medicine suite. Rambam Health Care Campus is the only hospital in Israel where Tc-99m labelled colloidal nanoparticles is injected in the operating room after anesthesia. This study aimed to evaluate the performance of intraoperative radio-tracer injection in terms of SLN mapping accuracy, while additionally providing information on its financial implications, procedural efficiency, safety, and potential advantages relevant to its consideration as an alternative to standard preoperative protocols.
Materials and Methods
Study population and setting

This was a single-arm retrospective study, which included data of patients aged >=18 years who underwent breast cancer surgery at Rambam Health Care Center, Haifa, Israel, between 2020 and 2023. The study's protocol was authorized by the local research ethics committee (0176-24-RMB-D, 2024). The need for informed consent was waived due to the study's retrospective nature.

- Safe delivery and storage of Tc-99m at the operation bay: Technetium's cabinet in the operating room (A); technetium transferred from the nuclear medicine unit is stored in a dedicated suitcase (B) within a lead container (C). Surgeons certified to inject the technetium are required to use a radiation reader and a dedicated shield for the syringe (D).
Fig. 1

In 2019, regulatory approval was obtained to administer radio-tracers intraoperatively, replacing preoperative injection done previously in our nuclear medicine institute. Three surgeons were trained and approved by the hospital radiation safety officer for handling and injecting radioactive materials. A protocol was established dictating the safe transfer of radioactive material between the nuclear medicine department and the operating theater. Syringes with unfiltered Tc-99m sulphur colloid were stored within a dedicated lead-shielded case (Fig. 1), which was placed in a predetermined closet file within the operating theater.

All patients requiring SLN biopsy were eligible. We excluded from further analysis patients with ipsilateral breast cancer recurrence who had previously undergone ipsilateral SLN biopsy and were in need of preoperative lymphoscintigraphy localization.
Procedure

SLN biopsy was performed in clinically node-negative (cN0) patients, while SLN biopsy and targeted axillary dissection (TAD) were used for initially node-positive (cN1) patients who underwent neoadjuvant therapy (NAT). Immediately following anesthesia, 1 mCi (0.2 ml) of unfiltered Tc-99m sulphur colloid were injected intradermally into the nipple areolar complex. Diluted patent blue was injected subcutaneously. SLN retrieval was performed in the usual manner, detecting the SLNB by blue dye and a hand-held gamma detector. Lymphoscintigrams were not performed.
Data collection
Demographic, clinical, surgical, and pathological data were retrospectively collected and securely stored on a password-protected database.
Data analysis

Data were recorded in Excel (Microsoft Excel  2010 Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA) and analyzed using GraphPad Prism version 6.00 for Windows (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA) and IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 28.0 (released 2021; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Descriptive statistics assessed SLN identification rates, stratified by intraoperative Tc-99m success and dye use. Associations with SLN detection were analyzed using Fisher's exact test, chi-square, and Mann-Whitney tests. Significant variables underwent logistic regression, with odds ratios (OR) and 95 % confidence intervals (CI) reported. Candidate variables that could reasonably affect SLN identification were included in the association analyses, including patient factors (age, BMI, ethnicity, prior surgery on the same breast), tumor factors (T stage, N stage, receptor status), and treatment factors (neoadjuvant therapy and breast surgical procedure). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

A total of 350 patients who underwent 352 intraoperative unfiltered Tc-99m sulphur colloid injections were included in this retrospective analysis. The demographic and clinical characteristics of the cohort are detailed in Table 1.

The median age of the cohort was 59.8 years, with the majority of patients being female (98.3 %) and postmenopausal (62.2 %). Invasive ductal carcinoma was the most common histological subtype (80.8 %). The majority of patients presented with early-stage disease and clinically negative lymph nodes. One-hundred-thirty-five (38.6 %) patients were treated with NAT, mostly chemotherapy (85.9 %). Breast-conserving surgery was performed in 66.2 % of cases. One patient, referred for risk-reduction mastectomies, underwent sentinel lymph node biopsy following a preoperative diagnosis of atypical ductal hyperplasia on core biopsy in one of the breasts. Four patients with long-standing stable oligometastatic disease underwent SLN biopsy following multidisciplinary team decision.

Table 2 describes the detection rates for SLNs' with the radio-tracer and patent blue. For the entire cohort (upfront surgery and post NAT), radioactive lymph nodes were identified following intraoperative unfiltered Tc-99m sulphur colloid injections in 89.5 % (315/352) procedures. In 13 additional procedures, the use of patent blue dye successfully identified the SLNs increasing the identification rate with dual tracers to 93.2 % (328/352).

In twenty-four patients (24 procedures), in which SLNs were not identified following dual tracing with the radio-tracer and patent blue, axillary dissection was performed in twenty. No further dissection was performed in three patients following successful identification and surgical removal of previously biopsied positive nodes, confirmed by intraoperative specimen imaging demonstrating the clip (i.e., targeted axillary dissection). In one patient, no further exploration of the axilla was performed. Metastatic lymph nodes were diagnosed in seven patients within this subgroup.

Significant differences were observed in the successful identification of SLNs between patients undergoing upfront surgery and those undergoing surgery following NAT. SLNs identification rate following radio-tracer injection in the upfront surgery setting was 92.2 % vs. 85.1 % for those who underwent prior NAT (p = 0.048). Adding blue dye increased the identification rate to 95.9 % and 88.8 % respectively (p = 0.015).

Subanalysis of 136 procedures in 135 patients treated with NAT reveals differences in the successful identification of SLNs between patients whose preoperative clinical staging was N0 and N1-3. Successful identification with radiotracer was 94.3 % and 78.3 % for N0 and N1-3, respectively (p = 0.014). Additional blue dye led to successful identification in 96.2 % and 83.1 %, respectively (p = 0.027).

Possible risk factors for failure of intraoperative radio-tracer injection are summarized in Table 3. Failure of intraoperative unfiltered Tc-99m sulphur colloid injection to identify the SLNs was associated with Arab or Druze ethnicity, advanced T- and N-stages, and NAT. When these factors were evaluated together in a multivariate analysis, only T-stage and N-stage remained significantly associated with failure to identify the SLNs.
- Sentinel lymph node identification rates by either Tc-99m alone, or Tc-99m and blue dye in all procedures (A), upfront surgeries (B), or surgeries following neoadjuvant therapy (C).
Fig. 2

SLNs identification rate improved within the years whether in patients undergoing upfront surgery or following NAT (Fig. 2). By 2023, identification rates of SLNs with dual tracing was 98.2 %, 94.6 %, and 96.7 % in upfront surgeries, surgeries following neoadjuvant treatment, and all surgeries, respectively.

Throughout the study period and up to the time of writing this manuscript, no radiation safety incidents, procedural errors, or malpractice events were reported. This reflects the effectiveness and reliability of the safety protocols implemented in our institution, as well as the strict adherence to radiation handling guidelines by all members of the clinical team. When considering the additional costs associated with imaging and physician interpretation of the images, the 352 procedures included in this study correspond to an estimated cost avoidance of approximately 387,200 Israeli Shekels (about USD 112,640).
Discussion

The status of axillary lymph nodes remains a critical prognostic factor guiding therapeutic decisions in breast cancer management. SLN biopsy has replaced traditional ALND as the gold standard for axillary staging in most cases. Our study shows that using intraoperative Tc-99m radiocolloid injection yields SLN detection rates of 89.5 % and when combined with blue dye injection 93.2 % was achieved. The results for the subgroup of patients undergoing upfront surgery were comparable with the detection rate shown in early-stage breast cancer. In patients who underwent NAT using dual tracing, our detection rate was 88.8 %, largely due to lower detection rates in those with metastatic lymph node disease before NAT.

Williams et al. and Dauphine et al. are two studies from the same institution.

Intraoperative injection of Tc-99m radiocolloid for SLN detection has emerged as a viable alternative to preoperative administration and several studies have demonstrated its efficacy (Table 4). The largest study by Berrocal J et al. is a single center study that over two decades included 2338 patients who received intraoperative injection of Tc-99m labelled colloidal nanoparticles with an overall success rate of 99.8 % in identifying at least one sentinel lymph node. Similar success rates were identified by others who reported smaller series. Our detection rate was slightly lower than that of the above-mentioned intraoperative radio-tracer injection studies. This could partially be attributed to the learning curve we experienced as depicted in Fig. 2, and the fact that we included patients who underwent neoadjuvant therapy.

Our findings suggest that advanced tumor stage (T3-T4) and positive lymph node involvement (N+) are the most significant predictors of failure to identify the SLN using intraoperative Tc-99m labelled colloidal nanoparticles injection. Differences in SLN identification between patients undergoing surgery first or SLN biopsy following NAT were also reported in the SENTINA trial in which patients were allocated to several treatment arms, two of which are relevant to our discussion. All of the procedures in this trial were performed following radiocolloid injection. Additional blue dye injection was optional. The first relevant arm included patients with clinically node-negative disease who underwent surgery first. The overall surgical detection rate with radiocolloid was 98.8 %, which is slightly superior compared to the 95.9 % surgical detection rate following radiocolloid injection in our study. The second relevant arm included patients with clinically node-positive disease who underwent SLN biopsy following NAT. The overall surgical detection rate in these patients was 77.4 %, with radioactive colloid alone. This identification rate is similar when compared to 78.3 % observed in our study. One must take into account that, unlike the SENTINA trial, not all of our patients allocated to SLN biopsy following NAT had clinically node-positive disease. Of note, the median number of lymph nodes removed in the SENITNA trial was 2, comparable to our results.

Avoiding unwarranted discomfort for the patients by the preoperative injection of the radiotracer to the breast led us to abandon the radiotracer's injection before surgery in favor of an injection after anesthesia in the majority of our patients. Intraoperative Indocyanine Green (ICG) Fluorescence is an alternative that may be injected intraoperatively with or without concomitant injection of the radiotracer. In these two studies, SLN identification rate with ICG alone was 97.9 % and 91.5 % in all patients and in patients following neoadjuvant chemotherapy, respectively.

Current guidelines recommend omitting routine SLN biopsies in selected patients who are 50 years or older, postmenopausal, with grade 1-2, hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, and undergoing breast conserving therapy. These recommendations are based on the SOUND and INSEMA trials, in which SLN biopsy was omitted in 697 patients with T1-2 node-negative tumors and in 962 patients with T1 node-negative tumors, respectively. When outcomes were assessed against those of patients who underwent SLN biopsies, no differences in disease survival were observed after a median follow-up of 5.7 and 6.1 years. Relative to the original trial inclusion criteria, the ASCO guidelines limited eligibility based on the observation that most patients enrolled in these trials were 50 years or older, and had small, hormone-responsive tumors. In this patient population with favorable tumor biology, the probability of a significant axillary disease burden is low, and axillary staging has a questionable impact on adjuvant therapy decisions. Although current guidelines support omitting SLN biopsy in many of the patients included in our study, this does not diminish the relevance of our primary objective, which was to evaluate the efficacy of intraoperative radiotracer injection in identifying SLNs. In all other patients who do not meet the eligibility criteria for omission of SLN biopsy, avoiding axillary dissection when SLNs are not identified should be considered sparingly, particularly when the morbidity of the operation outweighs omitting axillary staging.

Radio-tracer injection following anesthesia does not allow isotope imaging. Preoperative imaging may be important in certain circumstances, mainly recurrent breast cancer, where aberrant drainage is more common. Otherwise, and unlike other malignancies such as melanoma, the objective of this procedure in most of the patients undergoing breast cancer surgery is to identify the sentinel lymph nodes located in the axilla. Injecting the radio-tracer in the operating room and a search using the probe (without imaging) does not impair the ability to find the sentinel node.

Intraoperative injection offers financial as well as logistical advantages that should not be overlooked; advantage in scheduling and without travelling at the day of surgery. According to Thompson et al., preoperative injection in the US at 2008 already incurred an additional charge of $1325 attributed to imaging, injection, and interpretation of images by a physician. In our medical center, the savings associated with intraoperative Tc-99m labelled colloidal nanoparticles injection amount to approximately 1100 Israeli Shekels (approximately USD 320) per patient, derived from multiple factors that streamline the process.
Conclusions

Our study demonstrates that intraoperative injection of Tc-99m labelled colloidal nanoparticles is an acceptable alternative to preoperative injection in terms of detecting SLNs. These findings suggest that the established practice of preoperative injection can be safely implemented, offering means to reduce patient pain and anxiety as well as associated costs.

passages.text: Development and Validation of a Urinary Exosomal miRNA Diagnostic Panel for Early Detection of Esophageal Cancer
ABSTRACT

Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, with early detection being challenging. Although endoscopic screening can aid in diagnosis, its invasiveness and cost limit widespread compliance. To address this, we developed and validated a non-invasive diagnostic panel based on urinary exosomal microRNAs (miRNAs) for early ESCC detection. Urine samples were prospectively collected from ESCC patients and healthy controls across five institutions, and exosomal miRNA profiles were obtained using small RNA sequencing. A diagnostic panel was constructed using machine learning with recursive feature elimination in a proof-of-concept (POC) cohort comprising 99 ESCC and 93 control samples, and its performance was evaluated by five-fold cross-validation. This panel was subsequently tested in a blinded validation cohort of 50 ESCC and 61 control samples. In the POC cohort, the multi-miRNA panel achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.90. In the validation cohort, the AUC was 0.85 (95% CI: 0.77-0.92), with 84% sensitivity and 66% specificity. The panel showed high sensitivity across disease stages:100% for Stage 0, 91% for Stage I, and 73% for Stages II-IV:and its performance was not significantly affected by sex, body mass index, alcohol use, or smoking. Furthermore, in early-stage cases, the diagnostic score significantly declined after treatment (p = 0.026). These findings suggest that the urinary exosomal miRNA panel may offer a practical screening approach for the early detection of ESCC.

Using a machine learning-based approach in a multi-institutional prospective cohort, we identified a robust miRNA signature that demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Our 57-miRNA panel achieved an AUC of 0.90 in the proof-of-concept cohort and 0.85 in an independent validation cohort, with a sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 66%. Notably, sensitivity for Stage 0 and Stage I disease was 100% and 91%, respectively.

Introduction

Esophageal cancer (EC) poses a significant global health challenge, with approximately 600,000 new cases and over 500,000 deaths in 2020. Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), its predominant subtype, accounts for over 80% of cases in high-incidence regions such as East Asia and South Africa. Despite treatment advances, the prognosis remains poor owing to late-stage diagnoses. Although diagnostic techniques such as endoscopy have improved, early-stage ESCC often goes undetected because of a lack of symptoms, with many cases diagnosed after symptom onset or incidentally during other cancer evaluations. Consequently, a significant proportion of at-risk individuals do not receive timely screening, emphasizing the importance of improving approaches for early detection.

While endoscopic screening is the gold standard, its invasiveness, cost, and limited accessibility reduce its feasibility for asymptomatic populations. In parts of Asia, upper GI endoscopy is relatively affordable; however, concerns about cost-effectiveness and compliance limit its use. Thus, alternative non-invasive, cost-effective screening tools are urgently needed.

Liquid biopsy technologies, which analyze biomarkers in body fluids, have emerged as promising non-invasive cancer diagnostics. Among them, exosomal microRNAs (miRNAs) stand out owing to their stability and role in cancer pathogenesis. Large-scale studies have shown the diagnostic potential of serum miRNA panels across multiple cancers, including ESCC. A meta-analysis also supports the value of circulating miRNAs as EC biomarkers. However, most studies focus on blood samples, which require invasive collection. In contrast, urine is non-invasive, easy to collect repeatedly, and free from blood cell contamination, making it ideal for biomarker discovery. A recent study demonstrated that isolating exosomal miRNAs from urine markedly increases miRNA yield and facilitates more efficient marker discovery by RNA sequencing compared to cell-free urine.

In this study, we aimed to develop and validate a urinary exosomal miRNA diagnostic panel for ESCC using small RNA sequencing and machine learning approaches, with a focus on detecting early-stage disease and enabling future non-invasive screening strategies.
Material and Methods
Study Design and Population

This prospective, multicenter, case-control observational study was conducted at five medical institutions. Patients diagnosed with ESCC were enrolled from three institutions between January 2020 and March 2023: National Cancer Center Hospital East, Institute of Science Tokyo, and Tokyo Metropolitan Tama Medical Center. Healthy control (HC) participants were recruited from three separate institutions: Tsujinaka Hospital Kashiwanoha, Kasuga Clinic, and National Cancer Center Hospital East. The inclusion criteria for patients with ESCC were as follows: aged 20 years or older, treatment-naive, and a confirmed diagnosis of ESCC through pathological examination of biopsy specimens obtained via endoscopic examination. Patients with concurrent malignancies detected using endoscopic or computed tomography (CT) imaging were excluded. Participants were assigned to the HC group if they were aged 20 years or older and had no evidence of malignancy, confirmed through upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, chest radiography, and abdominal ultrasound examinations. Urine samples were provided by participants during their visit to each institution and were immediately preserved at -20 C or -80 C. For patients with EC, urine samples were collected prior to treatment. Additionally, post-treatment urine samples were obtained from patients treated at the National Cancer Center Hospital East. All urine samples were shipped to Craif Inc. within 6 months of collection for subsequent processing and analysis. All participants provided written informed consent before enrollment, and the study adhered to the ethical standards outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review boards of the respective hospitals.
Clinical Practice and Definition of Clinicopathological Characteristics

Prior to treatment, all patients with ESCC underwent comprehensive clinical assessments, including medical history taking, endoscopy, and CT imaging, to evaluate lifestyle factors (such as alcohol consumption and smoking history) and key tumor characteristics. Based on these imaging evaluations, patients were classified according to the TNM staging system (Union for International Cancer Control, 8th edition), and treatment was administered according to standard treatment guidelines. The tumor characteristics of ESCC were determined from pathological findings in patients treated with endoscopic or surgical resection. For patients who underwent chemoradiotherapy or chemotherapy alone, the tumor characteristics were recorded based on pretreatment evaluations. Healthy participants were also interviewed to assess lifestyle factors. Individuals who consumed more than 20 g of alcohol per day were classified as heavy drinkers, whereas those who consumed 20 g or less per day were classified as light drinkers.
Urine Sample Processing and Exosome miRNA Profiling by Small RNA Seq and qRT-PCR

Urine sample processing and exosomal miRNA profiling were conducted as previously described. Briefly, approximately 3.5 mL urine samples were centrifuged at 2000  g  for 30 min at 4 C to remove debris. The supernatant was mixed 1:1 with Total Exosome Isolation Reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and incubated at room temperature with shaking, followed by centrifugation at 3000  g  for 1 h at 4 C. The resulting extracellular vesicle pellet was resuspended in 300 muL phosphate-buffered saline and stored at 4 C until RNA extraction. Total RNA was extracted using the MagMAX mirVana Kit and KingFisher Apex System, eluted in 5 muL nuclease-free water, and stored at -80 C. Small RNA libraries were prepared using the QIAseq miRNA Library Kit (QIAGEN), quantified with the Qubit dsDNA HS Assay Kit, pooled equally, and sequenced on a NextSeq 550 System (Illumina) with 75-nt single-end reads. Raw reads were processed with UMI tools for adapter trimming and UMI extraction. Reads > 19 bp were aligned to the human miRNA reference (miRge 3.0) using Bowtie v1.2.3, allowing one mismatch in a 25-bp seed. Identical UMIs mapped to the same miRNA were collapsed for quantification. For RT-qPCR validation, reverse transcription was performed using the TaqMan Advanced miRNA cDNA Synthesis Kit with 5 muL RNA. Pre-amplified cDNA was analyzed on a QuantStudio 5 System using FAST Advanced PCR mix. Eighteen miRNAs, including two references, were quantified using RT-qPCR with probe assays of confirmed performance. Ct values were called with fixed thresholds; failed amplifications were excluded. Triplicates were averaged after removing outliers (+-1 Ct from the median). Expression was calculated as DeltaCt normalized to the mean of the pre-specified reference miRNAs, and log2 fold changes were computed from mean DeltaCt values between ESCC and HC groups. The hsa-miR-374a-5p and hsa-miR-30d-5p were selected as reference miRNAs previously identified as reference candidates in circulating miRNA studies and confirmed to exhibit consistent and abundant expression in urinary samples of the present cohort.
Study Flow for Marker Discovery, Training, and Validation

This study followed a structured workflow to ensure a systematic approach for biomarker discovery, model training, and validation (Figure 1). Urine samples were collected from 161 patients with ESCC and 180 healthy individuals. The samples were evaluated using rigorous quality control (QC) checks, and only those that met the required standards were included in the final analysis, resulting in 149 ESCC and 152 HC samples. The samples were divided into two cohorts in an approximately 2:1 ratio, forming a proof-of-concept (POC) cohort and a validation cohort. Within the POC cohort, sex-matched participants (99 ESCC and 93 HC samples) were selected to ensure comparability between cases and controls. In the discovery phase, miRNA expression profiles were analyzed to identify miRNAs significantly associated with ESCC by comparing the expression patterns between ESCC and HC samples. Subsequently, a training phase was performed to establish a diagnostic miRNA panel. In this phase, recursive feature elimination (RFE), a feature selection method in machine learning, was used to refine the miRNA panel by systematically identifying the most relevant miRNAs that contributed to ESCC classification. In this approach, all miRNAs were initially included in the model, and their contributions to classification performance were iteratively assessed, with the least important miRNAs removed step by step until an optimal set was identified, while maintaining diagnostic accuracy. The performance of the constructed miRNA panels was evaluated using five-fold cross-validation (CV). In the final validation phase (50 ESCC and 59 HC samples), the constructed miRNA panel was independently evaluated in a blinded setting, with diagnostic information withheld from the evaluators to ensure an objective assessment. In addition, the diagnostic performance of the miRNA panel was further assessed across clinically relevant subgroups, including tumor characteristics and background factors.

Analysis of Post-Treatment Dynamics of the Urinary miRNA Panel

To investigate the dynamic changes in urinary exosomal miRNA panel scores following curative treatment, we conducted a post-treatment analysis in a subset of patients selected from both the POC and validation cohorts that underwent pretreatment sample analysis. Among 43 patients with early-stage ESCC who received curative treatment (endoscopic resection or surgery), five post-treatment samples failed QC checks. As a result, a total of 38 paired pre- and post-treatment urine samples were included in the analysis. Curative treatment was defined as follows: for endoscopic resection, pathological confirmation of tumor invasion confined to the epithelium or lamina propria mucosae (EP/LPM) with negative horizontal and vertical margins; for surgical resection, pathological Stage I disease with tumor-free proximal, distal, and deep resection margins. Changes in miRNA panel scores before and after treatment were assessed using paired comparisons. Additionally, subgroup analyses were performed based on tumor size, stage, and treatment-to-sampling interval (the time from treatment to post-treatment sample collection).
Statistical Analysis

Differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2, defining differentially expressed miRNAs as those with adjusted p < 0.05 and absolute log2 fold change > 0.5. Functional enrichment analysis was conducted using the miRNA Enrichment Analysis and Annotation Tool 2.1, applying over-representation analysis based on WikiPathways. A Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. A linear support vector classifier was trained to distinguish ESCC from HC. miRNAs with > 2 counts in >= 80% of POC samples were retained, and the count data were normalized using the median-of-ratios method, log2-transformed with a pseudo-count of 1, and standardized prior to model training. RFE with five-fold CV was performed over 100 iterations; in each iteration, 80% of samples were used for CV and 20% held out to monitor overfitting. The optimal feature number was determined as the largest size not showing a significant performance drop from the full feature set in repeated CVs. Prediction scores were obtained via out-of-fold prediction in the POC cohort and hold-out prediction with the final model in the validation cohort. Model performance was assessed using AUC of ROC curves, and the cutoff was determined using Youden's index. Associations with background variables were examined using multivariate linear regression after dichotomizing each variable to enhance interpretability. Student's t-tests and Fisher's exact tests were used for group comparisons. AUCs were compared using Hanley and McNeil's method, with CIs derived from standard errors. For proportions, CIs were calculated using Wilson's score interval. Post-treatment score changes were analyzed by one-sided paired t-tests and were visualized with box plots.
Results
Study Participant Characteristics

The clinicopathological characteristics of the POC and validation cohorts are shown in Table 1. In both cohorts, patients with ESCC were significantly older than HCs (mean age: 68.4 vs. 58.6 years in the POC cohort and 71.5 vs. 53.4 years in the validation cohort). Additionally, compared with HCs, patients with ESCC had higher rates of smoking and heavy drinking:known EC risk factors :with current smoking at 23% vs. 10% and heavy drinking at 60% vs. 15% in the POC cohort; and 22% vs. 14% and 64% vs. 17%, respectively, in the validation cohort. Only one participant in each group had a malignancy in the preceding five years. There was no statistical difference in the presence of surgical history between the ESCC and HC group in either the POC or validation cohort. While ESCC cases overall showed male predominance (80% and 78%), a sex-matched subset was selected in the POC cohort (80% vs. 74%) to reduce confounding. Furthermore, age-related confounding was minimized by including relatively younger patients with ESCC and older HCs in the POC cohort. Tumor locations were consistent with clinical distributions, with approximately half of the cases in the mid-thoracic region (52% POC, 48% validation) and approximately 30% in the lower thoracic region (27% POC, 32% validation). Over half of ESCC cases were early stage (Stage 0/I: POC: 30%/32%; validation: 12%/44%), while 30%-36% were advanced (Stage III/IV: POC: 17%/13%; validation: 20%/16%), demonstrating broadly similar staging distributions between cohorts. Approximately half underwent endoscopic therapy (53% POC, 46% validation), while the rest received curative treatments including surgery or chemoradiotherapy, reflecting the predominance of early-stage disease.

Identification of Candidate Urinary miRNA Biomarker at the Discovery Phase

A comprehensive small RNA-sequencing analysis was performed on urinary exosomal RNAs. Differential expression analysis identified 34 miRNAs that exhibited significant changes between ESCC and HC groups, with 21 upregulated and 13 downregulated in the ESCC samples (Figure 2A). Notably, hsa-miR-194-3p exhibited robust upregulation, with a log2 fold change of 1.42 (adjusted p-value = 5.37 x 10-13). In contrast, among the downregulated miRNAs, hsa-miR-3613-5p and hsa-miR-135b-5p showed log2 fold changes of -0.70 (adjusted p-value = 6.29 x 10-4) and -0.67 (adjusted p-value = 2.64 x 10-5), respectively (Table S1). Of these 34 differentially expressed miRNAs, several:including upregulated miRNAs such as hsa-miR-194-3p, hsa-miR-181a-3p, hsa-miR-106b-3p, and hsa-miR-100-5p:have been previously linked to EC, whereas others may represent novel candidate biomarkers. Fold changes and diagnostic performance metrics for each miRNA are detailed in Table S1. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering based on these 34 miRNAs distinguished ESCC from HC samples (Figure 2B), supporting their potential as diagnostic biomarkers. The RT-qPCR was performed on a selected set of eighteen representative miRNAs including the two references to validate the RNA sequencing results, demonstrating a strong correlation with the small RNA-seq measurements (Figure S1A). In addition, the directionality and magnitude of the fold changes were largely consistent between the two platforms (Figure S1B). The fold change values in RT-qPCR were highly consistent when compared with those obtained using global mean normalization, supporting the appropriateness of the selected reference miRNAs (Figure S1C,D). Subsequent over-representation analysis of the predicted target genes for the differentially expressed miRNAs revealed significant enrichment in several key signaling pathways implicated in carcinogenesis, including epidermal growth factor receptor (ErbB), phosphoinositide 3-kinase-protein kinase B (PI3K-AKT), transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta), and Wnt (Figure 2C). Additionally, pathways associated with inflammatory responses, such as cytokine and chemokine signaling, as well as the IL-5 and IL-11 pathways, were significantly enriched (Figure 2C). These findings underscore the biological significance of the identified miRNA panel and support its potential as a non-invasive biomarker for the early detection of ESCC.

Construction of a miRNA Diagnostic Panel at the Training Phase

We utilized a set of 202 miRNAs detected above the threshold, regardless of differential expression status, to construct a miRNA diagnostic panel. Through iterative elimination using the RFE approach, 57 miRNAs were ultimately retained without compromising the diagnostic performance (Figure 3A and Table S2), achieving a mean AUC of 0.90 (five-fold CV, SD = 0.05) (Figure 3B). For comparison, a panel of only the 34 differentially expressed miRNAs yielded a slightly higher AUC of 0.92 (SD = 0.04) (Figure S2A). Thereafter, we evaluated the contribution of each miRNA to the diagnostic capability of the 57-miRNA panel (Figure 3C). The top three contributors were hsa-miR-192-5p/215-5p, hsa-miR-194-5p, and hsa-miR-125a-5p, with the first two miRNAs being among those that showed significant differential expression. A multivariate analysis confirmed that only the presence of cancer was independently associated with panel positivity, while other factors such as age, sex, body mass index (BMI), smoking, and alcohol had little or no impact (Figure 3D). These findings demonstrate that the RFE-based selection of miRNAs can maintain strong diagnostic accuracy and provide a robust multi-feature signature independent of most patient background factors.

Diagnostic Performance of the Constructed miRNA Panel for ESCC Detection at the Validation Phase

The correlation of miRNA expression changes between the POC and validation cohorts indicated consistent expression patterns between ESCC and HC for the 34 POC-significant miRNAs (r = 0.70, 82% sign concordance) and the 57-miRNA panel (r = 0.64, 72% sign concordance) (Figure 4A). Among the miRNAs with significantly differential expression in the POC cohort, 11 (9 of the 21 upregulated miRNAs and 2 of the 13 downregulated miRNAs) showed similar significant changes in the validation cohort (Table S3). The 57-miRNA panel constructed from the POC cohort achieved a favorable AUC of 0.85 (95% CI, 0.77-0.92) in the validation cohort (Figure 4B), outperforming the 34-miRNA panel based on differentially expressed miRNAs (AUC = 0.78, Figure S2B). Using the Youden index-derived cutoff (0.10), the panel showed a sensitivity of 87% (five-fold CV, SD = 6%) and specificity of 85% (SD = 8%) in the POC cohort, and 84% sensitivity (95% CI, 71%-92%) and 66% specificity (95% CI, 53%-77%) in the validation cohort (Figure 4C). Panel scores were consistently elevated in the ESCC group across all stages (Figure 4D). Stage-specific analysis (Figure 4E) showed particularly high diagnostic accuracy in early-stage ESCC (AUC 0.95 for Stage 0 and 0.90 for Stage I), while AUCs were slightly lower for Stages II-IV (0.67, 0.86, and 0.68, respectively), likely because of the limited number of cases at Stages II and IV. Nevertheless, no significant differences in overall diagnostic accuracy were observed between early and advanced stages (Figure 4F). The diagnostic performance stratified by tumor characteristics and background factors is summarized in Figure 5, and the corresponding score distributions are shown in Figure S3. No significant differences in AUC were observed across tumor locations (cervical/upper thoracic (Ce/Ut) vs. middle thoracic (Mt), Mt vs. lower thoracic (Lt), and Ce/Ut vs. Lt, Figure 5A), tumor sizes (< 20 mm, 20-40 mm, >= 40 mm, Figure 5B), age (< 55 vs. >= 55, Figure 5C), sex (Figure 5D), BMI (< 22 vs. >= 22, Figure 5E), or alcohol use (light/no vs. heavy drinkers, Figure 5F). A near-significant association was observed for smoking status (current vs. past/non-smoker, p = 0.028, Figure 5G). These findings indicate that the diagnostic accuracy of the 57-miRNA panel is consistent across various clinicopathological and demographic subgroups.

Post-Treatment Dynamics and Cancer-Specificity of the Urinary miRNA Panel Score

In a cohort of 38 patients with early-stage ESCC who achieved curative treatment, we evaluated the alterations in urinary exosomal miRNA panel scores before and after treatment. Most patients in the cohort were at Stage 0 (71%) and underwent endoscopic resection (82%), with a mean tumor size of 31.5 mm and an average treatment-to-sampling interval of 43.6 days (Table S4). Panel scores significantly declined post-treatment, from 1.13 +- 0.61 to 0.86 +- 0.89 (p = 0.026, paired t-test), after confirming that the paired differences (Post-Pre) followed an approximately normal distribution using the Shapiro-Wilk test (p = 0.78) (Figure 6A). Subgroup analyses based on tumor size, clinical stage, therapy type, and treatment interval showed consistent score reductions (Figure 6B-E). Notably, post-treatment scores declined significantly in patients with tumors > 20 mm, Stage 0 disease, endoscopic resection, or a treatment-to-sampling interval > 30 days, which may, at least in part, reflect the relatively larger sample sizes within these subgroups. These results suggest that the miRNA panel score is highly specific for early-stage ESCC and may serve as a dynamic marker of therapeutic efficacy and tumor burden.

Discussion

In this study, we developed and validated a urinary exosomal miRNA biomarker panel for the early detection of ESCC. Using urine:a minimally invasive and easily accessible specimen:we addressed the limitations of traditional screening methods such as esophagogastroduodenoscopy, which are associated with low patient compliance. Our miRNA panel showed high diagnostic accuracy across tumor stages and clinicopathological profiles and functioned independently of conventional risk factors such as smoking and alcohol intake. Its non-invasive nature offers strong potential for enhancing screening adherence and enabling earlier diagnosis of ESCC.

ESCC is often diagnosed at advanced stages owing to nonspecific early symptoms, with early-stage cases typically discovered incidentally during post-treatment surveillance or evaluations for other malignancies. Although blood-based liquid biopsies have been explored, they require venipuncture and hospital visits, thus limiting routine use. Saliva-based panels have also been proposed but face challenges including contamination, dryness, and oral bleeding. Urinary miRNA-based biopsies offer a favorable alternative, combining stability, reproducibility, and ease of collection. However, existing research is limited and often based on small sample sizes. Our multicenter, large-scale study provides robust validation of urinary exosomal miRNAs as diagnostic markers for ESCC.

Among differentially expressed miRNAs in our discovery (POC) cohort, hsa-miR-194 emerged as a notable biomarker. hsa-miR-194-3p and hsa-miR-194-5p were consistently upregulated in discovery and validation cohorts, contributing significantly to the diagnostic accuracy of the panel (Figure 3C; Tables S1 and S2). These findings are in line with prior serum-based miRNA studies in ESCC. Functionally, miR-194 has been shown to activate the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway in breast cancer by targeting and inhibiting SOX17, thereby promoting tumor proliferation and invasion. This is particularly relevant, as our pathway analysis also identified Wnt signaling as a key pathway associated with the identified miRNAs. Another significant cluster was hsa-miR-192-5p/215-5p, which showed strong and reproducible upregulation in the POC and validation cohorts, and contributed substantially to the diagnostic performance of the panel (Figure 3C). Given that miR-192 belongs to the same miRNA family as miR-194, a shared regulatory mechanism in esophageal tumorigenesis is plausible. Previous studies have linked miR-192 to diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic roles in cancers such as hepatocellular carcinoma, colorectal cancer, and lung cancer, although this is the first report of altered miR-192 expression in ESCC.

Although the diagnostic panel composed solely of differentially expressed miRNAs showed statistically significant changes, the magnitude of individual miRNA expression differences was modest, limiting their diagnostic utility when used independently. To enhance classification accuracy, we employed RFE, a machine learning approach that selects the most diagnostically relevant miRNAs through iterative optimization. The resulting RFE-based panel demonstrated improved robustness in CV while maintaining high diagnostic performance. This finding supports previous studies highlighting the superiority of machine learning-driven biomarker selection in constructing reliable miRNA panels, particularly in large-scale prospective cohorts.

A major strength of our study lies in its carefully constructed cohort. By recruiting from institutions where routine gastroscopy is practiced, we enriched our study population with early-stage ESCC (Stage 0/I) cases. HCs underwent comprehensive endoscopic screening to rule out undiagnosed malignancies. Additionally, we excluded individuals with concurrent cancers, particularly head, neck, and gastric cancers, which are commonly associated with ESCC, ensuring ESCC-specific biomarker assessment. The high diagnostic performance of our urinary miRNA panel in early-stage ESCC is likely attributable to the cohort design, as more than 60% of patients in the POC cohort had stage 0-I disease, emphasizing early detection. Furthermore, several pathways identified in our functional analyses, including Wnt, PI3K-AKT, and TGF-beta signaling, have been implicated in carcinogenic processes of ESCC, which may partly explain the panel's sensitivity to early-stage disease. Notably, the miRNA panel identified an independent risk signature for ESCC, distinct from traditional risk factors such as smoking and alcohol. This finding indicates that the panel captures novel biological signals associated with ESCC development. Combining it with lifestyle factors could enhance risk stratification and screening precision. Furthermore, our analysis of post-treatment samples showed a significant decline in miRNA panel scores after curative therapy. This reduction was more pronounced in patients with larger tumors or samples collected after longer intervals, suggesting that the panel reflects tumor burden rather than transient treatment effects, reinforcing its cancer specificity.

Nevertheless, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, differences in urine collection and storage protocols across centers may have affected miRNA stability and expression. Although we attempted to standardize sample handling, further optimization is needed for broader clinical implementation. To improve consistency in future multi-center studies and to strengthen the translational potential of urinary miRNA biomarkers, it will be important to establish standardized operating procedures and pre-analytical guidelines. Second, while the panel demonstrated high sensitivity, it showed moderate specificity, likely due to miRNA secretion from cancerous and normal cells. Specificity may be improved in future applications by integrating urinary miRNA profiles with lifestyle risk factors (e.g., alcohol consumption and smoking) and/or with other molecular biomarkers, such as circulating tumor DNA or protein-based markers. Such multimodal approaches could enhance diagnostic accuracy and reduce false positives in screening settings. Third, although internal validation supported the robustness of our panel, external validation using independent cohorts from diverse geographic regions is essential. The relatively small sample size in our validation phase also highlights the need for larger prospective trials. Furthermore, the study population consisted entirely of Japanese participants, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. This homogeneous cohort was appropriate for initial validation; however, the urinary miRNA panel should be further validated in larger, ethnically and geographically diverse populations to confirm its generalizability and clinical applicability.

In conclusion, we demonstrate that a urinary exosomal miRNA panel is a promising, non-invasive tool for the early detection of ESCC. It showed consistent performance across tumor stages and functioned independently of traditional risk factors. Our stringent cohort design, which included the exclusion of concurrent malignancies and comprehensive screening of non-cancer controls, reinforces the validity of our findings. Future research should focus on refining this panel, optimizing cutoff values, and evaluating its integration into clinical workflows. Such advancements could significantly improve early detection, reduce ESCC-related mortality, and ultimately enhance patient outcomes.
