passages.text: Toxins in disguise: Neuropeptide mimicry across animal venoms

Neuropeptides and peptide hormones form a highly diverse class of signaling molecules found across the animal kingdom that regulate key physiological processes, including growth, metabolism, reproduction, and behavior. Many venomous animals have evolved "doppelganger toxins" that mimic these endogenous peptides, allowing them to manipulate the physiology of their prey or predators. These toxins typically act on the same receptors as the peptides they mimic, most commonly G protein-coupled receptors, but also receptor tyrosine kinases, membrane-bound guanylyl cyclases, and ion channels. Although doppelganger peptides have been described in other ecological contexts, this review focuses on venom-derived mimics, summarizing their molecular characteristics, evolutionary context, and biological functions. We catalogue examples spanning conserved bilaterian neuropeptides to lineage-specific families and discuss their translational potential in medicine and pest control.
Introduction

Neuropeptides and peptide hormones (hereafter referred to collectively as neuropeptides) are essential signaling molecules found across the animal kingdom that regulate diverse processes such as growth, metabolism, reproduction, pain, learning, and social behavior. Because of their central role, these signaling systems are vulnerable to external manipulation. Many venomous animals exploit this through toxins that structurally and functionally mimic the neuropeptides of their prey or predators. Through this molecular mimicry, the venomous animal can hijack key aspects of the target's physiology and behavior in ways that enhance its own survival and success.

Beyond venoms, such neuropeptide-mimicking "doppelganger peptides" have also been identified in parasites, pathogens, and in the context of sexual conflict. In addition, a large body of work has examined neuropeptide-like toxins in the sometimes poisonous skin secretions of frogs and toads, which have been comprehensively reviewed elsewhere and are not covered here.

In this review, we focus on doppelganger toxins found in animal venoms. We begin with an overview of their biological roles, followed by a comprehensive survey of documented examples. While we have attempted to cover all known cases, the fragmented nature of the literature means that some examples may inevitably have been missed.
Diversity of venomous animals and their toxins

The deployment of venom as a tool for predation, defense, and competition is a highly successful adaptation that has evolved independently in nearly every major branch of the animal kingdom. While snakes, spiders, scorpions, bees, wasps, and jellyfish are among the most familiar venomous organisms, venoms are also found in a wide array of less conspicuous taxa, including cone snails, centipedes, assassin bugs, shrews, platypuses, and some marine worms (see for a more complete overview of venomous lineages). Venoms are complex cocktails of individual components called toxins, which are delivered to other organisms, typically prey or predators, to manipulate their normal physiological function for the benefit of the venomous organism. Venoms can include small molecules such as amines and purines, bioactive peptides, including many neurotoxins, and proteins such as enzymes, and in some cases viral-like components. Although the precise composition varies widely across lineages and species, proteinaceous and peptide toxins typically form the dominant functional components in most venoms studied to date. Many toxins act combinatorially although the complex interactions between individual venom components remain poorly understood.

Toxins are made by specialized cells but the nature and organization of these cells differs greatly across venomous animals. In cnidarians such as jelly fish, toxin-producing cells called nematocysts are dispersed across the animal and deliver their toxins by direct injection. In many other cases, venoms are produced in specialized venom glands of varying complexity, as seen in snakes, spiders, cone snails, and others.

Functionally, venoms can serve multiple biological roles. Snakes, spiders, and cone snails primarily use venom to immobilize and kill prey, most venomous fish use their venom defensively, hematophagous animals, such as ticks and vampire bats use venom to facilitate blood feeding, and parasitic wasps use venom to immobilize hosts that will serve as living food for their larvae. Some venoms are used for inter-species competition, as in the platypus, and certain scorpions sting during mating. Because these diverse functions often coexist within a single species, venoms can contain toxins with specific ecological function, such as offensive or defensive components.

Among active toxins, neuropeptide-mimicking doppelganger peptides stand out as a striking strategy, allowing venomous animals to specifically hijack conserved physiological signaling pathways in their targets. In some animals, such as the Gila monster and many cone snails, doppelganger peptides can constitute major components of the venom, underscoring their importance to venom function.
Neuropeptide diversity and evolution

Neuropeptides are among the earliest signaling molecules in animals, and their diversity is reflected in the evolutionary relations of the animal kingdom. Broadly, animals are divided into pre-bilaterians: cnidarians (e.g., jellyfish, sea anemones, corals), placozoans, ctenophores (comb jellies), and sponges, and bilaterians, which encompass most extant animal species. The Bilateria clade is further subdivided into two superphyla: Deuterostomia, which includes vertebrates (chordates), echinoderms (e.g., sea urchins and starfish), and hemichordates (e.g., acorn worms); and Protostomia, which includes many phyla, such as arthropods, nematodes, tardigrades, priapulids, mollusks, annelids, bryozoans, nemerteans, and platyhelminthes. Critically, neuropeptides have been uncovered in all animal phyla.

Comparative genomics and transcriptomics have revealed that some neuropeptides originated early in animal evolution, prior to the division of protostomes and deuterostomes. Examples include insulin-like peptides, tachykinins, and neuropeptide Y/F. At the same time, clade-specific neuropeptides are also common, such as endothelin and endorphins that are deuterostome-specific, and corazonin and allatotropin that appear to be restricted to protostomes. Lineagespecific innovations such as proctolin in arthropods and egg-laying hormone in molluscs are also known.

In some cases, ancestral neuropeptides have also been lost in certain lineages, such as somatostatin-related peptides (SSRP) in arthropods and nematodes, while other peptides, such as tachykinins and vasopressin/oxytocin-type peptides have diversified considerably in some lineages. This patchwork of conservation, loss, and innovation highlights the dynamic evolutionary history of neuropeptide signaling and provides a framework for understanding how doppelganger toxins exploit conserved versus lineage-specific peptide systems (Fig. 1, Table 1).

Despite these insights, our understanding of neuropeptide evolution remains incomplete and is continually being refined as new omics and functional data become available. It is therefore most likely that additional evolutionary relationships will be uncovered in the future, reshaping current perspectives on both conserved and lineage-specific signaling systems. Likewise, the evolutionary origins of doppelganger peptides are only partially understood. In general, doppelganger toxins evolve either de novo, from a "recruitment event" of the venomous animal's own neuropeptide gene, or through horizontal gene transfer (see for a figure illustrating these mechanisms). Recruitment is a complex and heterogenous process, where for instance some neuropeptides might take on a secondary "moonlighting" function as a toxin or a gene duplication can facilitate neofunctionalization. As illustrative examples, distinct evolutionary routes have been documented for the emergence of doppelganger toxins. In the cone snail, Conus geographus, the neurotensin-mimicking toxin Contulakin-G evolved a neurotensin-like motif de novo within a venom peptide scaffold from the C-superfamily of toxins and has no evolutionary connection to neurotensin, which is a chordate specific hormone. In contrast, crustacean hyperglycemic hormone (CHH)-like toxins arose through recruitment and duplication of endogenous neuropeptide genes followed by venom-specific expression and diversification, as supported by phylogenetic methods and conserved gene structure. A third mechanism is exemplified by tick adrenomedullin, which originated from a horizontal gene transfer from a vertebrate host lineage and was subsequently co-opted as a secreted bioactive toxin in some ticks. Although only a few cases of doppelganger evolution have been documented in detail and the origin of most remain unresolved, the phylogenetic distribution of neuropeptides can be helpful for generating hypotheses about a doppelganger peptide's origin when it is unknown. If a venomous species already encodes a given neuropeptide system (Fig. 1), the origin of doppelganger peptides can often be traced back to a recruitment of the endogenous precursors, while absence of the system makes de novo evolution or horizontal transfer more likely, although peptides with shorter motifs can be an exception. The octopus tachykinins provide one such example, having evolved de novo even in the presence of an endogenous counterpart.
Molecular targets and biological functions of doppelganger toxins

Most neuropeptides exert their effects by binding to G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). However, notable exceptions exist: insulin and insulin-like growth factors act through receptor tyrosine kinases, several neuropeptides activate membrane-bound guanylyl cyclases, while certain RFamide peptides have been shown to modulate ion channels such as acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) and other members of the degenerin/epithelial sodium channel (DEG/ENaC) superfamily.

A central goal in venom research is to identify the molecular targets of toxins. This is often more straightforward for doppelganger toxins than for other venom components, as their molecular targets typically mirror those of the endogenous peptide they mimic, though it is possible that the target has deviated for some peptides.

Doppelganger toxins can serve diverse biological roles, functioning offensively to subdue prey, defensively to deter predators, or in parasitic and parasitoid interactions as agents of development, paralysis, and feeding. However, the specific ecological function is highly dependent on the peptide being mimicked and the receptor being targeted.

It is important to note that venomous animals have evolved additional mechanisms to disrupt neuropeptide signaling systems beyond the use of doppelganger peptides. Here, we do not discuss indirect effectors of neuropeptide action, although many have been reported in venoms, such as insulinotropic peptides from various venoms and bradykinin-potentiating peptides from snake venom. Likewise, we do not cover peptides that act on neuropeptide receptors without sharing any recognizable similarity to the endogenous peptide; examples include the somatostatin 3 receptor (SSTR3)-targeting toxin, tau-CnVA, from the cone snail Conus consors or the vasopressin 2A receptor (V2AR)-targeting toxin, mambaquaretin-1, from the green mamba Dendroaspis angusticeps.
Applications of doppelganger toxins

Neuropeptide receptors are highly attractive pharmacological targets with more than one third of all approved drugs targeting GPCRs, many of which are peptide receptors. While most approved drugs are small molecules, recently there has been growing interest in peptide-based therapeutics based on modified neuropeptide analogs (such as lipidated or cyclized analogs) to increase stability and bioavailability. Notably, evolution has already addressed many of these challenges through doppelganger toxins, which are naturally selected for high stability and potent effects in their target organisms. This evolutionary approach is particularly relevant for human therapeutics when the neuropeptide system targeted by a doppelganger peptide is conserved in humans, providing a blueprint for drug design.

Several doppelganger toxins have already been translated into therapeutics. A key example is exendin-4, a GLP-1 mimetic from the Gila monster Heloderma suspectum, which served as the first GLP-1 receptor agonist approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes. Exendin-4 incorporates structural features that enhance receptor potency and resistance to enzymatic degradation, and although produced in the salivary glands from which toxins are delivered to prey and predators, its physiological role in the lizard may relate to endogenous metabolic regulation, as high levels are detected in circulation after feeding. Other doppelganger toxins also show significant promise as therapeutics. Dendroaspis natriuretic peptide (DNP) from the green mamba Dendroaspis angusticeps is a potent vasodilator that lowers arterial pressure in vivo, likely facilitating prey capture by disrupting cardiovascular function. DNP mimics vertebrate natriuretic peptides while engaging human receptors in unique ways due to its extended C-terminal region. These properties have inspired hybrid analogs such as cenderitide, which has advanced to early-phase clinical trials for cardiovascular disease. Contulakin-G, a neurotensin-like peptide from fish-hunting cone snails, is far more potent than neurotensin in mammalian pain models and previously entered phase 1 trials for chronic pain. Although it is a potent analgesic in both animals and humans, the biological role of this toxin in the snail remains unknown. Venom insulins from Conus geographus and other fish-hunting cone snail species provide another striking example of evolutionary innovation: these peptides rapidly activate the insulin receptor to induce hypoglycemic shock in fish prey, and their inherently monomeric structures, lacking the dimerization-promoting elements of human insulin, have inspired ultrafast-acting therapeutic analogs currently in preclinical development. Finally, cone snail somatostatin-like toxins, known as consomatins, exhibit high stability and subtype selectivity at human somatostatin receptors and provide analgesia in rodent models of pain, offering templates for next-generation pain therapeutics. This group of somatostatin doppelganger targets the somatostatin receptor 4 and is likely used by the snails to inhibit the painful escape response of fish prey, whereas another somatostatin doppelganger from the venom of C. geographus acts in concert with the insulin doppelganger present in the same venom to inhibit glucagon secretion via activation of the somatostatin 2 receptor, thereby exacerbating the hypoglycemic effect of the insulin toxin.

Beyond medicine, doppelganger toxins have potential as specific biopesticides against agricultural pests and disease vectors. A major challenge in pesticide development is achieving strong target specificity to affect only the pest organism without harming humans, pollinators, or other non-target species. Many neuropeptides are restricted to particular lineages making them attractive targets, as doppelganger toxins can exploit these signaling pathways to achieve selectivity and limited activity in humans. To date, the only doppelganger toxin pursued for pest control is the CHH-like spider venom peptide Ta1a, but others are likely to follow in the future.
Doppelganger peptide catalogue
Doppelganger peptides of metazoan neuropeptide families
Doppelganger peptides of epidermal growth factor peptides

Since its discovery as a growth factor released from mouse salivary glands, epidermal growth factor (EGF)-like peptides have been found widely across metazoans both as secreted peptides, such EGF and Spitz, but also as domains in larger proteins. These peptides signal through EGF receptors, members of the receptor tyrosine kinase family. Both the number of ligands and receptors vary widely among metazoans. For example, humans possess four receptors and eleven ligands, while the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans has a single receptor and ligand. EGFs are well-known for mediating developmental signals both during embryo-genesis and in adult processes, and recent evidence also implicates them in hypersensitivity and pain.

The peptide toxin MIITX2-Mg1a is a major component of the venom of the Australian giant bull ant, Myrmecia gulosa. It has evolved to structurally and functionally mimic vertebrate EGF and acts as a potent agonist of the mammalian EGF receptor, ErbB. Consistent with recent studies implicating EGF-ErbB signaling in pain, MIITX2-Mg1a was found to induce long-lasting pain hypersensitivity. From an ecological perspective, it is striking that the EGF most similar to MIITX2-Mg1a is found in the echidna, a primary predator of the bull ant. This finding strongly suggests that MIITX2-Mg1a evolved to engage the echidna EGF receptors in a manner similar to endogenous echidna EGF, functioning as a defensive strategy.
Doppelganger peptides of glycoprotein hormone

Glycoprotein hormones are heterodimers composed of alpha and beta subunits, each stabilized by intramolecular disulfide bonds that form a cystine-knot fold. The subunits associate noncovalently to form the functional heterodimer, which maintains structural stability while enabling receptor binding and signaling. Glycoprotein hormones are evolutionarily ancient and found across metazoans. In vertebrates, these hormones regulate metabolism and development. In invertebrates, its precise physiological roles are less well defined but may also involve endocrine signaling and growth regulation. Glycoprotein hormones signal via leucine-rich repeat-containing GPCRs (LGRs), whose large ectodomains mediate hormone recognition and downstream G protein signaling.

Proteomic analyses of the venom of the snail-hunting cone snail Conus victoriae identified peptides derived from the glycoprotein hormone alpha subunit. Transcriptomic analyses further revealed expression of a transcript encoding the corresponding beta subunit in the venom gland. Transcripts for both subunits were also detected in additional cone snail species, including the worm-hunting species Conus tessulatus and Conus virgo. These findings indicate that GPH doppelganger are expressed across multiple cone snail lineages. However, it remains unresolved whether these toxins act as functional heterodimers or as individual subunits, whether they undergo glycosylation as observed in other invertebrates, and what their physiological relevance is in envenomation.
Doppelganger peptides of insulin peptides

The insulin superfamily encompasses insulin-like peptides (ILPs) in protostomes and insulin, insulin-like growth factors (IGFs), and relaxins in chordates. These peptides and their receptors represent one of the most conserved hormonal systems in animals. All members share a cysteine-rich architecture, existing as either two-chain or single-chain peptides stabilized by disulfide bonds that adopt a structural fold strikingly conserved across bilaterians. In mammals, insulin primarily regulates glucose metabolism, IGFs mediate growth and development, and relaxins control reproduction, tissue remodeling, and cardiovascular physiology. The discovery of insulin and its subsequent life-saving use to treat diabetes represents one of the landmark medical breakthroughs of the 20th century, underscoring the profound biomedical relevance of this peptide family. In vertebrates, insulin and IGF-1 act through receptor tyrosine kinases, whereas relaxins engage GPCRs. The biological functions of protostome ILPs remain less well understood. ILPs are often highly diversified, particularly in insects and nematodes and can signal through the insulin receptor or leucine-rich repeat-containing GPCRs (LGRs), the latter considered homologous to vertebrate relaxin receptors.

The first example of a doppelganger peptide targeting the insulin signaling system came from the fish-hunting cone snail, Conus geographus. This species expresses several different insulin-like peptides in its venom to induce hypoglycemic shock in prey by lowering blood glucose, slowing movement, and facilitating capture. Although closely mimicking the fish and human hormone, C. geographus insulins have unique features that make them fast acting and more bioavailable than the native human peptide. Since then, many other insulin doppelganger have been identified in other fish-hunting cone snails and also in species that prey on worms and mollusks. Humanized analogs of these venom insulins, such as mini-G1 and Vh-Ins, are being investigated for therapeutic development of ultrafast-acting insulins for diabetes.

Beyond cone snails, insulin-like peptides have been reported in the tentacles of the venomous sea anemone, Oulactis sp., though it remains unclear whether these are specifically adapted for envenomation or represent an insulin-like peptide with endogenous function. In snakes, genome and venom-gland transcriptome analyses of the king cobra, Ophiophagus hannah, have revealed selective expression of an IGF-like sequence, suggesting a potential venom function. Several groups have corroborated the presence of IGF-like sequences in king cobra venom, but their exact chemical identity and biological function remain unknown.
Doppelganger peptides of RFamides

RFamides are short peptides named by their arginine-phenylalanine dipeptide motif at the C-terminus with the phenylalanine being amidated. RFamides are among the most widely distributed neuropeptides, with representatives found across all bilaterian phyla as well as cnidarians. Despite their broad distribution, the evolutionary relationships among them remain unresolved. This diverse superfamily includes well-known peptides such as cnidarian RFamide, FMRFamide, cholecystokinin, kisspeptin, and others. Because of this diversity, RFamide receptors and their biological roles are highly varied and too extensive to cover here in detail; for a detailed overview see.

Several RFamide peptides with diverse activities have been identified in cone snail venoms, beginning with Conorfamide-Sr2 (CNF-Sr2) from Conus spurius. CNF-Sr2 induces hyperactivity in mice and impairs locomotion in mollusks, while another RFamide doppelganger from the same species inhibits Shaker and human Kv1.3 potassium channels with modest potency. CNF-Vc1 from Conus victoriae also causes hyperactivity in mice and elevates intracellular calcium in subsets of dorsal root ganglion neurons. Both CNF-Vc1 and CNF-Sr1 activate the Mas-related GPCR MrgprC11, whereas CNF-Vc1 and CNF-Tx2 from Conus textile activate the human receptor MrgprX1, again with modest potency. In zebrafish larvae, CNF-Ep1 from Conus episcopatus rapidly abolishes swimming at low doses and also induces hypoactivity in mice. Overall, most cone snail RFamide doppelganger show only modest potency at vertebrate targets, likely reflecting the evolutionary distance between vertebrates and the natural prey of these species (annelids and gastropods).

Although a comprehensive evolutionary study of these cone snail peptides is lacking, the C. textile, C. victoriae, and C. episcopatus toxins, and possibly also the C. spurius peptides, derive from the same toxin gene superfamily that does not appear to be related to any endogenous neuropeptide gene, suggesting that these peptides evolved de novo.

FMRFamide-like toxins have also been identified in parasitoid wasps, and lepidopterans. A subset of these can activate human neuropeptide FF receptors and exhibit insecticidal effects when injected in Drosophila melanogaster.
Doppelganger peptides of bilaterian neuropeptide families
Doppelganger peptides of neuropeptide Y/F

Neuropeptide Y/F (NPY/F) peptides are ubiquitous across Bilateria and are typically called NPY in deuterostomes and NPF in protostomes with their effects mediated by several different GPCRs. In chordates, NPY plays key roles in vasoconstriction and a range of metabolic processes that generally promote growth. These functions are broadly conserved in protostomes.

A group of cone snail toxins, the cono-NPYs, mimic NPY/F peptides and were first identified in Conus betulinus. The C. betulinus doppelganger induced hyperactivity in mice but the target was not determined. Other toxin fragments derived from a cono-NPY doppelganger expressed in Conus textile, a species that also expresses the conorfamide gene family, elicit pain by enhancing acid-sensing ion channel 3 (ASIC3) currents with moderate potency. Similar peptides, also likely belonging to the NPY doppelganger family, As1b and As22b, induced ASIC1a peak current potentiation and, interestingly, also inhibited the neuronal alpha7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) and the muscle-type nAChR at higher potency. Transcripts encoding cono-NPYs have since been identified in various other species, but their biological activities have not been tested.

NPY/F-like peptides have been detected in the saliva of certain leeches, where they cause a dose-dependent reduction in inflammatory cytokine release. Additionally, an NPY doppelganger is one of the most highly expressed toxins in the venom gland of the fangblenny, Meiacanthus grammistes and the venom of Meiacanthus atrodorsalis.
Doppelganger peptides of somatostatin and related peptides

Somatostatins are short cyclic neuropeptides conserved across chordates, where they regulate endocrine function, inhibit hormone release, and modulate neuronal excitability through activation of several somatostatin-family GPCRs. Their structure is defined by an intramolecular disulfide bond that stabilizes the bioactive conformation. Because of their central role in suppressing hormone secretion, and the overexpression of somatostatin receptors in several cancers, synthetic somatostatin analogs have been developed as therapeutics for neuroendocrine disorders and cancer. In chordates, several related peptides have been described, including cortistatin, which also signals via somatostatin receptors, and urotensin and urotensin-related peptide, which act on urotensin receptors. Until recently, somatostatin and related peptides (SSRPs) were thought to be restricted to deuterostomes, but this hypothesis changed with the discovery of SSRP doppelganger in cone snail venom.

The first example from venom came from the deep-water, fish-hunting cone snail Conus rolani, whose venom contains consomatin Ro1. Strikingly, consomatin Ro1 more closely resembles therapeutic somatostatin drug analogs than the native hormone itself. Since this discovery, hundreds of somatostatin doppelganger have been identified in many cone snail species. Some act as potent agonists of the human somatostatin receptor 4 (SSTR4) and produce pain relief in mammalian pain models. Others potently activate the human somatostatin receptor 2 (SSTR2) and act in combination with insulin doppelganger to reduce blood glucose levels in prey. Evolutionary analysis revealed that SSRP doppelganger originated through the recruitment of a previously unrecognized neuropeptide gene encoding the snail's endogenous SSRP. This finding uncovered the existence of SSRP signaling systems across diverse protostome phyla.
Doppelganger peptides of tachykinin

Tachykinins are a well-characterized family of neuropeptides found throughout bilaterian animals and have been extensively studied in vertebrates. In humans, nine different tachykinins are encoded by three distinct precursor genes and act via three known tachykinin receptors, all of which are GPCRs. In mammals, tachykinins play key roles as neuromodulators in the central nervous system and mediate diverse processes such as pain perception, stress responses, memory, and reproduction. Tachykinins are also present in non-vertebrate deuterostomes and protostomes, where related receptors have been deorphanized. In invertebrates, tachykinins have similarly been implicated in processes such as nociception, memory, and reproduction.

Tachykinin doppelganger peptides have evolved independently in at least four animal lineages. Certain octopuses produce tachykinin-like peptides in their venom that appear to have evolved convergently and are not evolutionarily related to the animal's endogenous tachykinins. These peptides induce contraction of isolated strips of guinea pig ileum. The social wasps Polistes lanio lanio and parasitoid wasps have evolved tachykinin doppelganger in their venom. The crude venom of P. lanio increases vascular permeability in mouse dorsal skin, likely in part due to tachykinin doppelganger acting as antagonists of the neurokinin 1 receptor. The Brazilian armed spider Phoneutria nigriventer has also been found to produce multiple tachykinin doppelganger. These peptides were identified through mass spectrometry, and their biological function remains unknown.

Lastly, tachykinin doppelganger peptides, called sialokinins, are also known from the saliva of the yellow fever mosquito Aedes aegypti. These peptides are equipotent to mammalian substance P, a tachykinin neuropeptide, when tested for their ability to induce muscle contraction of guinea pig ileum and are believed to promote vasodilation of the target animal to aid in blood feeding.
Doppelganger peptides of vasotocin

The vasotocin peptide family, initially discovered in 1906, comprises short, disulfide-bonded peptides, including oxytocin, vasopressin, isotocin, and several other lineage-specific variants. Terminology in this family can be confusing, particularly in molluscs and other protostomes, because the term conopressin, originally coined for cone snail venom doppelganger, is also used for endogenous vasotocins. Strictly speaking, however, conopressin should refer only to the cone snail doppelganger, while endogenous protostome peptides should be referred to as vasotocins.

Vasotocins are encoded on larger precursors that also include a conserved neurophysin domain, a feature found across all bilaterians. These peptides signal through a well-defined family of GPCRs. Across animals, vasotocins regulate a wide range of physiological functions, including osmoregulation and smooth muscle contraction, but are best known for their conserved roles in modulating social behavior and reproduction in diverse animals, including vertebrates, nematodes, insects, and molluscs.

As noted above, many cone snail species produce conopressin toxins that mimic vasotocin peptides. Injection of conopressins in mice and annelids can trigger intense scratching or stereotyped mating behaviors, respectively, though the precise biological role of conopressins remains unclear. Anecdotal reports suggest that the venom of nemertean (ribbon worms) may also contain vasotocin-like toxins. This idea is supported by the recent identification of an unusually high number of divergent putative vasotocin peptides in nemerteans. Although these peptides were initially described as endogenous regulators, it is plausible that some could function as molecular mimics in venom.
Doppelganger peptides of deuterostome neuropeptide families
Doppelganger peptides of bradykinin

Bradykinin is a nonapeptide generated from kininogen precursors through proteolytic cleavage, and it plays central roles in vasodilation, pain, and inflammation. It acts through bradykinin B1 and B2 receptors, both GPCRs, producing smooth muscle contraction, vascular permeability, and nociceptive signaling. Across vertebrates, this system is critical for regulating vascular tone, inflammation, and injury responses.

Bradykinin-like peptides have been isolated from the venoms of some species of wasps and ants. Given their similarity to chordate bradykinins, these doppelganger likely act as defensive toxins that induce vasodilation, hypotension, pain, and inflammation in vertebrate predators. Indeed, when tested in rats, several of these doppelganger isolated from the solitary wasp Cyphononyx fulvognathus showed hyperalgesic effects in the paw pressure test after intraplantar injection which could be reversed when adding B1 and B2 receptor antagonists. Similar effects were recently observed with two other bradykinin-like doppelganger, Thr6-BK, Da1a, in mouse models of pain. Evolutionary analyses revealed that these peptides do not share common ancestry with vertebrate bradykinin. Instead, they independently evolved from toxin-encoding genes to target the bradykinin receptors of predators to induce pain.
Doppelganger peptides of calcitonin gene-related peptide and adrenomedullin

Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) is a neuropeptide widely expressed in chordates and produced by alternative splicing of the calcitonin gene. It is a potent vasodilator and neuromodulator, acting through the calcitonin receptor-like receptor, a GPCR, in complex with receptor activity-modifying proteins (RAMPs). CGRP is best known for its role in pain pathways and is a major therapeutic target in migraine. Evolutionarily, CGRP belongs to an ancestral calcitonin peptide family, that includes calcitonin, amylin, and adrenomedullin in chordates. These peptides share structural similarities and are involved in various physiological processes such as calcium homeostasis, glucose metabolism, and cardiovascular regulation.

Mimicry of CGRP has been described in the vampire bat, Desmodus rotundus, a blood feeder that possesses submandibular glands that produce various bioactive compounds to facilitate the hematophagous lifestyle. Vampire bat-derived CGRP (vCGRP) was shown to activate human CGRP receptors and G protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK1/2) channels. The vasorelaxant efficacy and potency of vCGRP were similar to those of human CGRP, and it was hypothesized that this activity facilitates feeding by promoting continual blood flow.

Another documented case occurs in blood-feeding soft ticks of the genus Ornithodoros. These ticks modulate blood flow by secreting adrenomedullin (ADM) doppelganger in their saliva, acquired via horizontal gene transfer from vertebrate hosts. Adrenomedullin itself is a multifunctional hormone with potent hypotensive and angiogenic effects. Functional assays in rats showed that one of the ADM doppelganger peptides from Ornithodoros moubata induces a profound, dose-dependent drop in blood pressure upon intravenous administration in rats, with activity greater than that of mammalian ADM. This enhanced vasodilatory effect suggests that Ornithodoros ticks use ADM doppelganger as powerful vasodilatory hormone mimics to incapacitate host defenses and secure prolonged blood meals.
Doppelganger peptides of endorphins/enkephalins

Opioid peptides are central regulators of nociception, stress, reward, and key autonomic processes such as gut motility and cardiovascular function across chordates, comprising three major families: endorphins, enkephalins, and dynorphins. Endorphins, such as beta-endorphin, are derived from proopiomelanocortin, enkephalins (Met- and Leu-enkephalin) from proenkephalin, and dynorphins from prodynorphin. These precursors are evolutionarily related, having diversified from an ancestral opioid peptide gene early in chordate history. Despite their different lengths and processing, all opioid peptides share a highly conserved Tyr-Gly-Gly-Phe (YGGF) motif at their N-terminus, which is essential for binding to their target, the opioid receptors. Opioid receptors are GPCRs of the rhodopsin-like family and include the mu-, delta-, and kappa-opioid receptors. These mediate diverse physiological effects in the CNS, including analgesia, reward, mood regulation, stress, and dysphoria. The opioid system has long been exploited as a therapeutic target for pain, but while opioid-based drugs remain among the most effective analgesics, their clinical use is limited by serious side effects, including respiratory depression, tolerance, constipation, and possible dependence. Beyond the CNS, opioid signaling also plays a major role in the gastrointestinal tract, where activation of mu-opioid receptors inhibits peristalsis, decreases intestinal secretion, and increases fluid absorption. These effects contribute to the constipating side effects of therapeutic opioids but may also suggest an ancient role of the opioid system in regulating digestion and gut motility.

The fangblenny, Meiacanthus atrodorsalis and Meiacanthus grammistes, tropical fish that use venom to deter predators, express multiple opioid-like peptides in their venom gland that derive from a proenkephalin gene. Although the individual peptides were not tested, whole venom significantly inhibited cyclic AMP production in cells overexpressing mu- and delta-opioid receptors, with no activity at kappa receptors. Venom activity was largely blocked by the broad-spectrum opioid antagonist naloxone in delta-expressing cells, but not in mu-expressing cells, suggesting that the venom's opioid doppelganger preferentially target delta receptors, and that the observed mu receptor activity may be mediated by a different component that does not directly engage the orthosteric receptor binding pocket.

Analysis of the venom of the Asian scorpion Buthus martensii (Olivierus martensii) revealed the presence of a gene precursor that encodes two short peptides (BmK-YA and His 4-BmK-YA), each present by four repeats, that share significant sequence similarity with chordate enkephalins, including the YGGF motif. Functional studies demonstrated that BmK-YA preferentially activates delta-opioid receptors with higher efficacy than morphine, while showing weaker potency and efficacy at mu- and kappa-opioid receptors. Interestingly, His 4-BmK-YA, which only differs by a single amino acid substitution in position 4 (histidine instead of methionine) had no activity at the human opioid receptors.
Although the biological role of opioid doppelganger in venoms remains unknown, these toxins may deter chordate predators through modulating pain circuits or inducing digestive discomfort.
Doppelganger peptides of endothelin

Endothelins are potent vasoactive peptides best known in vertebrates for their role in regulating blood vessel constriction and blood pressure. They are small disulfide-bond containing peptides, processed from larger precursors by endothelin-converting enzymes. In mammals, endothelins act through two GPCR receptors, the endothelin receptor A (ET-A) and B (ET-B). Although first characterized in mammals, endothelin-related peptides have been identified across chordates. Their important role in modulating vascular tone has made them targets for drug development in cardiovascular disease.

The first endothelin doppelganger, sarafotoxins, were identified in the venom of the burrowing asp, Atractaspis engaddensis, a venomous snake. These short peptides share high sequence and structural similarity with chordate endothelins and act as potent agonists of the ET-A and ET-B receptors. Injection of sarafotoxins in mammalian models produces rapid vasoconstriction, hypertension, and potentially lethal cardiovascular collapse. Longer peptides were later described from the venom of Atractaspis microlepidota microlepidota. Although these peptides have much lower potencies at the endothelin receptors than sarafotoxins isolated from A. engaddensis, they induce potent in vivo toxicity in mice possibly due to a different molecular mechanism of action. Outside of the genus Atractaspis (family Atractaspidae), no clear examples of venom-derived endothelin mimics have been reported, although many venomous animals employ different molecular strategies to modulate cardiovascular function.

passages.text: Doppelganger peptides of glucagon-like peptide 1

Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) is a member of the glucagon peptide family, derived from proglucagon processing, and acts as a potent incretin hormone by stimulating insulin secretion, inhibiting glucagon release, and slowing gastric emptying. In vertebrates, GLP-1 signaling through the GLP-1 receptor, a class B GPCR, plays essential roles in glucose homeostasis and appetite regulation. Clinically, GLP-1 analogs were originally developed to treat type 2 diabetes and have more recently emerged as highly effective therapeutics for obesity, with potential indications in cardiovascular disease, dementia, and other conditions.

In several venomous species, GLP-1-like peptides have been co-opted as bioactive components of venom. Several GLP-1 doppelganger have been described from the venom of the Gila monster, Heloderma suspectum, and a related species, the Mexican beaded lizard, Heloderma horridum. One of these peptides, exendin-4, from H. suspectum has been extensively investigated. Exendin-4, potently activates the human GLP-1 receptor but, unlike human GLP-1, it possesses several structural modifications that enhance its stability and potency, including a C-terminal extension and the absence of a proteolytic cleavage site found in most other GLP-1 peptides. These properties ultimately enabled exendin-4 to become the first approved GLP-1 analog for diabetes treatment. Despite decades of study, the physiological role of exendin-4 in the Gila monster remains unclear and an endogenous physiological role cannot be ruled out.

GLP-1 doppelganger have also been described in monotremes, including the platypus, Ornithorhynchus anatinus, and echidna, Tachyglossus aculeatus, which express a single GLP-1 peptide in both the intestine and venom gland. Specific modifications in monotreme GLP-1 confer resistance to proteolytic cleavage, a feature also seen in Exendin-4. The monotreme GLP-1 peptide robustly stimulates insulin secretion in cultured rodent pancreatic islets, demonstrating that it retains classical incretin activity despite sequence differences from mammalian GLP-1. However, binding assays reveal that the peptide has relatively low affinity for the canonical GLP-1 receptor compared with human GLP-1. These adaptations suggest that monotreme GLP-1 has been shaped by the dual pressures of metabolic regulation and venom function, representing a unique evolutionary strategy distinct from the gene duplication and diversification observed in Gila monster Exendin-4.
Doppelganger peptides of natriuretic peptides

Natriuretic peptides (NPs) are a vertebrate hormone family that includes atrial (ANP), brain (BNP), and C-type (CNP) natriuretic peptides. They share a disulfide-stabilized ring structure and primarily regulate salt and water balance, vascular tone, and blood pressure. Each NP is encoded by a distinct protein precursor. Proteolytic processing of these precursors generates both the mature cyclic peptide and, in some cases, additional bioactive fragments (e.g., NT-proANP and NT-proBNP), which can circulate and serve as clinical biomarkers of cardiac stress. NPs exert their effects through three membrane-bound natriuretic peptide receptors (NPRs). NPR-A is the primary receptor for ANP and BNP, while NPR-B preferentially binds CNP. Both are guanylyl cyclase-coupled receptors that trigger intracellular cyclic GMP (cGMP) production, leading to vasodilation, natriuresis, and diuresis. A third receptor, NPR-C, lacks guanylyl cyclase activity and primarily functions as a clearance receptor, regulating NP half-life, although it can also couple to Gi proteins to modulate signaling pathways such as inhibition of adenylyl cyclase. Through this tripartite receptor system, NPs act as key homeostatic regulators of cardiovascular and renal function.

Several venomous animals, including snakes, lizards, and platypus, have been reported to utilize NP mimics in their venoms. The first NP doppelganger was identified from the Eastern green mamba, Dendroaspis angusticeps, and various others have been identified since. Dendroaspis NP (DNP) promotes smooth muscle relaxation and, when administered to dogs, reduces mean arterial pressure, suggesting a potential use as a drug lead for cardiovascular disease. DNP shares sequence homology with the three mammalian natriuretic peptides, but differs in its receptor activation profile, a distinction attributed to its extended C-terminal region. Characterization of DNP inspired the development of a chimeric analog combining elements of DNP and human CNP, termed cenderitide. This engineered peptide functions as a dual activator of the NPR-A and NPR-B, producing the natriuretic and diuretic effects typical of DNP while also retaining the antiproliferative and antifibrotic activities associated with CNP. Cenderitide advanced into clinical trials for use in patients with stable chronic heart failure and myocardial infarction.

NPs have also been found in the venomous salivary gland secretions of the helodermatid, varanid, and anguid lizards. Notably, in helodermatid species like the Mexican beaded lizard, H. horridum, and the Gila monster, H. suspectum, the NP gene encodes a natriuretic peptide together with multiple "helokinestatin" peptides that antagonize bradykinin-induced smooth muscle relaxation. Functionally, NP-like toxins from lizard venoms induce systemic vasodilation and rapid hypotension in prey, similar to snake venom NPs, although receptor-binding profiles for these lizard-derived peptides have not yet been characterized directly.

The male platypus, O. anatinus, also secretes a natriuretic-like peptide in its venom. This peptide, OvCNP, produces edema in the rat paw and causes mast cell degranulation, which probably contributes to the development of the painful response following platypus envenomation. Interestingly, unlike any other known DNP-like peptide, the platypus doppelganger exists in two forms, one of which, OvCNPb, contains a D-amino acid. This discovery represented the first report of a D-amino acid in a biologically active peptide from a mammal.
Doppelganger peptides of neurotensin

Neurotensin (NT) is a chordate peptide with diverse functions in both the central nervous system and peripheral tissues. It is broadly distributed throughout the brain, especially in regions like the hypothalamus, amygdala, and nucleus accumbens, where it modulates neuronal excitability, influences dopamine signaling, and produces effects such as analgesia, hypothermia, and increased locomotion. In the gastrointestinal tract, NT is produced by enter-oendocrine N cells, and co-expressed and co-released with other key gut hormones, including GLP-1 and peptide YY (PYY), to regulate digestion, appetite, and glucose metabolism. NT acts through two class A GPCRs, neurotensin receptor 1 and 2 (NTSR1 and NTSR2), and interacts with neurotensin receptor 3 (NTSR3, also known as sortilin), which belongs to the Vps10p-domain receptor family.

Neurotensin (NT) mimicry has been reported in the fish-hunting cone snail C. geographus, which releases its venom into the water to induce a hypoactive, sedated state in prey. Although its precise ecological function in envenomation remains unresolved, Contulakin-G produces potent central analgesia in animal models of pain. The toxin carries an O-glycosylation that is critical for its in vivo activity with accumulating evidence indicating that the analgesic effects are mediated via NTSR2 receptors in the spinal cord, leading to downstream inhibition of R-type calcium channels (Cav2.3). Contulakin-G advanced to clinical trials for central neuropathic pain and showed encouraging efficacy but development was discontinued following the closure of the company responsible for its commercialization.
Doppelganger peptides of protostome peptide families
Doppelganger peptides of allatotropin / myoactive tetradecapeptide

Peptides of the allatotropin/myoactive tetradecapeptide (MAPT) family have been isolated from molluscs, annelids, and arthropods, and several other protostome lineages. These peptides exert both excitatory and inhibitory effects on various muscle tissues, including the smooth muscles of the esophagus and gut. In insects, allatotropin is a potent stimulator of juvenile hormone release and also enhances smooth muscle contraction. The GPCR has been deorphanized in insects and annelid and predicted in multiple other protostomes.

Doppelganger toxins have been found in the cone snail Conus vitulinus, where they are known as conomaps. Notably, conomap-Vt contain an unusual post-translational modification, incorporating a D-phenylalanine residue. Functionally, conomap-Vt induces contraction of the buccal mass, crop, penis retractor muscle, and foot tissue in the mollusc Pomacea bridgesi.
Doppelganger peptides of crustacean cardioactive peptide

Crustacean cardioactive peptide (CCAP) is a cyclic, amidated peptide that was first isolated from the pericardial organs of the shore crab. Homologs have since been identified in arthropods, molluscs, annelids, and nemerteans, but appear to be lost in several other protostome phyla.

Functionally, CCAP accelerates heart activity in crabs and Drosophila. It also stimulates midgut and hindgut contractions in cockroaches and stick insects, respectively, and modulates oviduct and spermatheca contractions in locusts. These effects are mediated by CCAP receptors, which belong to the GPCR family.

Doppelganger toxins of CCAP have been isolated from the worm-hunting cone snail Conus villepinii, where they are termed conoCAPs. Unlike the native peptide, conoCAP decreases heart rate in D. melanogaster larvae and can induce severe arrhythmia and death at higher concentrations. Intravenous injection of conoCAP in rats produces a modest reduction in heart rate and blood pressure, while the native CCAP peptide shows no such effect.
Doppelganger peptides of CCWamide

The CCWamide-agatoxin pair represents one of the cases where a doppelganger toxin was discovered before the endogenous peptide hormone it mimics was known. The U8-agatoxin was first isolated from the venom of the funnel spider Agelenopsis aperta and was later found to have homologs in the nervous systems of various arthropods, where they are commonly referred to as CCWamides. Recent studies have shown that CCWamides are widely distributed among protostomes and are evolutionarily related to these agatoxin doppelganger. However, neither the receptor nor the biological function of these peptides have yet been determined.
Doppelganger peptides of crustacean hyperglycemic hormone superfamily

Crustacean hyperglycemic hormone (CHH) and its related peptides (molt-inhibiting hormone, gonad-inhibiting hormone, and vitellogenesis-inhibiting hormone) were originally discovered in the eyestalks of crustaceans through bioactivity-guided assays. Homologous peptides, termed ion-transport peptides (ITPs), were later identified in other ecdysozoans, a group within protostomes that includes arthropods, nematodes, and other phyla, and more recently in lophotrocozoans, another major protostome group that includes molluscs, annelids, and other phyla. These peptides are typically 60-80 amino acids long with ecdysozoan members characterized by six conserved cysteine residues and five alpha helices, whereas lophotrochozoan homologs usually have four cysteines and four helices. Although only a subset has been functionally characterized, CHH superfamily peptides display a broad spectrum of biological roles, including regulation of metabolism, ion and water homeostasis, development, stress responses, immunity, and reproduction. In D. melanogaster, the ITP receptor was recently identified as a membrane guanylyl cyclase, whereas in Bombyx mori, Gq-coupled GPCRs were found to be the target.

An unusually large number of doppelganger peptides related to the CHH superfamily have been discovered in venomous species, including spiders, centipedes, parasitoid wasps, remipedes, lepidopterans, and cone snails. These venom-derived peptides generally retain the disulfide bond patterns and overall three-dimensional fold of their ancestral CHH-like precursors, although in some cases, such as centipede and spider toxins, one of the alpha helices has been lost; a structural change hypothesized to contribute to their toxic function. The presence of CHH-like doppelganger toxins across so many lineages suggests that the CHH signaling pathways may be particularly prone to molecular mimicry. Latrodectin, the CHH doppelganger toxin from black widow spiders, is perhaps unsurprisingly not toxic to mice, and anecdotally appears to lack hyperglycemic effects when injected into crabs, crayfish, or shrimp. Other doppelganger, such as the Ta1a-toxin of Tegenaria agrestis are insecticidal though their mode of action may differ from that of the ancestral CHH peptide.
Doppelganger peptides of corazonin

Corazonin was first identified as a cardioacceleratory peptide in cockroach. The peptide is widely distributed among insects and other arthropods but appears to be absent in coleopterans. Since its initial discovery, corazonin has been found to play diverse roles in social behavior, metabolism, and stress responses. Its receptors are GPCRs ancestrally related to the gonadotropin-releasing hormone receptors found in vertebrates.

Corazonin doppelganger toxins have been identified in several lepidopterans caterpillars as well as in the parasitoid wasp Ampulex compressa, a species that parasitizes cockroaches and uses its venom to manipulate their behavior for the development of its offspring. In caterpillars, these peptides are likely deployed as defensive toxins against predators, whereas in the wasp, they likely function in host manipulation. These distinct ecological contexts suggest differences in the toxic functions of these peptides. However, the precise mechanisms and physiological functions of these peptides in each system remain to be determined.
Doppelganger peptides of diuretic hormone 31

Diuretic hormone 31 (DH31) is evolutionarily related to calcitonin and is found across most protostome lineages. In insects, DH31 is produced by neurosecretory cells in the central nervous system and binds to class B GPCRs, which are primarily expressed in nervous tissue and the digestive tract. While DH31 is best known for its role in promoting diuresis, it also contributes to other physiological processes, including digestion, stress tolerance, and regulation of circadian rhythms.

DH31-like peptides have been identified transcriptomically from the venom glands of centipedes, spiders, and the venomous caterpillar Doratifera vulnerans, however, none of these venom-derived peptides have been functionally characterized. Endogenous DH31 induces significant fluid secretion in most insect species tested, raising the possibility that DH31-like doppelganger in venom may exert similar physiological effects on prey.
Doppelganger peptides of eclosion hormone

Eclosion hormone is an arthropod-specific peptide first discovered in giant silk moths. Together with ecdysis-triggering hormone, it initiates ecdysis, the shedding of the exoskeleton during molting, through engaging with its target receptor guanylyl cyclase.
An eclosion hormone-like toxin has been identified in the venom of the parasitoid wasp A. compressa, though its function has not yet been investigated.
Doppelganger peptides of elevenin

Elevenin was first identified in the L11 neuron of the abdominal ganglion of the Californian sea hare Aplysia californica. Since then, elevenin homologs have been found in numerous protostome phyla, including Mollusca, Annelida, Nematoda, and Arthropoda. Although its biological roles remain poorly understood, elevenin has been reported to function as an environmental signal that inhibits olfaction in C. elegans, and to regulate body coloration in the brown planthopper, Nilaparvata lugens. The elevenin receptor was first deorphanized in the annelid P. dumerilii, with homologous receptors subsequently characterized in other protostomes, including A. californica.

Elevenin doppelganger toxins are currently known only from venomous conoidean snails, first identified through proteotranscriptomic analyses of the venom of the cone snail C. victoriae. They have also been detected in the related but highly derived Pygmaeconus lineage. Notably, although elevenin itself is absent in vertebrates, intracranial injection of C. victoriae elevenin in mice induces hyperactivity.
Doppelganger peptides of myosuppressin

Myosuppressins belong to the broader group of FMRFamide-like peptides, which are widespread across metazoans. Myosupressins were first identified in cockroaches and have since been found in various other arthropods and protostomes, where they typically inhibit muscle activity through GPCR-mediated signaling.

Doppelganger toxins similar to myosuppressin have been identified and isolated from the venom of the parasitic wasps Sphex argentatus and A. compressa, of which the amidated toxin from S. agentatus was shown to cause spontaneous contractions of locus oviducts. Given myosuppressin's role in suppressing muscle contractions, it is likely that these toxins contribute directly to the paralysis of the wasps' prey/host.
Doppelganger peptides of proctolin

Proctolin is a short, five-amino acid peptide hormone that regulates muscle contraction in the digestive, reproductive, and circulatory systems of arthropods. Its native receptor was identified as a GPCR in D. melanogaster.

A proctolin doppelganger toxin has been isolated from the venom of the scorpion Tityus serrulatus, where it functions as an inhibitor of the peptidase neprilysin. Proctolin-like peptides have also been identified through proteomics in the venom of the spider wasp Pepsis decorata, a parasitoid that provisions its larvae on immobilized spiders, although the biological function of these peptides remains unknown.
Doppelganger peptides of prohormone-4

A short, bioactive peptide encoded by the prohormone-4 (PH4) precursor, was first identified computationally in the honey bee (Apis mellifera) genome and later confirmed in the brain, where it has been implicated in modulating behavior. Its receptor, however, remains unknown.
Doppelganger peptides of PH4 have been identified in the venom of the cone snail C. victoriae, but their biological function has yet to be determined.
Doppelganger peptides of pre-bilaterian peptide families
Doppelganger peptides of ShK-like peptide
A recently discovered neuropeptide from the sea anemone N. vectensis, ShK-like 2, was shown to be expressed in neurons in early development and induce contraction of the polyps.

A related and highly similar peptide, ShK-like 1, which evolved from a gene duplication event of ShK-like-2, can be found in the venom of N. vectensis and is lethal to zebrafish larvae. The discovery of ShK-like 2 represents another example of a case where the toxin was identified first and prompted the identification of the endogenous neuropeptide that gave rise to it.
Doppelganger-related peptides

Although most doppelganger were identified by their similarity to known neuropeptides, in some cases, such as the Shk-like 1/Shk-like 2 and agatoxin/CCWamide examples discussed further above, the toxin was discovered first, preceding the identification of the endogenous neuropeptide. These anecdotal cases recently inspired a systematic approach using cone snail doppelganger toxins as probes to identify previously unknown neuropeptides in cone snails and other protostomes. The resulting peptides, termed doppelganger-related peptides (DREPs), are named for structural features they share with their toxin counterparts. Although their biological roles remain to be experimentally confirmed, multiple lines of evidence support their classification as bona fide neuropeptides.
Hairpin doppelganger and their related neuropeptides

Hairpin doppelganger were first described from the venom of the snail-hunting cone snail C. victoriae. The C. victoriae toxin, contryphan-Vc1, adopts a unique single disulfide-directed beta-hairpin fold, a highly heat-stable motif that also forms the structural core of several multi-disulfide peptide frameworks, including the inhibitor cystine knot. Additional hairpin doppelganger have since been identified in two other snail-hunting species, and homologous peptides, hairpin DREPs, were also confirmed in non-venomous mollusks as well as in annelids. In A. californica, hairpin DREP is expressed broadly across neuronal transcriptomes and in the salivary gland, with lower expression levels detected in the foot. In the squid Doryteuthis pealeii, hairpin DREP shows high expression in neuronal tissues, but also in some non-neuronal secretory tissues. Expression of hairpin DREP was also detected in the nerve cord and neural ganglion of the earthworm Lumbricus rubellus.
Medial doppelganger and their related neuropeptides

Medial doppelganger, found in the venom of several snail-hunting cone snails, contain two short domains that may yield two active peptides, each stabilized by a disulfide bond and C-terminal amidation. Homologous peptides, called medial DREPs, were identified in non-venomous mollusks and annelids, with expression observed in the pleural ganglion of the sea hare A. californica.
R-superfamily doppelganger and their related neuropeptides

Cone snail R-superfamily toxins, short peptides with two disulfide bonds, show sequence similarity to the mature peptide region of an uncharacterized protein in the genome of the owl limpet Lottia gigantea. Although this relationship was not fully explored, sequence homology searches readily identify related sequences in other non-venomous mollusks, strongly suggesting that these cone snail toxins are doppelganger of a still-unrecognized molluscan DREP. A related toxin, teretoxin Tan14.1, was later discovered in the venom of the auger snail Terebra anilis. While homologous sequences have not yet been reported outside of Mollusca, the fact that cone snail species expressing these toxins, namely C. villepinii and C. austini, prey on worms suggests that this putative neuropeptide may also exist in annelids and possibly other protostome phyla. Interestingly, structurally related toxins with weak activity against voltage-gated potassium channels have also been identified in the scorpion Heterometrus laoticus. However, whether the snail and scorpion toxin families share an evolutionary origin remains unresolved.
Tail doppelganger and their related neuropeptides

Tail toxins, which contain a single disulfide bond with a short cyclic loop located toward the C-terminus, were identified from the venom glands of several worm-hunting cone snails. Corresponding homologous peptides, called tail DREPs, were detected in non-venomous mollusks and annelids, with high expression in the calciferous and digestive tissues of L. rubellus.
Triangle doppelganger and their related neuropeptides

Triangle doppelganger toxins, which contain a single disulfide bond, were identified from the venom gland transcriptomes of worm-hunting cone snails, alongside homologous sequences - termed triangle DREPs - found across mollusks, annelids, arthropods, and platyhelminths. Tissue-specific transcriptomes revealed high neuronal expression of triangle DREPs in D. pealeii as well as in the nerve cord and neural ganglion of L. rubellus.
Conclusion

Once only anecdotally reported, neuropeptide mimicry by doppelganger peptides in venomous animals and other ecological contexts is an increasingly recognized phenomenon, with many additional examples likely still to be discovered. This review provides an overview of the currently known cases. Despite this growing list, the biological roles of most doppelganger peptides remain poorly understood, particularly those that mimic protostome-specific neuropeptides. Demonstrating biological activity in a target organism represents an important first step, however, fully elucidating their native physiological functions, ecological relevance, and evolutionary significance is essential. Addressing these knowledge gaps will likely be a focus of future research that will deepen our understanding of the diverse uses and potential applications of these peptides.

The top portion represents a dendrogram of venomous lineages in which doppelganger toxins (shown as blue triangles) have been identified, and the known occurrences of the corresponding neuropeptides are shown on the right and as yellow triangles in the figure. Doppelganger-related peptides (DREPs) and their proposed neuropeptide counterparts are shown in transparent blue and yellow, respectively, as these have not yet been experimentally validated.

Overview of neuropeptides with known doppelganger peptide counterparts identified in animal venoms. Neuropeptides are listed in the order in which they appear in the main text. Doppelganger-related peptides are not included in this table.
