passages.text: Immune checkpoint genes (ICGs) are responsible for balancing stimulatory and inhibitory pathways and are crucial for maintaining self-tolerance and modulating the type, intensity, and duration of immune responses. Mounting evidence shows that in cancer, immune checkpoint pathways are activated to suppress immunological activity against tumors and inhibit immune responses. Immune checkpoint blockade represents a type of epoch-making immunotherapy that uses various antibodies to block immune checkpoint pathways.

Although cuproptosis and immune checkpoints are high on the priority list of cancer research, little has been done to investigate whether or not cuproptosis-related immune checkpoint genes (CRICGs) can help predict the prognosis and guide the treatment of NSCLC. In this study, a predictive model was established with 4 CRICGs that were identified with bioinformatics approaches, and a prognostic nomogram was developed using the risk scores generated from the predictive model, which was found to effectively predict the prognosis of patients with NSCLC. Besides, the study results suggested correlations between the 4 CRICGs and ICI levels in the tumor microenvironment (TME). Eight small-molecule drugs (SMDs) were further selected to treat NSCLC by targeting these CRICGs.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Data collection

The training dataset included mRNA expression and clinical data of tumor tissue samples from NSCLC patients (including lung adenocarcinoma [LUAD] and lung squamous cell carcinoma [LUSC]) available on The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) data portal (https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/). The validation dataset was comprised of GSE30219 downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/). Cuproptosis-related genes (CRGs; n = 13) were obtained from a published work, and ICGs (n = 79) were from another study. Expression levels of these CRGs and ICGs were determined via R-4.2.0, followed by a correlation analysis using the "limma" package with the correlation coefficient >= 0.3 and P < .05 to quantify the expression levels of CRICGs.
2.2. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) and protein-protein interaction (PPI)

The CRICGs underwent gene ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses using the "clusterProfiler," "org.Hs.eg.db," "ggplot2," and 'enrichplot' packages. A false discovery rate or P-value < .05 was defined as significant enrichment. The STRING database (http://www.string-db.org/) was utilized to predict protein-protein interaction (PPI) and draw PPI networks in combination with Cytoscape.
2.3. Development and performance evaluation of the predictive model based on cuproptosis-related immune checkpoint genes (CRICGs)

The "survival" R package was employed to analyze and screen for CRICGs of prognostic value. Subsequently, a univariate Cox regression analysis was performed on the prognosis-related CRICGs. Then, a least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-penalized Cox regression analysis was carried out using the "glmnet" package to develop a prognostic risk model. The risk score can be calculated via the following formula:

Wherein Coef1, 2, 3, ..., n stand for coefficients of mRNA1, 2, 3, ..., n in the LASSO Cox regression model. The NSCLC patients were divided into high- and low-risk groups by the median risk score (median cutoff). In the survival analysis, a Kaplan-Meier (KM) curve was depicted to compare the prognosis between the high- and low-risk groups. The "survivalROC" package was utilized to compute a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve for performance evaluation of the prognostic risk model. The predictive performance was further evaluated using NSCLC samples from the GEO database as the validation dataset.
2.4. Construction of prognostic nomogram

Uni- and multivariate Cox regression analyses of the risk scores and clinical data of the NSCLC patients were performed using the "survival" package to measure the prognostic value of such risk scores. The "pheatmap" package, chi-square test, and Fisher's test were implemented to verify whether the CRICGs used for constructing the risk model were involved in the development and progression of NSCLC. The "regplot" and "rms" packages were utilized to plot a prognostic nomogram of NSCLC based on the risk scores and clinical data for 3- and 5-year survival analysis. A calibration curve was created to assess the predictive performance of the prognostic nomogram.
2.5. Gene set enrichment analyses

Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was conducted using the "enrichplot," "org.Hs.eg.db," "ggplot2," and 'clusterProfiler' packages to explore potential molecular mechanisms in the high- and low-risk groups. Statistical significance was set at P < .05 or false discovery rate < 30%.
2.6. Analysis of immune cell infiltration (ICI) in the tumor microenvironment (TME)

Seven algorithms, including tumor immune estimation resource (TIMER), xCell, CIBERSORT, CIBERSORT-ABS, MCP-counter, quanTIseq, and EPIC, were integrated to analyze the differences between the high- and low-risk groups in ICI levels in the TME. Following that, the "ggpubr" package was applied to quantify the expression levels of 47 common ICGs - which were obtained from a previous study - in the high- and low-risk groups (given that CRICGs are already known to play a role in the immune response to NSCLC, is it necessary to measure the expression levels of these ICGs?) The TIMER database (https://cistrome.shinyapps.io/timer/) was employed to investigate the correlations between the 4 CRICGs and 6 types of ICI in the TME.
2.7. Screening for potential therapeutic agents and drug susceptibility testing (DST)

The Enrichr database (https://maayanlab.cloud/Enrichr/) was utilized to screen for SMDs that displayed therapeutic potential for NSCLC and had associations with the selected CRICGs. The Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) database (http://www.cancerrxgene.org/) was used in combination with the "ggplot2," "ggpubr," and "pRRophetic" packages to illuminate the differences between the high- and low-risk groups in susceptibility to targeted therapy and chemotherapy.
2.8. Statistical analysis

All statistical analyses were performed utilizing the R software (version 4.0.2). Intergroup comparisons were examined by the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test. P < .05 indicated a difference of statistical significance.
3. Results

The study flow diagram is shown in Figure 1. The training dataset contained the mRNA expression and clinical data of 1041 patients with NSCLC (LUAD + LUSC) available in TCGA. The validation dataset was formed by the survival data of 233 NSCLC samples of the GSE30219 dataset from the GEO database.
Flow chart of data collection and analysis. CRICG = cuproptosis-related immune checkpoint gene, ICG = immune checkpoint gene, ROC = receiver operating characteristic, TCGA = The Cancer Genome Atlas.
3.1. GSEA and PPI network analysis of CRICGs

The NSCLC gene expression matrix that visualized the expression levels of 13 CRGs and 79 ICGs was downloaded from TCGA. Correlations between CRGs and ICGs were analyzed using the "limma" R package and 58 CRICGs were identified eventually.
3.2. GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses of potential functions of CRICGs

Results of the GO enrichment analysis showed that under biological process terms, the 58 CRICGs were primarily enriched in the following processes: coenzyme metabolic process, tricarboxylic acid cycle, and acetyl-CoA metabolic process. Cellular component enrichment for all CRICGs was dominated by mitochondrial matrix, oxidoreductase complex, and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase complex. Enriched categories for molecular function included oxidoreductase activity, acting on the aldehyde or oxo group of donors, NAD or NADP as acceptor, oxidoreductase activity, acting on the aldehyde or oxo group of donors, and transition metal ion transmembrane transporter activity (see Fig. 2A). KEGG pathway enrichment for the 58 CRICGs was mainly found in the signaling pathways linked to the citrate cycle (tricarboxylic acid cycle), carbon metabolism, and pyruvate metabolism (see Fig. 2B).

Enrichment analyses and protein-protein interaction network of differentially expressed CRICGs. (A) GO analysis; (B) KEGG analysis; and (C) protein-protein interaction network of differentially expressed CRICGs. CRICG = cuproptosis-related immune checkpoint gene, GO = Gene Ontology, KEGG = Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes.

The STRING database revealed that there were 58 nodes and 171 edges in the PPI network based on the 58 CRICGs. With an average local clustering coefficient of 0.611 and a PPI enrichment P-value < 1.0 e-16, the PPI network was constructed using Cytoscape (see Fig. 2C), where nodes in red and green colors represent CRGs and ICGs, respectively.
3.3. Identification of prognosis-related CRICGs and construction of predictive model

A multivariate Cox regression model was utilized to assess potential associations of the 58 CRICGs with the overall survival (OS) of patients with NSCLC. Finally, 5 CRICGs were identified to have significant associations with NSCLC prognosis, including CD209, TNFRSF9, SIRPA, HLA-DMA, and HLA-DMB. On this basis, a forest plot was constructed as shown in Figure 3A. Following that, a predictive model of NSCLC prognosis was developed with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator Cox regression and 4 CRICGs, namely CD209, TNFRSF9, SIRPA, and HLA-DMB (see Fig. 3B). In the predictive model, the risk score is computed by the formula: risk score = (0.0827 x CD209 expression level) + (0.0778 x TNFRSF9 expression level) + (0.0167 x SIRPA expression level) + (-0.0296 x HLA-DMB expression level).

Identification of prognostic CRICGs by univariate Cox regression analysis and LASSO-penalized Cox regression analysis. (A) Forest plot shows candidate CRICGs. (B) LASSO regression analysis was used for dimensionality reduction for the 5 prognosis-associated CRICGs. X axis shows lambda and Y axis shows error. CRICG = cuproptosis-related immune checkpoint gene, LASSO = least absolute shrinkage and selection operator.
3.4. Performance evaluation of predictive model

NSCLC patients in the training dataset were classified into a high-risk group (n = 387) and a low-risk group (n = 388) using the median risk score as the cutoff point (see Fig. 4D). The KM survival curve indicated that survival time was significantly longer in the low-risk group than in the high-risk group (P < .001; see Fig. 4A). Moreover, the risk score system (Fig. 4C) also suggested a negative correlation between the risk score and NSCLC prognosis. The ROC curve (Fig. 4B) showed that the predictive model based on the 4 selected CRICGs demonstrated favorable efficiency and accuracy in predicting the 5-year survival of patients with NSCLC from TCGA (AUC5 = 0.621). Finally, a heatmap was generated to visualize the differences between the high- and low-risk groups in the expression levels of the 4 CRICGs (see Fig. 4E).

Performance evaluation of the predictive model based on cuproptosis-related immune checkpoint genes (CRICGs) using the training dataset. (A) The Kaplan-Meier (KM) survival analysis shows a significant difference in survival time between the high- and low-risk groups of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients in the training dataset; (B) evaluation of predictive performance in the training dataset for 5-year overall survival (OS) based on time-independent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis; (C) risk score system of NSCLC samples in the training dataset; (D) risk score distribution for NSCLC samples in the training dataset; and (E) heatmap of differences between the high- and low-risk groups in the expression levels of the 4 CRICGs in the training dataset. CRICG = cuproptosis-related immune checkpoint gene, NSCLC = non-small cell lung cancer, OS = overall survival, ROC = receiver operating characteristic.

The 4 CRICGs were assessed likewise for prognostic value using a GEO dataset for validation, with samples in the validation dataset being separated into a high-risk group (n = 116) and a low-risk group (n = 117) by the median risk score (see Fig. 5D). In line with the results yielded by analysis of the training dataset, the KM curve of the validation dataset suggested longer survival in the low-risk group (P < .001; see Fig. 5A). The risk score system displayed a negative correlation between the risk score and NSCLC prognosis (see Fig. 5C). As shown in the ROC curve, the predictive model delivered good performance, with AUC1 = 0.606, AUC3 = 0.587, and AUC5 = 0.606 (see Fig. 5B). Differences in the expression levels of the 4 CRICGs between the high- and low-risk groups were plotted as a heatmap (see Fig. 5E).

Performance evaluation of the CRICG-based predictive model using the validation dataset. (A) The KM survival analysis shows a significant difference in survival time between the high- and low-risk groups of NSCLC patients in the validation dataset; (B) evaluation of predictive performance in the validation dataset for 1-, 3-, and 5-year OS based on time-independent ROC analysis; (C) risk score system of NSCLC samples in the validation dataset; (D) risk score distribution for NSCLC samples in the validation dataset; and (E) heatmap of differences between the high- and low-risk groups in the expression levels of the 4 CRICGs in the validation dataset. CRICG = cuproptosis-related immune checkpoint gene, KM = Kaplan-Meier, NSCLC = non-small cell lung cancer, OS = overall survival, ROC = receiver operating characteristic.
3.5. Risk score as an independent prognostic factor in NSCLC

Uni- and multivariate Cox regression models were employed to assess the eligibility of the CRICGs that were used for constructing the predictive model as an independent prognostic factor in NSCLC. The univariate Cox regression analysis showed that the risk score, T staging, overall staging, and pathological patterns were strongly associated with the survival of patients with NSCLC (see Fig. 6A). The multivariate Cox regression analysis suggested that the risk score served as an independent prognostic factor for the survival of NSCLC patients (see Fig. 6B).

Validation of the risk score of the CRICG-based predictive model as an independent prognostic factor in NSCLC. (A) Univariate Cox regression analysis of the associations of the prognosis with the risk scores and clinical characteristics of NSCLC patients; (B) multivariate Cox regression analysis of the associations of the prognosis with the risk scores and clinical characteristics of NSCLC patients. CRICG = cuproptosis-related immune checkpoint gene, NSCLC = non-small cell lung cancer.
3.6. Associations between the predictive model and clinical characteristics of NSCLC patients

The chi-square and Fisher's tests were conducted to investigate whether or not the 4 CRICGs applied to the predictive model were involved in NSCLC development and progression. Figure 7A, B demonstrates significant differences in T staging (P = .034), N staging (P = .021), and overall staging (P = .018) between the high- and low-risk groups, indicative of a higher risk score with the advancement of cancer stage at diagnosis; Moreover, there were significant differences in pathological patterns (P < .001), indicating a stronger likelihood of LUSC patients having a higher risk score than LUAD patients.

Correlation analysis between the risk scores and clinical characteristics of NSCLC patients. (A) Heatmap of correlations of clinical characteristics with high- and low-risk groups and the 4 CRICGs; (B) correlations between age, sex, T staging, N staging, overall staging, pathological patterns, and the risk score. CRICG = cuproptosis-related immune checkpoint gene, NSCLC = non-small cell lung cancer.

Further, a subgroup analysis was carried out to investigate the associations between such CRICGs and NSCLC prognosis in each subgroup. The risk score of the predictive model delivered better performance in the T1 + T2 (P = .002), N0 (P = .045), N1 + N2 + N3 (P = .031), stage I + II (P = .038), stage III + IV (P = .025), and LUSC (P = .044) subgroups but was less predictive of prognosis in the LUAD and T3 + T4 subgroups (see Fig. 8).
Kaplan-Meier curves of OS differences stratified by T stage, N stage, TNM stage and pathological classification between the high-risk groups and low-risk groups. TNM = tumor-node-metastasis.
3.7. Construction and performance evaluation of prognostic nomogram

A prognostic nomogram was constructed using such parameters as age, sex, pathological patterns, overall staging, and the risk score of the predictive model to predict 3- and 5-year survival in individual NSCLC cases (see Fig. 9A). Further, the predictive performance of the nomogram was evaluated, and a calibration curve was created as shown in Figure 9B. The calibration curve represents the performance of an ideal prognostic nomogram, where 1-, 3-, and 5-year survival probabilities highly match with actual outcomes.

Construction and performance evaluation of nomogram. (A) Nomogram to predict 3- and 5-year survival in NSCLC patients. (B) Calibration curve to evaluate the predictive performance of the nomogram for 3- and 5-year survival in NSCLC patients. NSCLC = non-small cell lung cancer.
3.8. Gene set enrichment analyses

GSEA was performed to look further into potential differences between the high- and low-risk groups in mechanistic signaling pathways. The results revealed a predominance of tumor-related GnRH, Chemokine, ErbB, cAMP, and PPAR signaling pathways in the high-risk group; in the low-risk group, the GSEA showed enrichment for basal cell carcinoma, chemical carcinogenesis-DNA adducts, Hippo signaling pathway, Wnt signaling pathway, and breast cancer among all genes (see Supplementary Material 1, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R148).
3.9. Analysis of ICI in the TME

Numerous types of ICI in the TME were discussed in this study to analyze their associations with the risk score of the predictive model. A heatmap of immune cells showing different infiltration levels in the high- and low-risk groups was generated by integrating 7 algorithms, including TIMER, xCell, CIBERSORT, CIBERSORT-ABS, MCP-counter, quanTIseq, and EPIC (see Fig. 10). The TIMER algorithm suggested that the low-risk group had a significantly higher infiltration level of B cells but substantially lower infiltration levels of CD8+ T cells, neutrophils, and myeloid dendritic cells than the high-risk group.
Different types of immune cell infiltration (ICI) in the tumor microenvironment (TME) in the high- and low-risk groups. ICI = immune cell infiltration, TME = tumor microenvironment.

Given the importance of immune checkpoints in immunotherapy, this study also analyzed the associations between the risk score of the predictive model and the expression levels of 47 ICGs. As shown in Figure 11, BTLA, CD40LG, CD48, CD160, HHLA2, IDO2, and TNFRSF15 expression levels are significantly higher in the low-risk group; CD200, CD276, ICOSLG, NRP1, PDCD1LG2, TNFS4, TNFRSF8, and TNFRSF9 expression levels are significantly higher in the high-risk group.

The relationship between risk score and immune checkpoints. (A-O) The relationship between BTLA, CD40LG, CD48, CD160, CD200, CD276, HHLA2, ICOSLG, IDO2, NRP1, PDCD1LG2, TNFS4, TNFRSF8, and TNFRSF9 TNFRSF15 expression levels and low-/high-risk group.

The TIMER database was used for the analysis of potential associations of the 4 CRICGs for constructing the predictive model with different types of tumor-infiltrating immune cells in the TME, including B cells, CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and dendritic cells (see Fig. 12A-D).

Analysis of associations between the 4 CRICGs and 6 types of ICI in the TME based on the tumor immune estimation resource (TIMER) database. (A-D) Associations of CD209, HLA-DMB, SIRPA, and TNFRSF9 expression with ICI levels of B cells, CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and dendritic cells in the TME. CRICG = cuproptosis-related immune checkpoint gene, ICI = immune cell infiltration, TIMER = tumor immune estimation resource, TME = tumor microenvironment.
3.10. Screening for potential therapeutic agents and DST

Eight SMDs were deemed to be the most promising candidates in the analysis of SMDs associated with the 4 CRICGs of the predictive model using the Enrichr database, including Fucose TTD 00008125, Epichlorohydrin CTD 00005906, Maltotetraose BOSS, Styrene oxide CTD 00000717, Alpha-d-Mannose TTD 00001913, Benzene CTD 00005481, Pemetrexed CTD 00003054, and 6-Deoxy-d-galactose BOSS (see Table 1).
Eight small molecule drugs (SMDs) identified from the Enrichr database.

Drug susceptibility testing (DST) was conducted using the GDSC database to analyze potential differences between the 2 groups in susceptibility to 138 therapeutic agents. As shown in Figure 13, NSCLC is more susceptible to common targeted therapy and chemotherapy with erlotinib, gefitinib, PF.02341066 (crizotinib), BIBW2992 (afatinib), paclitaxel, docetaxel, gemcitabine, etoposide, and vinorelbine among the 11 most frequently used anticancer drugs. Moreover, the 50% inhibitory concentrations (IC50) were all higher in the high-risk group, suggesting higher resistance of NSCLC to these anticancer agents in the high-risk group.

Drug susceptibility testing (DST) in the high- and low-risk groups. (A-K) Differences between the high- and low-risk groups in susceptibility of NSCLC to targeted drugs including erlotinib, gefitinib, PF.02341066 (crizotinib), BIBW2992 (afatinib), and common chemotherapy drugs including paclitaxel, docetaxel, gemcitabine, etoposide, and vinorelbine. DST = drug susceptibility testing, NSCLC = non-small cell lung cancer.
4. Discussion

Lung cancer is the most common malignancy and the biggest cancer killer among men, and it is the second most prevalent and second leading cause of cancer deaths among women worldwide. Particularly, the vast majority of lung cancers are NSCLC. Given the recent breakthroughs achieved by the research on epidermal growth factor receptor-tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors, NSCLC patients are provided with a wider range of treatment options and demonstrate significantly improved survival probabilities. However, drug resistance remains a real challenge leading to treatment failures. This requires further studies on interactions and mechanisms of substances in the TME to discover more effective therapeutic targets and prognostic biomarkers.

Cuproptosis, as a novel form of cell death, is gaining traction among researchers. Ample evidence shows that in malignant tumors, copper accumulation is associated with tumor cell proliferation and growth, metastasis, and angiogenesis in the TME. Immune checkpoint blockade has been heatedly discussed as a robust denominator approach to cancer therapy targeting immune checkpoint pathways. Cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated antigen 4, programmed death 1 (PD-1), and programmed death-ligand 1 are most extensively studied among all inhibitory receptors. Anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated antigen 4 and PD-1/programmed death-ligand 1 antibodies like ipilimumab, pembrolizumab, and nivolumab have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for clinical application as immunotherapies. Despite the pronounced efficacy of such medications, there is still a large number of cancer patients who cannot benefit from immunotherapy. Therefore, it is essential to improve the diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of lung cancer patients with more effective biomarkers.

This study focused on the role of CRICGs that combined cuproptosis and ICGs in predicting the prognosis and guiding the treatment of patients with NSCLC. The associations between 13 CRGs and 79 ICGs from open-source databases were analyzed to determine the expression levels of CRICGs. After univariate Cox and LASSO regression analyses, 4 prognosis-related CRICGs were identified and used for constructing the predictive model. Among these CRICGs, CD209 expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells is shown to have a positive correlation with the treatment outcomes of patients with leukemic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma; TNFRSF9 expression in regulatory T cells is found to be associated with NSCLC patients' OS and response to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy, suggesting the immunomodulatory effect of TNFRSF9 on regulatory T cells in cancer patients; SIRPA expression is proved to have a strong association with the prognosis and metastasis of colorectal cancer; HLA-DMB in tumor cells is reported to play a role in the increase in tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells, and both are closely associated with the survival probabilities of patients with advanced serous ovarian cancer.

In this study, NSCLC samples were stratified by the median risk score into high- and low-risk groups for performance evaluation of the predictive model in combination with KM curves, ROC curves, and a validation dataset. Then, the risk score was validated as an independent prognostic factor for OS of NSCLC patients. A prognostic nomogram was constructed using the risk scores and clinical data such as age, and TNM staging, which demonstrated ideal performance in predicting 3- and 5-year survival in NSCLC patients. According to the median risk score, NSCLC patients were assigned to high- and low-risk groups, and the GSEA results suggested enrichment for tumor-related pathways among the CRICGs. The ICI analysis further revealed the differences in infiltration levels of several types of immune cells between the high and low-risk groups. Eight CRICG-targeting SMDs with therapeutic potential were identified from the Enrichr database. Finally, the DST data from the GDSC database showed that the high-risk group appeared to demonstrate higher resistance to the frequently used NSCLC-targeted drugs and chemotherapy.

The present study has the following limitations: it has not investigated the underlying mechanism of CRICGs regulating the biological behavior of NSCLC cells; multicenter clinical cohorts are required to validate the utility of the predictive model.
5. Conclusions

In conclusion, the predictive model based on 4 selected CRICGs can accurately predict the prognosis of NSCLC patients. With the risk score of the predictive model being an independent prognostic factor for OS, NSCLC patients differing in immune responses and drug reactions can be divided into high- and low-risk groups by the risk score, offering new insights as to the clinical treatment and prognosis of NSCLC.

passages.text: Olink Proteomic Profiling of Vitreous Humor and Plasma From Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy Patients Identifies a Novel Inflammatory Molecular Endotype
Purpose

To characterize proteomic profiles and underlying biological processes in vitreous humor and plasma of patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), diabetic patients without retinopathy (Non_DR), and non-diabetes mellitus patients (Non_DM), and to identify the molecular endotypes within PDR patients.
Methods

Proteomic profiling of paired vitreous humor and plasma samples from 47 PDR patients, 26 Non_DR patients, and 48 Non_DM patients were conducted with Olink platform. The Olink platform includes 13 panels targeting 1161 proteins. Gene set enrichment analysis was applied for enriched pathways, and the K-means clustering method was used to identify different PDR clusters based on vitreous proteomic profiles.
Results

Proteomic analysis revealed significant differences in the vitreous humor of PDR patients compared to those in the Non_DR or Non_DM groups, with elevation of carbonic anhydrase (CA) family members as potential contributors to PDR pathophysiology. Plasma samples from PDR group exhibited less profound differences in proteomic profiles compared to the other two groups. Clustering analysis of PDR vitreous samples identified three distinct clusters as molecular endotypes of PDR patients. Of those, Cluster 3 was characterized by enrichment in CCL/CXCL/IL6/IL18 chemokines and pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, which may contribute to more severe PDR phenotypes.
Conclusions

Significant differences in proteomic profiles were observed in PDR patients, especially in vitreous samples, with CA family members identified as potential therapeutic targets for PDR. Endotyping analysis of vitreous samples uncovered unique patient population with enriched CCL/CXCL/IL6/IL18 inflammatory pathways, highlighting the significance of local protein signature changes in PDR disease heterogeneity and its potential applications in patient stratification and therapeutic treatment.

Diabetic retinopathy (DR), a severe ocular complication of diabetes, poses a growing global healthcare burden because the worldwide prevalence of diabetes mellitus (DM) is approximately 14%, affecting an estimated 828 million adult patients in 2022. DR and its advanced stage, proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), affect approximately 34.6% and 6.96% of diabetic patients worldwide, respectively. In China, a recent meta-analysis reported prevalence estimates of about 23% for DR and 2.8% for PDR among diabetic patients. Longer duration of diabetes and worse glycemic control more likely lead to DR development.

PDR, characterized by pathological retinal neovascularization, may eventually cause severe vision loss or even blindness. Anti-VEGF therapy has supplanted pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) as the primary treatment modality for PDR. However, anti-VEGF therapy does not appear to improve retinal perfusion and may not prevent non-perfusion worsening or peripheral visual field loss. Novel therapies are required to address the unmet medical needs. Additionally, DR disease progression is a chronic and complicated process and PDR represents its ultimate and pivotal stage. Thus PDR patients are highly heterogenous in pathophysiology, clinical progression, and response to treatment. Exploration of PDR patient classification within the context of precision medicine will be of special significance in disease prognosis and treatment. High-risk PDR and non-high-risk PDR have been classified based on neovascularization size and the presence of hemorrhage in clinical practice. Immediate PRP or combination with other therapies such as anti-VEGF for eyes with high-risk PDR is recommended to reduce the risk of severe vision loss. Heterogeneity may significantly impact the PDR microenvironment. However, the relationship between intraocular proteomic profiles and clinical phenotypes, and their potential impact on treatment response or prognosis, remains unclear. A more comprehensive understanding of the proteomic changes associated with PDR disease progression, as well as the endotyping of PDR, is therefore crucial.

The vitreous humor, which reflects retinal pathophysiology, is one of the most widely used biofluids in PDR research. Disruption of the blood-retinal barrier in PDR allows the exchange of vitreous and plasma proteins. Thus exploring the proteomic landscape in plasma could potentially reflect pathological changes in retina and identify variations in the circulatory system. Existing proteomics studies have shed light on the pathways and biomarkers involved in angiogenesis, inflammation, oxidative stress, and cellular proliferation that potentially contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease. However, most of the current research relied on very limited sample size because of the difficulty in vitreous sample collection and primarily focused on either vitreous or plasma. Therefore a systematic evaluation of paired vitreous and plasma samples from a relatively large cohort of PDR patients will provide significant value in identifying novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets for PDR.

Previous proteomics studies in DR or PDR have predominantly relied on LC-MS as the detection method. Untargeted LC-MS is an unbiased profiling method with limitations in detecting low abundant proteins (ng/mL or even lower), which could play key roles as disease-specific biomarkers. Recent advances in protein quantification methods have enabled innovative and highly reliable approaches for high-throughput protein analysis. One of the most advanced platforms is the Olink platform using antibody-based proximity extension assay technology that has significantly advanced protein biomarker discovery. The Olink platform provides advantages in high specificity, high sensitivity, excellent scalability, and extremely low sample volume requirement (1 microL), which can greatly benefit operational feasibility for bio-samples like vitreous humor. The present study aims to investigate the underlying biological processes involved in both local and systemic pathologies of PDR and to uncover potential biomarkers and pathogenic pathways that may contribute to PDR progression.
Methods
Ethics

Human samples were collected with informed consent in accordance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. This study was approved by Novartis BioMedical Research and obtained ethical approval from the Ethics Committee/Institutional Review Board of Shanghai General Hospital with registration number [2020]264. All participants provided written informed consent, agreeing to the use of their clinical information and biological samples for research purposes.
Subject Enrollment and Sample Collection

A total of 131 patients who underwent vitrectomy as standard care between May 2018 and May 2019 at Shanghai General Hospital were enrolled in the study. The patients were grouped into three populations: The PDR group is our study-focused patient population, the Non_DR group included diabetic patients without diabetic retinopathy who underwent vitrectomy as control for PDR group, and the Non_DM group included non-diabetic patients who underwent vitrectomy as control for diabetics. In the Non_DR and Non_DM groups, the reasons for vitrectomy included rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, macular hole, retinoschisis, epiretinal membrane, vitreomacular traction syndrome, or vitreous hemorrhage. In the PDR group, indications for vitrectomy primarily included non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage (40 patients) and tractional retinal detachment involving or threatening the macula (seven patients).

Paired plasma and vitreous samples were collected from each patient before and during the surgery, respectively. Vitreous hemorrhage patients were present in all three groups. The cause of hemorrhage in control groups included as a result of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, traumatic retinal detachment, or polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy. Because hemorrhage is a major clinical endpoint for PDR patients and significantly contributes to PDR disease progression, hemorrhage patients were included in the study, except for two patients with retinal vein occlusion (RVO) in the Non_DM group, considering that hemorrhage from RVO patients typically occurs during the chronic stage and may significantly alter the vitreous proteomics. Vitreous sampling was performed by highly experienced surgeons, ensuring that samples were taken far from hemorrhage areas to avoid the interference of vitreous proteomics by direct leakage from hemorrhage. All samples were immediately flash-frozen and stored at -80 C until proteomic analysis. Plasma samples were also assessed for blood chemistry and hematological assessments. The samples from 10 patients were excluded from the analysis: two patients with RVO hemorrhage in the Non_DM group, three patients identified with very minimum retinopathy in the Non_DR group, and five patients received preoperative anti-VEGF treatment in the PDR groups. Thus 121 patients were included in the final analysis (47 PDR, 26 Non_DR, and 48 Non_DM).
Proteomic Profiling and Data Pre-Processing

Olink Target 96 platform was used to conduct proteomic profiling of the samples by antibody-based Proximity Extension Assay. The platform is composed of 13 panels (Cardiometabolic, Development, Cardiovascular II and III, Immune response, Inflammation, Metabolism, Neuro Exploratory, Neurology, Oncology II and III, Organ damage, and Cell regulation) devised to target a total number of 1161 proteins. Protein levels were quantified using normalized protein expression (NPX) value, which is in log2 scale. Sample quality control (QC) was performed by Olink's built-in system, which employed internal controls spiked into each sample. The sample QC was assessed by the deviation from the median of the controls of all samples in each panel. Samples with a deviation of less than 0.3 NPX from the median passed QC. Three plasma samples (1 Non_DR and 2 PDR) didn't pass the sample QC in more than half of the panels and were excluded. Data pre-processing was performed following Olink guidance, and limit of detection (LOD) was defined for each protein assay by Olink. Any protein with median NPX < (LOD + 1) in all samples was excluded from further analyses and defined as protein not detectable. For detectable proteins, all readouts below LOD were analyzed as LOD value. Because there is no housekeeping protein included in the Olink 96 platform, an internal protein normalization analysis was not feasible.
Proteomic Analysis

Proteomic analysis was performed by ANOVA with the built-in package Olink Analyze Vignette. Age and gender were considered as covariates in the analysis. Proteins with adjusted P value <= 0.05 and llog2(fold-change)l >= 0.5 were identified as significantly altered proteins. Benjamini-Hochberg method was used for multiple comparison adjustment.
Pathway and Network Analysis

Pathway analysis was conducted using gene set enrichment analysis with the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database to identify significantly (P <= 0.05) enriched pathways. For overlapping proteins, overrepresentation analysis was performed using the DAVID web platform. Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis was applied to explore functional interactions and identify key signaling networks.
PDR Clustering Analysis

K-means clustering method was used to identify clusters in PDR group based on the proteomic profiles from vitreous samples. One PDR patient has 67 undetectable proteins and was excluded from clustering analysis.
Statistical Analysis

Patient characteristics were analyzed using R packages (R 4.2.1) with statistical tests selected based on data normality. For comparisons among three groups, one-way ANOVA or the Kruskal-Wallis test was applied. For comparisons between two groups, the two tailed Student's t-test or the Mann-Whitney test was applied, accordingly. Pearson's correlation model was used to assess the correlation between plasma and vitreous, using data from the Non_DR and PDR groups. A significant threshold of P <= 0.05 was used for all tests.
Results
Participant Characteristics

The workflow of the present study is shown in the flow chart (Fig. 1). Paired vitreous humor and plasma samples from 131 patients were collected, of which samples from 121 patients were included in the analysis. Proteomic profiling of all samples was conducted by the Olink 96 platform, targeting 13 panels of 1161 proteins. In total, 695 proteins in vitreous hum and 909 proteins in plasma were detected and included in subsequent analysis.
Flow chart of the study design.

The demographic and clinical characteristics of participants among PDR, Non_DR and Non_DM groups are shown in Tables 1 and 2. Overall, the proportion of females was slightly higher than that of males across all groups without statistical significance. The PDR group exhibited the youngest age distribution. It is noted in the previous study that PDR was more severe in younger patients than in older patients. Because all PDR patients in our study required vitrectomy, which may indicate more-severe PDR, this could contribute to the relatively younger age in the PDR group. Significant elevations in blood glucose, hemoglobin A1C, and blood urea nitrogen levels were found in the Non_DR and PDR groups compared to the Non_DM group, consistent with the metabolic dysregulation associated with diabetes and renal dysfunction (Table 2).

Proteomic Profiles in PDR Vitreous and Plasma

The difference between each two groups in vitreous (Fig. 2) and plasma (Fig. 3) proteomics were analyzed. Despite no significant change being identified between Non_DM and Non_DR in vitreous (Fig. 2A), 574 and 518 proteins were significantly changed in PDR compared to Non_DR and Non_DM, respectively (Fig. 2A, Supplementary Fig. S1), in which 514 significantly altered proteins were shared in both comparisons (Fig. 2B). Most significantly altered proteins showed elevated levels in PDR vitreous compared with controls, with only a few exhibiting decreased levels, which emphasized dominant activation of disease-related proteomic changes in PDR. We therefore focused on the difference between the PDR and Non_DR groups in the following analyses to identify proteins potentially linked to the progression of diabetic retinopathy.

Proteomic analyses of PDR, Non_DR, and Non_DM vitreous. (A) Volcano plot showing significantly altered proteins in each comparison among three groups. The significantly altered proteins are colored in orange (Increased) or blue (Decreased) (cut-off: adjusted P <= 0.05 and llog2(fold-change)l >= 0.5). (B) Venn diagram presenting the overlapping number of significantly altered proteins between PDR versus Non_DM and PDR versus Non_DR. (C) Enriched KEGG pathways in PDR versus Non_DR by gene set enrichment analysis. Significant pathways are labeled with * (P <= 0.05). (D) Heatmap of top 20 significantly altered proteins (PDR vs. Non_DR) among three groups. The proteins are ranked by the value of log2(fold-change). NES, normalized enrichment score.

Proteomic analyses of PDR, Non_DR, and Non_DM plasma. (A) Volcano plot showing significantly altered proteins in each comparison among three groups. The significantly altered proteins are colored in orange (increased) or blue (decreased) (cut-off: adjusted P <= 0.05 and llog2(fold-change)l >= 0.5). (B) Venn diagram presenting the overlapping number of significantly altered proteins between PDR vs. Non_DM and PDR vs. Non_DR. (C) Enriched KEGG pathways in PDR vs. Non_DR by gene set enrichment analysis. Significant pathways are labeled with * (P <= 0.05). (D) Heatmap of top 20 significantly altered proteins (PDR vs. Non_DR) among three groups. The proteins are ranked by the value of log2(fold-change).

Widely reported PDR-associated proteins (e.g. VEGFA, PGF, and EPO) were found at significantly higher levels in the PDR vitreous compared to Non_DR (Supplementary Fig. S2). Pathway enrichment analysis between PDR and Non_DR indicated that chemokine signaling pathway, focal adhesion, complement and coagulation cascades and extracellular matrix receptor interaction were significantly increased in the PDR vitreous (Fig. 2C), consistent with the fact that angiogenesis, inflammation, and fibrosis are overrepresented in PDR. The top 20 significantly elevated proteins in PDR vitreous were identified as CA1, CA3, 4E-BP1, BLVRB, HO-1, PGF, CA2, DEFA1, CRKL, CD2AP, PGF, ADA, EPO, MB, CCL13, TGM2, FCN2, CASP-3, XG, and MBP-C (Fig. 2D), including factors with reported functions in angiogenesis and immune response.

The plasma proteomics showed less profound differences in PDR group. Specifically, 137 and 200 significantly altered proteins were identified in PDR plasma, compared to Non_DR and Non_DM groups, respectively (Fig. 3A, Supplementary Fig. S1B). Similar to vitreous, no notable disparities were observed between Non_DM and Non_DR groups (Fig. 3A). A total of 119 significantly altered proteins were commonly identified in both comparisons (Fig. 3B). GSEA analysis did not enrich any significantly increased pathway. A few pathways were significantly decreased in PDR plasma, including ERBB pathway, neurotrophin pathway, and regulation of cytoskeleton (Fig. 3C). The top 20 significantly altered proteins, including GH, NT-proBNP, KLK4, IGFBP-2, KRT19, MBP-C, NEFL, REG1A, PSG1, EDA2R, LAYN, Dkk-4, IL17C, SPINK1, SCARB2, TNFRSF19, GT, TFF3, CLEC7A, and CADM3, exhibited elevated levels in PDR compared to Non_DR (Fig. 3D). The less profound difference in PDR plasma indicates that PDR-related proteomic changes could be primarily localized rather than systemic. Considering the patients in the PDR group had strict glycemic control before surgery, this may have also attenuated systemic proteomic alterations at the time of surgery.
Circulating and Local Pathogenic Molecular Profiling in PDR

Paired vitreous and plasma analysis can reveal the proteomic changes transiting from circulation to the microvascular and vitreous ecosystem. There were 95 proteins significantly elevated in both PDR vitreous and plasma compared to the Non_DR group (Fig. 4A). Only cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and Wnt signaling pathway were significantly enriched from the overlapped proteins (Fig. 4B). To identify potential plasma biomarkers associated with disease pathophysiology, we conducted correlation analysis of the top 20 significant proteins in plasma to assess their correlations with vitreous. NT-proBNP, GH, REG1A, TNFRSF19, and SCARB2 showed significantly strong or moderate correlations between plasma and vitreous (P <= 0.001 and Pearson's r >= 0.6 or 0.4; Fig. 4C). NT-proBNP is a known biomarker for heart failure, and high-level NT-proBNP has been shown to associate with diabetes-related microvascular and macrovascular complications. GH was reported to stimulate the proliferation of retinal microvascular endothelial cells and promote neoangiogenesis in PDR. REG1A was reported as diabetic renal biomarker. These discoveries provided evidence that a particular or a panel of proteins could serve as biomarkers associated with disease pathophysiology. The transition of these molecules between circulation and vitreous indicates their potential involvement in the onset and development of PDR. Further validation study of these candidates could identify potential plasma biomarkers as a single or a panel of proteins. In contrast, LAYN, a fibrosis-related marker associated with progression of kidney failure in diabetes was elevated in PDR patients solely in plasma but not in vitreous, suggesting its systemic role as diabetic dysfunction biomarker without association with PDR.

Correlation between significantly altered proteins in plasma and vitreous. (A) Venn diagram presenting the overlapping number of significantly increased proteins (PDR vs. Non_DR) between vitreous and plasma. (B) KEGG pathways enriched from 95 overlapping significantly altered proteins by over representation pathway analysis. Significant pathways are labeled with * (P <= 0.05). (C) Correlation between plasma and vitreous for the top 20 significantly altered proteins in plasma (PDR vs. Non_DR). The log2(fold-change) and significance in either plasma or vitreous, the Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) and significance between plasma and vitreous, and if it is overlapping significant proteins between plasma and vitreous (Overlap, Yes or No; "-", not detectable) are shown in the table. (D) Boxplot showing protein levels of CA isoforms among three groups. Significant difference between groups is labeled as ***: adjusted P <= 0.001; **: adjusted P <= 0.01; *: adjusted P <= 0.05. log2(fc): log2(fold-change); adj P value: adjusted P value.

Within the 573 proteins significantly increased in PDR vitreous, 478 were only significantly elevated in vitreous, but not in plasma (Fig. 4A), implying much more complicated local pathophysiological changes in PDR. Notably, we found significant elevation of CA family members in PDR (Fig. 4D), including CA1, CA2, CA3, CA9, and CA14. CA1 and CA3 were the top two significantly elevated proteins in PDR vitreous (Fig. 2D and Supplementary Fig. S2A). CA1 and CA2 levels were dramatically increased in PDR vitreous but not in plasma. CA3, CA9, and CA14 were significantly elevated in both vitreous and plasma of PDR patients, with CA3 and CA9 showing a more pronounced increase in vitreous than in plasma. While CA12 showed significant increase in PDR plasma, it was undetectable in vitreous (Fig. 4D). Among the CA family members, only CA6 is secreted isoform, which was unfortunately undetectable in vitreous and unchanged in plasma. CA1, CA2 and CA3 are cytosolic isoforms, and CA4, CA9 and CA14 are membrane associated isoforms. Thus, elevation of these non-secreted isoforms of carbonic anhydrases in PDR vitreous potentially came from cell injury and release of the cytosolic and membrane-associated carbonic anhydrases into vitreous. Different CA isoforms have been reported in choriocapillaris, retinal pigment epithelium, Muller cells, as well as astrocytes. However, their expression across different retinal cell types requires further investigation. CA1 has been reported to be associated with diabetic retinopathy. The discovery of elevated carbonic anhydrases in the PDR vitreous shed light on the potential contribution of CA family in PDR pathogenesis.
CCL/CXCL/IL6/IL18 Inflammation Molecular Endotype Identified in PDR Vitreous

To enhance our understanding of the molecular heterogeneity of PDR, we used the K-means clustering method to identify molecular variations within PDR patients. Three distinct subgroups were automatically clustered based on the vitreous proteomic profiles (Cluster 1-3; Fig. 5A). To further understand the protein-level differences that distinguish the three clusters, proteomic comparisons between each pair of clusters were conducted. There were a substantial number of significantly increased proteins in Cluster 2 (603) and Cluster 3 (603) compared to Cluster 1. There were 232 proteins significantly increased in Cluster 3 compared to Cluster 2 (Fig. 5B). Among which, 209 proteins overlapped across the three comparisons, and exhibited an ascending gradient from Non_DR, Cluster 1, Cluster 2 to Cluster 3 (Fig. 5C). Interestingly, the known PDR-associated cytokines, VEGFA, PGF, and EPO, were also significantly increased from Non_DR to Cluster 1-3 (Supplementary Fig. S3A), indicating that Cluster 3 could be a progressive or more severe disease subgroup in PDR.

Endotyping analysis in PDR patients. (A) Three PDR clusters identified by K-means clustering based on vitreous proteins. (B) Venn diagram presenting the overlapping number of significantly increased proteins in each comparison among three PDR clusters. (C) Heatmap of 209 overlapping significantly altered proteins among three PDR clusters. (D) KEGG pathways enriched from 209 overlapping significantly altered proteins by over representation pathway analysis. Significant pathways are labeled with * (P <= 0.05). (E) PPI networks in each comparison among three PDR clusters. The 15 core PPI network proteins are marked as red. (F) Heatmap of 15 core PPI network proteins in Non_DR group and three PDR clusters.

Pathways in immune responses were highly enriched in the 209 overlapping proteins, including cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, chemokine signaling pathway, TNF signaling pathway, IL-17 signaling pathway, et al, (Fig. 5D), highlighting the prominent inflammatory response in Cluster 3. To further elucidate the molecular signatures across clusters, we performed PPI analysis using the top 100 significantly increased proteins identified in each pairwise comparison (Fig. 5E). Almost identical core PPI networks stood out from Cluster 3 versus Cluster 2 and Cluster 3 versus Cluster 1 network analysis, including a panel of 15 inflammatory cytokines (i.e., CCL3, CCL8, CCL13, CCL19, CCL20, CXCL1, CXCL5, CXCL6, CXCL8, CXCL9, CXCL10, CXCL11, CXCL13, IL6, and IL18), with an increased trend from Non_DR group to PDR Cluster 1-3 (Figs. 5E, 5F). CCL8, CCL13, CCL19, CCL20, CXCL1, CXCL5, CXCL10, CXCL13, and IL6 were also present in the PPI of Cluster 2 versus Cluster 1 network analysis. These collectively suggested a dominantly elevated core CCL/CXCL/IL6/IL18 inflammation pathway in Cluster 3, which could serve as a molecular signature to grade inflammatory progression of DR, and Cluster 3 could be considered as a distinct subgroup characterized with severe inflammation activation. No significant difference was found in plasma proteins among the three clusters in PDR (data not shown), indicating that such pathophysiological endotyping of PDR is unlikely to be distinguished by circulating protein biomarkers.
Discussion

Our study used the Olink proteomic platform to profile paired vitreous and plasma samples from PDR patients, in comparison to the Non_DR and Non_DM control groups. Profiling of the vitreous samples revealed that widely reported PDR associated cytokines VEGFA, PGF and EPO were at significantly higher levels in the PDR. Additional PDR associated proteins were identified, among which the protein levels of a panel of intracellular or membranous carbonic anhydrases (CA1, CA2, CA3, CA9, and CA14) were significantly elevated in PDR vitreous compared to Non_DR. The CA family consists of 15 distinct isoforms, each exhibiting unique structural and functional properties. Although many studies have documented the involvement of carbonic anhydrases in glaucoma and macular edema, their contribution in PDR is still largely unknown. PDR progression is characterized by pathological complications including vitreous hemorrhage and release of intracellular proteins into the vitreous humor, underscoring the pathological significance of protein leakage in ocular diseases. It was reported that CA1 and CA2 were elevated in PDR patients and intravitreous injection of CA1 in rats increased retinal vessel leakage and caused intraretinal edema. Although studies on CA3 and CA9 in DR are limited, CA3 is believed to play a protective role in oxidative stress and CA9 can be induced by hypoxia and is associated with proliferation, migration, invasion, and metastasis of cancer cells. Dorzolamide, a topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, has been validated in the treatment of glaucoma and cystoid macular edema associated with diabetic macular edema, retinitis pigmentosa, and choroidal vascular disorders. The effect of dorzolamide has also been investigated in DR and PDR patients in an investigator-initiated trial and most treated patients reported satisfactory outcomes with sustained positive functional vision. In particular, PDR patients who received combined therapy of dorzolamide with anti-VEGF or laser retinal photocoagulation revealed minor improvement in OCT and retinal biomicroscopic examination, despite retinal state remaining stable in the dorzolamide only group. The discovery in our study provided additional evidence that altered carbonic anhydrase could play a significant role in PDR, given its known effects on retinal fluid dynamics and metabolic homeostasis. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition may offer adjunctive benefits in PDR, particularly in cases with coexisting macular edema. Further investigation is warranted to determine whether and how vitreous carbonic anhydrases are involved in the onset and progression of PDR.

Proteomic endotyping analysis in PDR population revealed a unique PDR subgroup (Cluster 3) that exhibited elevation of inflammatory pathways and is potentially associated with a more severe disease phenotype. A core PPI network of 15 cytokines including CCL and CXCL chemokines and proinflammatory cytokines IL6 and IL18 was identified in the Cluster 3 PPI networks, suggesting an active immune cell recruitment in Cluster 3 PDR patients and strong inflammatory response. Interestingly, an increased trend from Non_DR to PDR Cluster 1 to Cluster 3 was observed not only for the 15 inflammatory panels (Fig. 5F), but also for the known PDR-associated cytokines (Supplementary Fig. S3A) and 209 significant proteins among Clusters 1, 2, and 3 (Fig. 5C). We hypothesize that the three molecular endotypes identified in this study may represent three different stages in the activation of PDR-associated signaling pathways, with Cluster 3 as the most advanced endotype.

Elevated levels of IL6 and IL18 in the vitreous have been reported to be associated with active PDR. IL6 is a critical factor in vascular inflammation in DR. IL18 may contribute to retinal angiogenesis, via VEGF-dependent or -independent signaling pathways. Interestingly, IL6 and IL18 differ in their protein profiles. Although IL6 was already high in Cluster 2, IL18 elevation was only evident in Cluster 3, suggesting the two key proinflammatory cytokines may play different roles in disease progression (Fig. 5E, Supplementary Fig. S3B). This could come from different types of immune cells recruited to the lesion at different stages, as suggested by the chemokine protein levels in the PPI network. Notably, neutrophil and T-cell chemokines (CXCL5, CXCL10) were already present in Cluster 2 versus the Cluster 1 PPI network, whereas macrophage (CCL3) and dendritic cell (CCL19, CCL20) chemokines were only present in the Cluster 3 PPI networks.

We recognize that there are limitations in the study. The 13 panels in Olink 96 platform may not fully represent the protein landscape of vitreous and plasma. The control of vitreous samples was not derived from entirely normal eyes but from patients experienced vitrectomy with other ocular conditions. Some of them may involve blood-retinal barrier breakdown and local pathological changes that could influence the vitreous proteomics. However, given the ethical and practical constraints in obtaining normal vitreous, this approach represents the most feasible clinical samples for the control groups. Although vitreous sample collection was away from the site of hemorrhage, the presence of vitreous hemorrhage may alter the proteomic composition of vitreous. Therefore the potential impact of hemorrhage on vitreous proteomics should be considered when interpreting our findings. These are also single event-based sample collections, which may or may not fully capture the temporal changes that occur during disease progression. The discoveries will need to be further validated with orthogonal analyses and independent PDR cohorts.

In summary, Olink profiling of vitreous samples and plasma revealed proteomic changes in PDR patients, which emphasized the local rather than systemic changes in proteomic profiles. A panel of CA family members was identified as potential contributors to PDR disease progression at different stages of PDR. Additionally, molecular endotyping within the PDR group identified a cluster characterized by the enrichment of CCL/CXCL/IL6/IL18 inflammatory pathways. The significantly altered proteins and molecular endotyping offer valuable insights into the underlying molecular mechanisms of PDR and may aid in the discovery of potential new therapies.
