passages.text: Previous generations of chromeno-pyridine-based inhibitors have demonstrated noteworthy anticancer potential; however, many of these molecules were limited by inadequate dual-target engagement, weak selectivity, and insufficient structural features to overcome EGFR- or HER2-driven resistance mechanisms. To address these shortcomings, the compounds investigated in the present study incorporate strategically designed structural modifications, including improved heteroatom positioning, electron-modulating substituents, and enhanced aromatic extensions that strengthen their ability to anchor deeply within the ATP-binding clefts of both EGFR and HER2. These refinements increase molecular planarity, broaden aromatic surface area, and promote stronger pi-pi stacking and hydrophobic stabilization with conserved residues. By integrating these features into a benzo-fused chromeno[3,4-c]pyridine scaffold, the present study aims to generate inhibitors with superior dual-target affinity, enhanced selectivity, and reduced susceptibility to common resistance mechanisms thereby offering a more promising platform for the development of next-generation EGFR/HER2 therapies.
Methods
Experimental

The synthesis and spectroscopic characterization (FT-IR, 1H-NMR, and 13C-NMR) of the (benzo)chromeno[3,4-c]pyridine derivative used in this study were adopted from the previously reported procedure by Thabet et al.. Briefly, the target compound was obtained through a multicomponent reaction involving dicyanomethane or ethyl cyanoacetate and compound 14 in accordance with the described synthetic protocol. The reaction mechanism involves a Michael addition of the activated methylene group to the electron-deficient double bond of compound 14, generating intermediates A and A'. Subsequent intramolecular nucleophilic attack of the amino group on a cyano moiety promotes cyclization, followed by tautomeric rearrangement and oxidative aromatization to yield the (benzo)chromeno[3,4-c]pyridine core. Hydrogens lost during the oxidative step are highlighted in the supplementary information (Figure S1). Spectroscopic confirmation reported by Thabet et al. showed characteristic FT-IR absorptions for C N ( 2220 cm-1), C = O ( 1730 cm-1), and aromatic C-H stretching ( 3060 cm-1). The 1H and 13C NMR spectra further supported the formation of the fused heterocyclic framework. These experimentally verified structural data were used as the basis for the computational analyses performed in the present study.
Molecular docking details

Molecular docking was performed to evaluate the binding interactions between the synthesized (benzo)chromeno[3,4-c]pyridine derivative and selected HER-family cancer-related receptor proteins. Protein preparation was carried out using BIOVIA Discovery Studio 2021. The receptor structures were downloaded from the Research Collaboratory for Structural Bioinformatics (RCSB) Protein Data Bank (PDB). During preparation, the active site region was defined to guide ligand placement and enable possible interactions within catalytic and allosteric regions capable of modulating receptor function. All crystallographic water molecules and co-crystallized ligands were removed to avoid interference during docking, and polar hydrogens were added to improve interaction accuracy. The refined structures were saved in PDB format. The optimized ligand geometry was generated using GaussView 6.0, and energy-minimized coordinates were exported in PDB format for docking analysis. Docking simulations were performed using AutoDock Vina, with grid boxes centered around the functional domains of each receptor. The grid center coordinates used for the docking runs were:with the exhaustiveness of 8 respectively. These coordinates ensured adequate sampling of the active site cavities and neighboring interaction hotspots. Following docking, 2D and 3D interaction diagrams (in Fig. 7a and b respectively) were generated using BIOVIA Discovery Studio 2021 and PyMOL for visualization and interpretation of binding modes.
Protein selection
The crystal structure of the selected protein as well as the studies compound (ligand) showing the atomic constitution.

Three HER-family protein structures (PDB IDs: 3PP0, 3RCD, and 4HRN) were selected based on their critical roles in oncogenic signaling, drug resistance, and targeted therapy development. These structures were retrieved from the Protein Data Bank with crystallographic resolutions of 2.25 A (3PP0), 3.21 A (3RCD), and 2.62 A (4HRN). High-quality structures (<= 2.5 A) typically yield more reliable docking interactions because they provide better-defined atomic positions and clearer electron-density maps, thereby enhancing binding accuracy. 3PP0 represents the wild-type EGFR tyrosine kinase domain in complex with the inhibitor lapatinib. 3RCD corresponds to a wild-type HER2 kinase domain co-crystallized with a dual EGFR/HER2 inhibitor. HER2 overexpression or amplification is a major driver of aggressive breast cancer subtypes and has also been reported in subsets of NSCLC. Because HER2 shares more than 80% structural similarity with EGFR in the ATP-binding site, dual inhibition is often required when tumors develop bypass activation through HER2 upregulation. Thus, 3RCD provides a well-characterized structural template for evaluating dual-targeted inhibition. 4HRN represents the HER2 receptor tyrosine kinase domain (wild-type) and is especially valuable for studying ligand interactions that stabilize the inactive conformation of the receptor. Altogether, these three protein structures capture the functional diversity and therapeutic relevance of the EGFR/HER2 signaling axis. Their involvement in tumor progression, acquired resistance to first-, second-, and even third-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and their high validation as drug targets justify their selection for structure-based virtual screening and binding affinity evaluation. Each protein structure was inspected for missing residues, incomplete chains, and steric clashes. Co-crystallized ligands, ions, and water molecules were removed, except those required for structural stability. Polar hydrogens were added, and Gasteiger charges were assigned using AutoDockTools. The processed structures were then saved in PDBQT format for docking simulations (Fig. 1).
ADMET profiling

ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity) analyses were performed to evaluate the pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles of the compound was evaluated using online web servers ADMElab 3.0. for ADME (i.e. absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) studies. Toxicity endpoints were predicted using Protox-II (version 3.0). While SwissADME was used to determine physicochemical properties, lipophilicity, hydrogen-bonding characteristics, and drug-likeness scores. The optimized molecular structure was converted to SMILES format using ChemCraft. The corresponding SMILES codes (Table 7) were uploaded into both platforms. Predicted ADMET descriptors including gastrointestinal absorption, blood-brain barrier permeability, cytochrome P450 enzyme interactions, water solubility, bioavailability score, and toxicity class were recorded and evaluated to determine suitability for potential drug development.

passages.text: Computational details

All quantum chemical calculations were performed using density functional theory (DFT) at the omegaB97XD/6-311++G(d,p) level to optimize the molecular geometry and evaluate electronic properties. The method (omegaB97X-D) was chosen because it provides a more accurate treatment of long-range interactions and dispersion forces unlike traditional hybrids like B3LYP, which often underestimate such effects. omegaB97X-D offers a more reliable and well-validated level of theory for the electronic structure and interaction analyses required in this study. Geometry optimization and molecular property calculations were carried out using Gaussian 09, with GaussView 6.0 used for visualization and modeling. Frontier molecular orbital (FMO) analysis was conducted to determine chemical reactivity and stability based on HOMO and LUMO energy levels. Natural bond orbital (NBO 3.0), analysis, as implemented in Gaussian, was used to assess charge distribution and intramolecular electron delocalization. Additional spectral analyses (NMR and FT-IR) were used to correlate computed molecular features with experimentally observed functional groups.

passages.text: Overlay of the study compound's 3D geometries optimized in gas phase and in the solvents water, cyclohexane, and tetrahydrofuran (THF).

Geometry optimization is a computational method deployed to determine the most stable arrangement of atoms in a molecule. This process involves adjusting the positions of atoms iteratively to minimize the molecule's energy, which results in a structure where forces on each atom are balanced, and the molecular system is at a local or global energy minimum. The study is an essential step that provides insight into the molecular structure, stability, and reactivity of compounds. The functional groups present in a compound play significant roles in determining its molecular behavior. The values presented in Table 1 show a comparison of bond lengths and bond angles for (benzo)chromeno[3,4-c]pyridine derivative in various solvents (cyclohexane, gas, tetrahydrofuran (THF), and water). This provides information on how solvation affects molecular structure (see Fig. 2). Key bonds such as C-C, C-H, C-O, and C-N were examined in the various solvents. C-C Bond: The C4-C8 bond length remained almost constant across all solvents, ranging from 1.394 to 1.397 A. This suggests that the core conjugated system is stable regardless of solvent polarity.

C-H Bond: The C3-H7 bond length also remained unchanged at 1.085 A in all environments, indicating that there is negligible solvent influence on localized C-H interactions. C-O Bond: There was a slight elongation in the bond length at the C49-O68, increasing from 1.206 A in the gas phase to 1.216 A in water, which suggests stabilization of oxygen lone pairs through dipole-dipole interactions. C-N Bond: The C49-N56 bond length showed a slight variation, with a maximum of 1.439 A in the gas phase and a minimum of 1.424 A in water; this slight variation reflects solvent-induced electronic effects. The bond angles across the different solvents exhibited slight variations. From Table 1, key bond angles were examined across the different solvents, such as C-C-C, C-H-C, C-O-C, and C-N-C. C-C-C Bond Angle: The C4-C8-C11 bond angle is widest in cyclohexane with 121.133  and the smallest in the gas phase with 120.859 , this slight variation indicates a solvent-induced flexibility. C-H-C Bond Angle: The C3-H7-C1 bond angle remained almost unchanged, with bond angles ranging from 34.124  to 34.192 , reinforcing the minimal impact of solvent polarity on local bond geometry. C-O-C Bond Angle: The C49-O68-C47 bond angle remained relatively small across all solvents, with a slight observed increase in THF due to minor angular relaxation from solvent interactions. C-N-C Bond Angle: The C49-N56-C50 bond angle exhibited minimal variations, with the largest value in the gas phase, 124.036 , and the smallest bond angle in THF, 123.998 . This suggests solvent stabilization effects on nitrogen. The results from the geometry optimization revealed that the compound exhibited a solvent-dependent variation, with the variations particularly in bonds involving electronegative atoms like oxygen and nitrogen. Polar solvents such as water and THF induced slight bond length contractions and angular adjustments due to enhanced solute-solvent interactions. These findings align with previous research on similar heterocyclic systems, which highlights the role of solvation effects in modulating molecular conformation and electronic properties.

Herein, the comparison between the experimental and theoretical as presented in Table 2 results provides deeper insight into the vibrational characteristics and functional groups present in the synthesized (benzo)chromeno[3,4-c]pyridine derivative. C N (cyanide) functional group, the experimental frequency was observed at 2226 cm-1, while the theoretical calculations predict slightly higher values at 2359.53 and 2359.91 cm-1. passages.text: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a powerful analytical technique in computational analysis used to determine the structural and electronic environments of molecules in a compound. NMR provides detailed information on the arrangement of atoms, functional groups, and molecular interactions in a system. By comparing the experimental and theoretical NMR values, researchers can validate computational models and gain insights into molecular behavior. NMR Analysis was carried out both experimentally and theoretically for 1H and 13C proton spectroscopic shifts of the studied compound, (benzo)chromeno[3,4-c] pyridine derivative. The results of the various chemical shifts were computed accordingly and presented in Table 3. The analysis of the NMR spectra of (benzo)chromeno[3,4-c] pyridine derivative showed a strong correlation between the experimental and theoretical values, this correlation demonstrates the reliability of computational methods in the prediction of chemical environments. From Table 3, the experimental 1H NMR data for the chromeno[3,4-b] benzene scaffold showed characteristic signals at 3.86 ppm (2H, s, CH2), 6.98 ppm (2H, s, NH2), 7.20-7.89 ppm (various ArH peaks), and 9.79 ppm (2H, s, NH). In other hand, the theoretical calculation was able to provide comparable values with H53 at 7.375 ppm, H55 at 7.385 ppm, and H52 at 7.702 ppm. Similarly, on the other scaffold (pyridopyran scaffold), the experimental 1H shifts aligned with the theoretical calculation, with H5 at 7.168 ppm, H7 at 7.489 ppm, and H9 at 7.843 ppm. This strong correlation between the experimental and theoretical results confirms that computational methods effectively capture the electronic environment of protons in the studied compound. The little observable deviations can be attributed to solvation effects, hydrogen bonding, and minor conformational differences in experimental conditions compared to theoretical calculations.

The experimental 13C NMR values for chromeno[3,4-b] benzene showed the following peaks: 26.6, 75.2, 110.4, 116.4, 126.6, 127.6, 128.5, 130.8, 135.7, 153.2, 157.9, 162.3, and 162.4 ppm. The theoretical 13C NMR values closely correlated with the experimental values, with C46 at 127.95 ppm, C44 at 130.47 ppm, and C40 at 132.54 ppm. For the pyridopyran scaffold, it was observed that the experimental values at C2 125.79 ppm, C4 126.39 ppm, and C6 128.07 ppm closely match the theoretical calculations. From the experimental and theoretical values, the observed correlation shows that the computational chemistry approach is reliable in predicting 13C NMR chemical shifts. The minor differences observed are attributed to solvent interactions, basis set limitations, and dynamic effects in solution-phase NMR experiments. Previous studies on similar heterocyclic frameworks, such as pyridopyrans and chromenopyridines, have reported comparable trends in NMR shift predictions using density functional theory (DFT). Literature findings indicate that DFT-based calculations often show deviations within a range of 0.2-0.5 ppm for 1H and 1-3 ppm for 13C shifts. Going by this range, the observed differences in Table 3, falls within that range. The consistency observed in the NMR analysis shows the stability of the compound in the chemical environments.

Frontier molecular orbital analysis
Visualization of the frontier molecular orbitals (HOMO and LUMO) of the studied compound, highlighting regions involved in electron redistribution.

Frontier molecular orbital (FMO) is a computational technique that offers data for explaining the molecular properties of compounds. The calculated energies of the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and that of lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) along with their energy gap and other global descriptors such as Ionization Potential (IP) and Electron Affinity (EA), Chemical Hardness (eta), Softness (Sigma), Electronegativity (-mu), Electrophilicity (Omega), and Fermi Level (EFL) provide insights into the behavior of a compound(s) whether reactive or stable. HOMO is an electron-rich region with a tendency to donate electrons, higher HOMO value (less negative) suggests a strong electron-donating ability, while LUMO, situated above the electron-rich region, is vacant and tends to accept electrons from HOMO as can be seen in Fig. 4 electrons move from HOMO to LUMO. The energy gap, which is the difference between these HOMO and LUMO two values, plays a crucial role in determining the compound's reactivity and stability. A lower energy gap signifies higher reactivity, whereas a higher energy gap suggests the compound's stability. Among the compounds evaluated, water was observed to have highest energy gap of 4.35 eV, making it the most stable. This stability is essential in biological systems, as water serves as a universal solvent, facilitating biochemical reactions. Its high stability ensures that it does not interfere with cellular functions, making it a vital component of all living organisms.

Natural Bond Orbital (NBO) analysis is a computational approach used to describe the electronic structure of molecules. The approach helps in providing insights into several electronic properties such as electron density distribution and the charge transfer between bonding (sigma) and antibonding (sigma*) orbitals, which significantly influence molecular stability. These interactions significantly influence the stability of molecules and are quantified using the second-order perturbation energy (E2). In the donor and acceptor interaction framework, electron donor (i) and acceptor (j) orbitals are identified based on interactions between bonding and antibonding orbitals. These interactions are primarily responsible for charge transfer between atoms or molecular fragments. The second-order perturbation energy is calculated using the equation below:where Fij represents the off-diagonal Fock matrix element, E(i):E(j) are the diagonal elements, and E(2) represent the second order perturbation energy of the chemical system. According to previous Literature, higher values of E(2) correspond to stronger interactions between the donor and acceptor orbitals, which have a direct impact on the molecular stability and adsorption properties. The NBO analysis of (benzo)chromeno[3,4-c] pyridine derivative in different solvents (cyclohexane, gas, THF, and water) in Table 5 provides critical insight into their stability and electronic interactions. The results from the NBO analysis showed variation in the donor-acceptor interaction, which influences the molecule's behavior in different environments, a crucial aspect for drug development.

The compound's strong stabilization in non-polar solvents is an indication of good lipophilicity, which is a favorable characteristic of substances capable of crossing cell membranes. Also, the moderate stabilization in polar solvents implies that the compound may have reasonable aqueous solubility, though potential formulation enhancements such as prodrug approaches or nanoparticle delivery systems may be needed to optimize the compound for drug delivery. Molecular electrostatic Surface potential analysis
Visualized molecular electrostatic potential (MESP) distributions for the investigated compounds.

The Molecular Electrostatic Surface Potential (MESP) provides a graphical representation of the charge distribution within a molecule and is useful for identifying potential sites of electrophilic and nucleophilic attack. In this study, MESP analysis was performed on the synthesized benzochromeno[3,4-c]pyridine derivatives in the gas phase and in three different solvents cyclohexane, tetrahydrofuran (THF), and water to evaluate solvent effects on electronic distribution (Fig. 5). Across all media, the MESP maps showed distinct variations in color, corresponding to differences in electrostatic potential. Consistent red regions were observed around oxygen atoms adjacent to nitrogen atoms, indicating zones of high electron density and strongly negative electrostatic potential. These areas represent nucleophilic sites capable of donating electron density to electrophilic species. The surrounding yellow regions indicate moderately negative electrostatic potential, representing less intense nucleophilic sites. Blue regions appeared predominantly around nitrogen atoms, signifying areas of positive electrostatic potential and identifying them as the most electrophilic centers in the molecules. Such positively polarized nitrogen atoms commonly act as hydrogen-bond donors and play key roles in biochemical interactions. Carbon and hydrogen atoms exhibited mostly green regions, which correspond to electrostatically neutral areas due to the low polarity of C-H bonds. Although these regions are not involved in major charge-based interactions, they contribute to hydrophobicity and influence molecular stability and membrane permeability. In all, the color patterns follow the standard MESP scale, where red indicates the most negative potential, yellow moderately negative, green neutral, and blue positive electrostatic potential. These observations provide insight into the electronic characteristics and reactive tendencies of the studied compounds.
Density of state (DOS)
Comparative DOS spectra of the compound in gas, cyclohexene, THF, and water phases.

The Density of States (DOS) analysis of the studied compound under different solvation conditions gas phase, cyclohexene, tetrahydrofuran (THF), and water provides valuable insight into how the surrounding environment influences its electronic structure. The DOS plots generated using GaussSum, as presented in Fig. 6 show the distribution of occupied and virtual molecular orbitals and how their energies shift in response to changes in solvent polarity. These variations are important because they directly affect the compound's electronic stability and reactivity. In the gas phase, the DOS profile exhibits a dense distribution of occupied orbitals with several pronounced peaks, reflecting a wide range of available electronic states. The HOMO-LUMO region appears relatively narrow, indicating a moderately small energy gap. This suggests that in the absence of solvation effects, the compound's electrons experience minimal stabilization, resulting in a relatively flexible electronic environment. Upon transitioning to cyclohexene, a non-polar solvent, the DOS pattern remains largely similar to that of the gas phase. Only minimal shifts in the energy levels are observed, indicating that non-polar environments exert limited influence on the molecule's orbital energies. Overall, cyclohexene does not significantly perturb the electronic architecture of the compound. This confirms that non-polar solvents interact weakly with the compound's charge distribution. A more noticeable change is observed in THF, a moderately polar solvent. In this environment, the DOS curve shows shifting of several occupied orbitals to lower energies, indicating enhanced stabilization from dipole-dipole interactions between the solvent and the compound. The virtual orbitals also display slight adjustments, suggesting that the solvent begins to influence both the valence and conduction regions. This increased stabilization reflects stronger solute-solvent interactions, which may slightly alter the HOMO-LUMO gap. The most pronounced electronic reorganization occurs in water, the most polar of the solvents examined. In aqueous solution, the occupied orbitals shift more deeply into negative energy values, signifying substantial stabilization of the electron density. The virtual orbitals also exhibit corresponding shifts, demonstrating that water exerts a strong electrostatic influence on both filled and empty molecular states. This significant modification of orbital energies suggests that the compound becomes more electronically stabilized in water, which can have important implications for its chemical behavior, solubility, and biological activity.

Molecular docking is a computational technique that is used in drug design, it helps to understand how well two molecules interact with each other, usually a protein and a ligand. This approach aids in understanding the strength of interaction that exists between these interacting species by virtually predicting the binding affinity, bond distance, and the number of conventional hydrogen bonds, as well as the type of interaction that exists between the interacting species. According to the literature, the higher negative values of the binding affinity suggest better interaction, vice versa. Hydrogen bonds play a crucial role in determining the specificity of ligand binding, and the bond distance typically from 2.0 to 3.0 A suggests that the interacting molecules are well-aligned and positioned for effective binding; thus, the shorter the bond distance, the stronger the ligand-protein interaction. As stated earlier, different types of interactions were observed, but more emphasis was placed on the conventional hydrogen bond due to its role in the biological system, which was highlighted above. From the result obtained in Table 6, among the selected proteins, 3rcd-Gas showed the highest binding affinity with a value of - 11 kcal/mol, indicating the strongest interaction with the protein. It formed three hydrogen bonds, involving amino acid residues such as SER783, ASP863, and SER728. Serine (SER) and aspartic acid (ASP) are crucial amino acids in protein interactions, often participating in enzyme catalysis and molecular recognition. The shorter bond distances, particularly ASP863:OD2 2.14766 A, suggest a highly stable interaction, enhancing the potential biological efficacy of 3rcd -Gas. 3pp0-Gas, with a binding affinity of - 8.8 kcal/mol, formed five hydrogen bonds, associated with ARG981 and GLU971. Arginine (ARG) is known for its role in forming strong electrostatic and hydrogen bonding interactions due to its positively charged guanidinium group, making it essential in protein-ligand binding. Glutamic acid (GLU), a negatively charged residue, further stabilizes the interaction, enhancing molecular recognition. Despite having more hydrogen bonds than 3rcd:Gas, its lower binding affinity suggests that the interactions may not be as strong or energetically favorable. 4hrn -Gas exhibited the weakest binding among the proposed compounds, with an affinity of -7.0 kcal/mol, forming only two hydrogen bonds with GLN61 and PHE112. Glutamine (GLN) plays a role in hydrogen bonding due to its amide side chain, while phenylalanine (PHE) contributes through hydrophobic interactions. The longer bond distances, particularly PHE112:O (2.94332 A), suggest weaker binding, making 4hrn-Gas less favorable than 3pp0-Gas and 3rcd-Gas.

Its strong activity against EGFR/HER2 family receptors and extensive structural characterization make it an appropriate benchmark for evaluating new anticancer candidates. High-resolution crystallographic data and well-documented binding interactions allow for accurate comparison of docking poses, interaction patterns, and binding energies. Moreover, the structural features of dacomitinib such as aromatic rings, heterocycles, and hydrogen-bonding functional groups closely resemble those found in many kinase-targeting molecules, making it mechanistically and chemically suitable for use as a reference inhibitor in this study. ADMET studies

To understand the potential therapeutic efficacy of certain compounds, an ADMET study is an important approach. The approach provides valuable insight into the pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiles of the studied compounds to be used as potential drug candidates. ADMET is an acronym that stands for Absorption, Digestion, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity. By examining the various ADMET parameters, researchers gain a comprehensive view of how the compound behaves within a biological system and its efficacy as a therapeutic agent. In this study, ADMET analysis was investigated on the (benzo)chromeno[3,4-c] pyridine compound to assess toxicity, physicochemical properties, and drug-likeness. The following tools such as Protox and SwissADME, were employed to predict and evaluate these properties. From the result obtained as presented in table x, the absorption parameters indicate favourable permeability properties. Caco-2 permeability (- 5.149) and MDCK permeability (0.0), both marked in green, suggest that the compound is capable of crossing epithelial barriers moderately well, despite its relatively large molecular weight (668.66 g/mol). The positive PAMPA and P-gp inhibitor results (both green) further support the idea that the compound has no major efflux-related absorption limitations. However, the high total polar surface area (TPSA = 186.14 A2) may pose challenges to oral bioavailability, a limitation that can be overcome through advanced drug delivery systems such as nanoparticle formulations, liposomal carriers, or parenteral administration routes. In terms of distribution, the compound exhibits a high plasma protein binding (PPB = 97.6%, red), which may reduce the free drug fraction available for pharmacological activity. Nonetheless, many clinically successful drugs show high PPB and still maintain therapeutic efficacy through appropriate dosing strategies. The steady-state volume of distribution (VDss = 1.843, green) suggests efficient tissue penetration, although blood-brain barrier permeability is predicted to be unfavourable (green), which is beneficial if the intended therapeutic target is non-CNS related. The metabolic profile reveals notable interactions with several cytochrome P450 enzymes. The compound is predicted to strongly inhibit CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP3A4, CYP2B6, and CYP2C8 (+++), while showing no inhibitory effect on CYP1A2 and CYP2D6. These metabolic interactions imply that the compound may undergo slower biotransformation and could potentially influence the metabolism of co-administered drugs. Such interactions do not disqualify the compound from drug candidacy but highlight the need for structural optimization or careful pharmacokinetic monitoring during development. Excretory parameters indicate a moderate plasma clearance rate (CL_plasma = 2.077) and a half-life (T1/2 = 1.086), suggesting that the compound may require frequent dosing unless modified through formulation or structural approaches to enhance retention time. When combined with the toxicity profile, a more comprehensive safety perspective emerges. The compound demonstrated favourable toxicological characteristics in areas such as immunotoxicity, mutagenicity, and cytotoxicity, all of which were predicted as inactive with confidence scores of 0.92, 0.54, and 0.67, respectively. These outcomes are important indicators suggesting a low likelihood of immune-related toxicity, genotoxicity, or cell-damaging effects:key requirements for early-stage drug safety. However, hepatotoxicity (0.56) and carcinogenicity (0.50) were predicted as active. Although these results warrant attention, they do not outright negate the drug development potential of the compound. Hepatotoxicity risks are not uncommon among approved therapeutics and can often be mitigated through structural modifications, prodrug approaches, or targeted delivery systems. Similarly, the carcinogenicity prediction should be interpreted cautiously, as in silico tools can occasionally produce false-positive outcomes; thus, experimental validation is recommended.

passages.text: The physicochemical properties of the studied compound showed a molecular weight of 668.66 g/mol and a total polar surface area (TPSA) of 186.14 A2. Although this poses an oral bioavailability challenge, other formulation strategies such as nanoparticle-based delivery, parenteral administration, as well as liposomal encapsulation can effectively enhance the absorption and circulation of the compound. From Table 7, it is observed that the compound violated Lipinski's and Ghose's drug-likeness rules, but this does not ultimately defeat the drug-likeness potential of the studied compound, as most successful drugs such as antibiotics, peptide-based drugs, and anticancer drugs, also violate these guidelines. The drug-likeness rule generally serves as a filter, but drugs with strong biological activities can still be optimized for improved pharmacokinetic effect.
Boiled-egg model and ADMET radar plot showing permeability, bioavailability, and physicochemical suitability of the compound.

The ADMET evaluation of the studied compound was further illustrated using the BOILED-Egg model and the ADMET bioavailability radar (see Fig. 8a, b), both of which provide visual insight into key pharmacokinetic properties relevant to drug development. The BOILED-Egg plot (see Fig. 8a) which predicts gastrointestinal absorption and blood-brain barrier penetration based on lipophilicity (WLOGP) and topological polar surface area (TPSA), clearly demonstrates that the compound falls outside both the white and yellow regions. The white region represents molecules with a high likelihood of passive gastrointestinal absorption, whereas the yellow region represents compounds that are likely to penetrate the blood-brain barrier. The placement of the compound outside these boundaries indicates poor passive intestinal permeability and an inability to cross the blood-brain barrier. This observation aligns with its relatively high TPSA value, suggesting that the compound is too polar to effectively diffuse across biological membranes. As a result, oral administration may be challenging, and alternative delivery methods such as liposomal encapsulation, nanoparticle-based systems, or parenteral routes may be required to enhance systemic exposure. On the other hand, the ADMET radar plot Fig. 8b provides a broader view of the compound's drug-likeness by assessing six physicochemical parameters: lipophilicity, size, polarity, solubility, saturation, and molecular flexibility. In an ideal scenario, a drug candidate would fall within the pink region of the radar, indicating compliance with optimal ranges across these parameters. However, the red polygon representing the studied compound extends beyond this region in several critical categories. Notably, the compound exceeds the acceptable limits for molecular size and polarity, both of which are consistent with its high molecular weight and large polar surface area. These characteristics typically limit oral bioavailability and membrane permeability. Additionally, the compound shows deviation in solubility, suggesting that it may face challenges dissolving efficiently in physiological fluids. Despite these limitations, the compound demonstrates acceptable lipophilicity and molecular flexibility, which are favorable for interaction with biological targets. The consensus average lipophilicity of the compound was evaluated and obtained to be - 0.53. This indicates that the compound exhibits relatively low lipophilicity, suggesting limited membrane permeability and reduced potential for passive diffusion across biological membranes.
Conclusions

This study focused on the In Silico Evaluation of (benzo)chromeno[3,4-c]pyridine Derivative as Dual EGFR/HER2 Inhibitors for Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer using DFT, molecular docking, ADMET, MESP, and Spectral analysis (NMR and FT-IR). In the molecular docking analysis, three proteins were selected, namely 3pp0, 3rcd, and 4hrn, which are known for their cancerous potential, and docked against the studied compound. The docking result showed a favorable interaction between the studied compound and the target protein, with protein 3rcd showing the highest binding affinity of - 11 kcal/mol, with the interaction having 3 hydrogen bonds. The interaction also showed a short bond distance of 2.14766 A at ASP863:OD2, suggesting a highly stable interaction, enhancing the potential biological efficacy of the studied compound. The interactions between the studied compound and the other selected proteins also showed favorable biological potentials. Comparing the docking result with that of the standard drug (Dacomitinib, a medication used in the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer), the studied compound ((benzo)chromeno[3,4-c]pyridines derivative 16) showed more favorable interaction, suggesting the potential of the studied compound as an effective therapeutic candidate. The structural analysis (geometry optimization) showed structural stability of the studied compound across different solvents (water, gas, cyclohexane, and THF), which is a critical feature for its biological efficacy. It was also observed that electronegative atoms exhibited solvent-responsive behavior, further supporting the suitability of the compound as a drug candidate. Also, FT-IR analysis confirmed the presence of key functional groups such as NH2/NH and C=O, which are critical for its biological activity, thereby indicating that the studied compound possesses favorable structural feature which are important for drug-like interactions. In the NMR analysis, there was a strong correlation between the experimental and theoretical values which confirms the electronic stability of the studied compound. The FMO analysis (electronic properties) revealed that the studied compound showed a moderate energy gap and favorable reactivity descriptors. Also, the NBO analysis on the other hand, showed a strong donor-receptor interaction of the studied compound, further backing the favorable potential of the compound to undergo interactions. The MESP analysis showed specific regions such as nucleophilic and electrophilic regions. The presence of these regions, makes the studied compound favorable for biological activities. The ADMET analysis indicated promising safety profiles and drug-likeness of the studied compound despite minor pharmacokinetic shortfalls. The findings from the various analyses supports the studied compound as an effective remedy for the treatment of non-small lung cancer.

passages.text: Recent advances in bispecific antibody-drug conjugates for breast cancer therapy
Purpose

Bispecific antibody-drug conjugates (BsADCs) represent a promising strategy to overcome limitations of conventional ADCs in breast cancer, such as tumor heterogeneity and inefficient internalization. This review summarizes recent advances and the therapeutic potential of BsADCs.
Methods

We conducted a literature review, focusing on BsADC candidates selected for clinical relevance (e.g., ZW49, BL-B01D1), mechanistic innovation (e.g., biparatopic targeting, engaging fast-internalizing receptors), and potential in challenging subtypes like triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC).
Results

BsADCs enhance drug delivery through dual targeting. Biparatopic HER2-targeting agents (e.g., ZW49, JSKN003) induce receptor clustering and robust internalization. BsADCs co-engaging rapidly internalizing receptors (e.g., HER2xCD63) hijack efficient endocytic pathways, showing activity even in low HER2-expression models. Furthermore, BsADCs targeting compensatory pathways, such as EGFRxHER3 (BL-B01D1) and TROP2xHER3 (JSKN016), have demonstrated breakthrough efficacy in TNBC. Optimization of linker technology and drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR) has improved stability and the therapeutic window, enabling the progression of several BsADCs into Phase III trials.
Conclusion

BsADCs are a transformative therapeutic modality for breast cancer. Their ability to enhance tumor selectivity, overcome heterogeneity, and target resistant pathways positions them as key players in the future oncology landscape, with ongoing trials poised to define their clinical role.
Introduction

Breast cancer is one of the most common malignant tumors among women worldwide, and the incidence rate is increasing year by year. The treatment landscape for breast cancer has profoundly evolved into an era of precise molecular subtyping and individualized therapy. Despite these advances, formidable challenges such as intrinsic and acquired drug resistance, profound tumor heterogeneity, and target escape remain the major bottlenecks to achieving durable clinical responses.

Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are immunoconjugates comprised of a monoclonal antibody tethered to a cytotoxic drug (known as the payload) via a chemical linker. ADC is a vector-based chemotherapy that allows the selective delivery of a potent cytotoxic agent within a tumor. Traditionally, ADCs were produced through stochastic conjugation, leading to a heterogeneous mixture of molecules with varying DARs and conjugation sites. However, there is a strong trend towards site-specific conjugation technologies (e.g., engineering cysteines, incorporating non-natural amino acids, or utilizing enzymatic conjugation). These methods generate homogeneous ADCs with defined DARs, which often exhibit improved pharmacokinetics, enhanced stability, and a broader therapeutic window compared to their heterogeneous counterparts.

Currently, ADCs are an important class of cancer therapeutics, with seventeen ADCs approved so far by the US Food and Drug Administration. Despite all the advancements in cancer therapy, inherent and acquired drug resistance continues to be major obstacles to successful treatment. Multiple mechanisms of resistance to ADCs have been reported, including antigen-related resistance, failure in internalization, impaired lysosomal function, drug-efflux pumps, and alterations of targets. A prospective approach to address the aforementioned challenges involves the conjugation of a linker-payload complex to Bispecific antibodies (BsAbs), giving rise to the concept of Bispecific antibody drug conjugates (BsADCs). The clinical rationale for this dual-targeting approach is powerfully demonstrated by the success of the trastuzumab and pertuzumab combination in HER2-positive breast cancer. By targeting domains IV and II of HER2 respectively, this standard-of-care regimen synergistically inhibits HER2 signaling and has become a standard-of-care in both metastatic and early-stage HER2-positive breast cancer, providing a strong proof-of-concept. In contrast to traditional ADCs, the unique dual epitope/target binding modes of BsADCs not only enable binding to co-expressed antigens in solid tumors to enhance selectivity but also significantly improve internalization. These distinctive advantages position BsADCs as a substantial force in the realm of next-generation ADCs. The rationale for enhanced internalization by BsADCs is multifaceted and represents a core advantage over conventional ADCs. As illustrated in Fig. 1, this enhancement can occur through several mechanisms: (1) Cooperative Internalization and Clustering: Biparatopic BsADCs binding two non-overlapping epitopes on the same antigen can cross-link and cluster receptors, forming large aggregates that are more efficiently internalized via endocytosis. (2) Leveraging Rapidly Internalizing Receptors: BsADCs targeting a tumor-associated antigen (e.g., HER2) and a second, rapidly internalizing receptor (e.g., CD63, PRLR) can exploit the efficient endocytic machinery of the latter, effectively 'shuttling' the ADC into the cell even if the primary tumor antigen has poor internalization kinetics.
Mechanisms of enhanced internalization by Bispecific antibody-drug conjugates (BsADCs)

(A) A conventional monospecific ADC shows limited internalization efficiency. In contrast, BsADCs enhance payload delivery through two primary strategies: (B) A biparatopic BsADC induces receptor clustering and robust internalization by binding two distinct epitopes on the same tumor-associated antigen. (C) A Bispecific ADC co-engages a tumor-specific antigen and a rapidly internalizing "shuttle" receptor (e.g., CD63), hijacking the latter's efficient endocytic pathway for improved cellular uptake. The internalized complexes are trafficked through early and late endosomes to lysosomes, where cytotoxic payloads are released.)

passages.text: This review primarily focuses on BsADCs in breast cancer that exemplify key strategic advances and have reached at least the stage of preclinical proof-of-concept. We have selected representative candidates based on the following criteria: (1) Clinical relevance: BsADCs that have entered clinical trials and generated reported data (e.g., ZW49, MEDI4276, BL-B01D1, JSKN016). (2) Mechanistic innovation: BsADCs that illustrate distinct targeting paradigms, such as biparatopic targeting for enhanced internalization (e.g., JSKN003) or engaging fast-internalizing receptors (e.g., HER2xCD63). (3) Therapeutic potential for challenging subtypes: Agents showing breakthrough efficacy in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) or against tumors with low antigen expression. While this selection is not exhaustive, it provides a comprehensive overview of the current landscape and the most promising design strategies in the field.
Structure of BsADC

The core structure of BsADC includes a Bispecific antibody (bsAb), a linker, and a payload. Following the binding to cancer cell-surface antigen, BsADC is internalized by receptor-mediated endocytosis, and the payload is released by the degradation of the linker or the antibody in the endolysosomal compartment. Therefore, the development of BsADCs requires careful consideration of multiple factors, including target antigen biology, antibody specificity, payload cytotoxicity and mechanism of action, linker stability and cleavage, and conjugation sites. Beyond these factors, an inherent consideration in Bispecific targeting is the potential requirement for co-expression of both target antigens on the same tumor cell for optimal activity. An inherent consideration in Bispecific targeting is the potential requirement for co-expression of both target antigens on the same tumor cell for optimal activity. This concept could, in theory, restrict the target cell population compared to a monospecific ADC. However, this potential limitation is counterbalanced by two key factors. First, the enhanced internalization and potency on double-positive cells may more effectively eradicate this critical subpopulation. Second, and crucially, the use of cleavable linkers enables the 'bystander effect', whereby membrane-permeable payloads released in double-positive cells can diffuse and kill adjacent tumor cells expressing only one or even none of the target antigens. This effect is vital for overcoming tumor heterogeneity and ensuring comprehensive tumor cell killing. The structure of BsADCs integrates several critical design components that collectively determine their therapeutic efficacy and safety profile. As summarized in Fig. 2, these include the Bispecific antibody format, linker chemistry, and cytotoxic payload, each offering distinct strategic advantages.
Key design components and strategies of Bispecific antibody-drug conjugates (BsADCs)

passages.text: Classification of Bispecific antibody formats, distinguishing between Bispecific (dual-antigen) targeting (e.g., HER2 x CD63) and biparatopic (dual-epitope) targeting (e.g., HER2 ECD2 x ECD4).

Linker technologies, detailing cleavable linkers including protease-cleavable (e.g., Val-Cit), reduction-sensitive (e.g., disulfide), and acid-labile (e.g., hydrazone) types, as well as non-cleavable linkers (e.g., SMCC).

Diverse payload classes, encompassing microtubule inhibitors (e.g., auristatins, maytansinoids), DNA-damaging agents (e.g., calicheamicin, duocarmycins, PBDs), topoisomerase I inhibitors (e.g., DXd, SN-38), and other emerging payloads (e.g., RNA polymerase II inhibitors such as amanitins).
Bispecific antibodies(BsAb)

Bispecific antibodies (bsAbs) bind two different epitopes on the same or different antigens. Through this dual specificity for soluble or cell-surface antigens, bsAbs exert activities beyond those of natural antibodies, offering numerous opportunities for therapeutic applications. A critical distinction must be made between Bispecific and biparatopic antibodies. Bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) constitute a broad category defined by their ability to bind two different antigens or epitopes. This category can be divided into two primary classes: those that engage two distinct antigens (e.g., HER2 and CD63), and biparatopic antibodies, which are a specialized subset that bind two distinct, non-overlapping epitopes on the same antigen (e.g., two different domains of HER2). Consequently, while all biparatopic antibodies are Bispecific, not all Bispecific antibodies are biparatopic. Both strategies are leveraged in BsADC design, with biparatopic targeting primarily aimed at enhancing receptor clustering and internalization, while Bispecific targeting across different antigens can engage distinct biological pathways or exploit differential internalization rates. Antibodies consist of two heavy chains and light chains, encompassing the Fc region and Fab region. When constructing ADCs, the fundamental requirements for the antibody skeleton include a suitable circulating half-life and low immunogenicity. More than 100 different bsAb formats have been reported according to a recent review. While their molecular architectures are different, virtually all of them can be grouped into one of the two large categories: fragment-based bsAbs and Fc-based bsAbs. Fragment-based bsAbs, consisting exclusively of antibody variable domains, are a major class of bsAb formats. They are in general smaller in size than Fc-based bsAbs and hence, show better tissue penetration in vivo. Meanwhile, the loss of binding to Fc gamma receptor (FcgammaR) reduces Fc mediated nonspecific drug uptake. Conversely, the loss of binding to the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) leads to a relatively short half-life in plasma. To circumvent this limitation, strategies such as PEGylation or the introduction of albumin-binding motifs are actively explored to prolong the plasma half-life of these smaller constructs. This creates a fundamental design trade-off: optimizing for superior tissue penetration often comes at the cost of plasma persistence, and vice versa. While there are a variety of different fragment-based bsAb formats, three of them have been more extensively investigated in preclinical and clinical studies: tandem scFvs, dual affinity retargeting (DART) proteins, and tandem diabodies (TandAbs). Fc-based bsAbs have homo- or heterodimeric Fc domains (and less frequently CH3 domains only) to which Fab, scFv or sdAb are attached through a peptide linker. Fc-containing BsADCs bring additional advantages such as antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC), immune phagocytosis, and cytokine release, which collectively contribute to tumor killing. However, the binding to FcgammaR during endocytosis may lead to the internalization of BsADCs in normal tissues, resulting in off-target toxicity. This risk can be mitigated through Fc engineering, such as introducing point mutations (e.g., L234A/L235A, or N297A) to reduce or ablate FcgammaR binding, thereby minimizing Fc-mediated, antigen-independent uptake. While this challenge is inherent to all Fc-containing ADCs, the dual-targeting nature of BsADCs necessitates particularly careful optimization of Fc function to balance potential efficacy (e.g., ADCC) against the risk of off-target toxicity. Fc-based bsAbs can be categorized into two large groups: symmetric and asymmetric. Symmetric Fc-based bsAbs typically have additional Fv or scFv moieties at the N- and/or C-termini of the polypeptide chains, making them larger than conventional IgG antibodies. On the other hand, asymmetric Fc-based bsAbs are produced by the preferential heterodimerization of two engineered Fcs, making them identical in size and shape to conventional IgG and each of the two arms of the bsAb recognizing a different antigen.

passages.text: The paramount considerations in the construction of BsADCs lie in the judicious selection of a suitable target combination. Target selection serves as a fundamental prerequisite for the successful development of ADCs, exerting a pivotal influence on the ultimate therapeutic window and systemic toxicity. Ideally, the target antigen for ADC needs to be overexpressed on cancer cell surfaces with no or negligible expression on normal healthy tissues. Owing to the unique dual targeting characteristics of BsADCs, a comprehensive consideration of the deep-level effects of antigen combinations is essential. This encompasses factors include internalization, recycling, turnover rates, lysosomal degradation, and obligate mechanisms.

passages.text: Linkers

The linker connects the antibody and the cytotoxic payload and is a key component in the function of BsADCs. The linker imparts the following characteristics to BsADCs: (1) high stability in the circulation, and (2) specific release of payload in the target tissue.

The first type is the cleavable linker, which is designed to be selectively cleaved in the tumor microenvironment or inside the cancer cell to release the cytotoxic payload. The most prevalent and clinically validated strategy utilizes enzymatically cleavable linkers, which leverage the high activity of specific lysosomal proteases (e.g., cathepsin B). Other important mechanisms include acid-labile linkers that hydrolyze in the markedly lower pH within endolysosomes (pH ~ 4.5-5.0) compared to blood (pH ~ 7.4), and reducible disulfide linkers that are cleaved by elevated concentrations of reducing agents like glutathione (GSH) in the cytosol. Based on these mechanisms, cleavable linkers are categorized into three major classes. Protease-cleavable linkers, exemplified by the Valine-Citrulline (Val-Cit) dipeptide, are stable in plasma and are selectively cleaved by lysosomal proteases such as cathepsin B following ADC internalization. This strategy is a cornerstone of many modern ADCs, including brentuximab vedotin. In contrast, acid-labile linkers (e.g., hydrazone) are designed to hydrolyze in the acidic compartments of the endo-lysosomal system; however, their susceptibility to hydrolysis at neutral pH can contribute to premature payload release and off-target toxicity, a limitation observed in the first-generation ADC gemtuzumab ozogamicin. Finally, disulfide linkers rely on the high reducing potential within the cell cytosol for cleavage by glutathione. The in vivo stability of disulfide linkers can be enhanced through structural engineering to introduce steric hindrance. Beyond targeted release, a pivotal advantage of cleavable linkers is their ability to generate membrane-permeable payload catabolites. This property enables the "bystander effect," whereby the cytotoxic agent can diffuse from an antigen-positive tumor cell to kill adjacent antigen-negative cancer cells. This effect is crucial for overcoming tumor heterogeneity. Ultimately, the central challenge for all cleavable linker technologies lies in balancing this potent efficacy against the risk of off-target toxicity from premature cleavage.

passages.text: The second type of linker is non-cleavable. In contrast to the cleavable linker, there are no chemical triggers in this structure, and the linker is part of the payload. Non-cleavable linkers (e.g., SMCC), characterized by high stability in plasma, can only undergo degradation in the lysosome to release the payload. This linker design typically results in superior plasma stability, which can contribute to an improved therapeutic index by minimizing premature payload release. However, it is important to note that non-cleavable linkers are not devoid of off-target toxicity. For instance, ADCs utilizing non-cleavable linkers have been associated with significant ocular toxicity, as seen with tisotumab vedotin, indicating that the released payload metabolite can still affect sensitive tissues.

passages.text: Cytotoxic payloads

The cytotoxic payload is the warhead that exerts cytotoxicity after internalization of BsADCs into cancer cells. Cytotoxic payloads, integral to BsADCs, play a crucial role in determining the overall antitumor effect and potential adverse reactions. The activity and physicochemical properties of the payload have a direct impact on the antitumor efficacy of ADC drugs. The mechanism of action of the payload is an important factor determining the performance of the ADC (e.g., adverse reactions). Besides, certain other characteristics of ADC payloads, such as cytotoxicity, immunogenicity, stability of storage during preparation and circulation, water solubility, and modifiability are also important.

passages.text: The ideal payloads should have the following characteristics. First, they should have adequately high cytotoxicity, typically with half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values in the picomolar (pM) to low nanomolar (nM) range (e.g., 0.01-1.01 nM) against target tumor cell lines. The fundamental reason ADC payloads require extreme potency is that the actual number of molecules reaching the cytosol of each tumor cell is exceedingly low. This is driven by two factors: the limited repertoire of safe and specific antigen targets, and the overall low delivery efficiency-collectively caused by the poor permeability of antibodies in solid tumors and the intrinsically inefficient internalization process. Second, payloads must be sufficiently hydrophilic or incorporate structural features (e.g., polar groups, solubilizing linkers) to achieve adequate water solubility (often targeting > 0.1-1.1 mg/mL) to prevent aggregation during ADC formulation and in circulation. Third, ADC payloads should have sufficiently low immunogenicity. Protein drugs have the risk to induce immunogenicity, which may negatively affect the ADC efficacy or even lead to mortality of the treated patients. Fourth, high stability is paramount. The linker-payload complex should be stable in the systemic circulation to minimize off-target toxicity from premature release, ideally exhibiting a long half-life (> 7 days) in plasma. An ideal linker must achieve a delicate balance between sufficient stability during circulation and efficient release of the cytotoxic payload specifically within the tumor. Furthermore, the conjugated ADC must demonstrate high chemical stability in formulation, with minimal degradation or aggregation, which can be assessed by techniques such as size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) and sedimentation velocity analytical ultracentrifugation (SV-AUC). Fifth, ADC payloads should have functional groups that can be modified without significantly affecting their potency. The payload must have a modifiable functional group or a site that can conjugate to the monoclonal antibody. The site of the modification must be carefully selected to preserve the potency of the parental drug. More importantly, when using non-cleavable linkers, the payload must retain its potency even after the antibody degrades. Finally, the ADC payloads should have bystander effects. Some ADC drugs are internalized and release small, uncharged, permeable membrane hydrophobic molecules, which spread through the cell membrane and kill tumor cells with negative expression of adjacent antigens. This process is known as the "bystander effect" and has important implications on tumor cells with uneven antigen-expression.

passages.text: Currently, cytotoxic payloads used in ADCs mainly include potent microtubule inhibitors, DNA-damaging agents, and immunomodulators. Microtubules are an important part of the cytoskeleton in eukaryotic cells. Microtubules play an important role in maintaining various cellular functions such as cell morphology, signal transduction, organelle transportation, cell motility, cell division, and mitosis, and are important targets for tumor therapy. Tubulin is the composition of microtubules, and tubulin inhibitors interfere with the dynamic combination of microtubules by binding to tubulin, arresting cells in the G2/M phase of the cell cycle, and ultimately leading to apoptosis. Compared to tubulin inhibitors, DNA-damaging agents (e.g., calicheamicin, duocarmycins) can act throughout the cell cycle and have demonstrated efficacy in solid tumors. It was historically hypothesized that due to their extreme potency, fewer molecules of DNA-damaging payloads would be required per cell to achieve cell kill. However, the clinical development of some ultra-potent DNA-intercalators like the pyrrolobenzodiazepine (PBD) dimers has been challenged by significant off-target toxicities, potentially related to their persistent DNA damage and the bystander effect. In contrast, topoisomerase I inhibitors (e.g., DXd, SN-38) have emerged as a highly successful class of DNA-damaging payloads, offering a favorable balance of high potency and manageable safety profiles, as evidenced by the success of ADCs like trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd).

passages.text: Drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR)

Drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR) represents the number of linker-drugs attached to a given antibody. There are substantial differences in the in vivo pharmacokinetics of various drug-carrying forms of ADCs (DAR = 0-8). For BsADCs, the DAR typically ranges between 2 and 4. This range strikes an optimal balance between potency and pharmacokinetic properties. Concrete preclinical and clinical data substantiate the significant impact of DAR on pharmacokinetic profiles. For instance, in a murine model, a site-specific trastuzumab-based ADC with a DAR of 6 exhibited a faster clearance and a shorter half-life compared to its DAR 4 counterpart when measuring conjugated antibody (the intact ADC). This phenomenon, often referred to as "DAR-dependent clearance," is attributed to increased hydrophobicity and non-specific uptake by the mononuclear phagocyte system at higher DARs. Clinical observations further support this; population PK modeling of the DM4-based ADC, tusamitamab ravtansine (DAR ~ 3.8), characterized the irreversible deconjugation from higher to lower DAR species as a key determinant of its overall disposition. Consequently, for less potent payloads, higher DAR values may be necessary to achieve sufficient cell-killing effects. However, a simple increase in payload conjugation at high DAR can lead to conjugate hydrophobicity, leading to faster clearance by the mononuclear phagocyte system and accelerated plasma elimination, rather than renal clearance which is predominant for small molecules.

B, C: BsADC-antigen complex gradually forms an endosome. (drugs release from cleavable linkers). D: BsADC-antigen complex is degraded within a lysosome. (drugs release from cleavable and non-cleavable linkers). E: The payload produces various cytotoxic effects, such as the following; E1, microtubule disruption; E2, DNA damage. passages.text: The mechanism of action of BsADCs, from cell surface binding to payload release and induction of cell death, including the bystander effect, is depicted in Fig. 3.
Progress of BsADCs in breast cancer research
BsADCs on HER2

Breast cancer is the most common cancer type among women worldwide, with HER2-positive breast cancer accounting for 15% to 20% of all breast cancer cases. Clinically approved HER2-targeting monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) and ADCs have significantly transformed treatment options for HER2-positive breast cancer, yielding clinical benefits. However, the expression heterogeneity of HER2 poses a limitation to the efficacy of current anti-HER2 therapies in cases of relatively low HER2 levels. This not only narrows the range of indications for HER2 therapy but also fosters drug resistance under therapeutic pressure81. Additionally, the potential resistance of HER2 to internalization diminishes drug efficacy. Fortunately, the dual binding model of BsADCs offers a promising solution to the current challenges of poor internalization and drug resistance in HER2-targeting for breast cancer.
Dual-epitope BsADC targeting HER2
ZW49:

ZW49 is generated from the conjugation of a novel N-acyl sulfonamide auristatin payload to the inter-chain disulfide bond cysteines of the Bispecific anti-HER2 IgG1 antibody ZW25 (now known by its generic name, zanidatamab), via a protease cleavable linker. Auristatin-based payloads, such as the conventional monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE), are exceptionally potent microtubule inhibitors with IC50 values typically ranging from 10 to 100 pM against various cancer cell lines. The strategic physicochemical modifications in this novel variant are designed to fine-tune its membrane permeability, thereby aiming to control the bystander effect and expand the therapeutic window. Zanidatamab is an asymmetric IgG1-like molecule produced using the Azymetric  platform, which incorporates engineered CH3 domains ("knobs-into-holes" and electrostatic steering) to ensure heavy-chain heterodimerization and correct assembly. This site-specific conjugation strategy, targeting the hinge cysteine residues, enables the generation of a highly homogeneous ADC population with a controlled DAR of 2-3, as characterized by hydrophobic interaction chromatography (HIC), minimizing the heterogeneity and aggregation risks common with stochastic conjugation methods. The conjugate exhibits high stability in circulation, as the protease-cleavable linker-which incorporates a valine-citrulline (Val-Cit) dipeptide sequence-remains intact in plasma. However, upon internalization and trafficking to the lysosome, the Val-Cit motif is efficiently cleaved by cathepsin B, enabling rapid payload release kinetics. This efficient intracellular release mechanism, combined with the membrane-permeable nature of the payload, is critical for mediating a potent bystander effect, allowing it to diffuse into and kill adjacent cancer cells that may have heterogeneous or low HER2 expression, thereby overcoming a key mechanism of tumor resistance. In cellular binding assays, it was confirmed that the payload conjugation to ZW25 did not affect the antibody's binding to HER2-expressing cells. Zanidatamab (formerly ZW25) was constructed using the IgG1-like heterodimeric Azymetric  Fc platform, with an anti-HER2-ECD4 single chain variable fragment (scFv) linked to heavy chain 1 and an anti-HER2-ECD2 fragment antigen-binding (Fab) domain on heavy chain 2. Zanidatamab can bind two HER2 via a trans receptor binding model, inducing the formation of large, polarized aggregate clusters. This not only improves the internalization effect but also promotes antibody hexamerization, achieving enhanced CDC effects. ZW49 incorporates a novel payload, N-acyl sulfonamide auristatin, making it well-tolerated. The favorable tolerability profile of ZW49 is attributed to strategic physicochemical modifications conferred by the N-acyl sulfonamide group on the auristatin payload. This moiety acts as a carboxylic acid bioisostere, which significantly reduces the payload's intrinsic lipophilicity compared to conventional auristatins like monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE). The resultant decrease in membrane permeability confines the cytotoxic activity more effectively within target cells, thereby mitigating the potent bystander effect-a known contributor to on-target, off-tumor toxicity in healthy tissues expressing low levels of HER2. This controlled bystander activity helps expand the therapeutic window. Furthermore, the enhanced hydrophilicity of the N-acyl sulfonamide auristatin likely improves the solubility of the conjugate and contributes to superior plasma stability by minimizing aggregation and non-specific interactions, which collectively reduce the risk of premature payload release and systemic exposure. The Bispecific antibody nature of ZW49 contributes to superior internalization compared to trastuzumab. Its Fc region imparts ADCC, ADCP, and CDC effects, while the hexamer mode of HER2 enhances CDC and internalization.

passages.text: Preclinical data indicates that ZW49 exhibits a potent tumor-killing effect and good tolerance without compromising HER2 affinity (highest non-severely toxic dose = 18 mg/kg). Currently, ZW49 is undergoing a phase I clinical trial (NCT03821233). Preliminary results have suggested promising efficacy in various types of HER2-positive tumors. In eight breast cancer patients with a median of six prior therapies treated at the cohort expansion recommended dose, an ORR of 13% was observed (1 of 8 patients).Toxicity analysis revealed two cases of G2 keratitis lasting more than 14 days; approximately 43% of patients exhibited keratitis, but all events decreased to G1 or eventually resolved. There were no interstitial lung disease (ILD) events or deaths related to treatment. However, subsequent clinical development of ZW49 appears to have been deprioritized in favor of other assets within the Zymeworks pipeline, and its future development strategy remains to be clarified. This strategic decision likely stems from a confluence of factors beyond the clinical data itself. Firstly, the competitive landscape for HER2-targeting ADCs became increasingly crowded, most notably with the approval and immense success of trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd), which set a very high bar for efficacy. Secondly, the observed limited efficacy (ORR of 13% in the phase I breast cancer cohort), coupled with a significant rate of ocular toxicity (keratitis), resulted in a potentially narrow therapeutic index for ZW49. Within this context, the parent antibody, zanidatamab (the Bispecific antibody component of ZW49), demonstrated compelling clinical activity both as a monotherapy and in combinations, presenting a broader and more immediate developmental path. Consequently, resources were strategically reallocated to prioritize zanidatamab and other next-generation candidates, reflecting a pipeline realignment based on commercial viability and a clearer path to registration.
MEDI4276:

MEDI4276 was constructed by attaching the single-chain variable fragment (scFv) of trastuzumab to the N terminus of the heavy chain of the anti-HER2 fully human mAb 39 S (IgG1kappa).Trastuzumab and 39 S bind to nonoverlapping distant epitopes on HER2. Thus, MEDI4276 contains four antigen-binding sites, two on each arm, that are capable of interacting with HER2. The presence of four high-affinity binding sites promotes efficient recruitment and clustering of HER2 molecules, even in tumor models with low HER2 expression. Such a biparatopic, tetravalent, monospecific antibody was shown to induce robust receptor clustering, internalization, lysosomal trafficking, and subsequent degradation of the complex. It is plausible that this dense clustering enhances the local concentration of lysosomal proteases, thereby facilitating more efficient cleavage of the protease-labile linker and subsequent payload release. The payload, AZ13599185 is a tubulysin variant that developed by AstraZeneca/MedImmune. Tubulysins are a class of ultra-potent cytotoxics, often exhibiting IC50 values in the low nanomolar to picomolar range, which is commensurate with the requirements for effective ADC therapy. Its efficient release within the cell, coupled with its inherent membrane permeability, is crucial for mediating the potent cytotoxicity observed, even in low HER2-expressing models. The mode of action of this small-molecule toxin is to inhibit microtubule polymerization during mitosis to induce cell death. The biparatopic antibody contains three site mutations in the Fc region, L234F, S239C, and S442C. The two engineered cysteine residues per heavy chain (S239C and S442C) enable site-specific conjugation of AZ13599185 to the antibody via a maleimidocaproyl linker, resulting in a biparatopic ADC with a DAR of 4. The mutation L234F in combination with the S239C mutation reduced FcgammaR binding. It is thought that these mutations may minimize the FcgammaR-mediated, HER2-independent uptake of ADC by normal tissues, thereby reducing off-target toxicity. It is noteworthy that these mutations are strategically located outside the FcRn binding interface; therefore, they are not anticipated to compromise FcRn-mediated recycling, thus preserving the antibody's extended plasma half-life. This design exemplifies a sophisticated strategy to decouple undesirable Fc effector functions from favorable pharmacokinetic properties.

passages.text: A first-in-human, phase 1, multicenter, open-label, dose-escalation study(NCT02576548) was conducted to evaluate the safety, pharmacokinetics (PK), immunogenicity, and antitumor activity of MEDI4276 in patients with HER2-positive advanced breast cancer or gastric cancer. This study showed that despite some clinical activity (albeit limited) in breast cancer, further clinical development of MEDI4276 is challenged by an unfavorable PK profile (insufficient to overcome a potential antigen sink) and high toxicity. MEDI4276 doses escalated from 0.05 to 0.9 mg/kg (60- to 90-minute intravenous infusion every 3 weeks). Primary endpoints were safety and tolerability; secondary endpoints included antitumor activity (objective response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival), pharmacokinetics, and immunogenicity. Forty-seven patients (median age 59 years; median of seven prior treatment regimens) were treated. The maximum tolerated dose was exceeded at 0.9 mg/kg with two patients experiencing dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) of grade 3 liver function test (LFT) increases, one of whom also had grade 3 diarrhea, which resolved. Two additional patients reported DLTs of grade 3 LFT increases at lower doses (0.4 and 0.6 mg/kg). The most common (all grade) drug-related adverse events (AEs) were nausea (59.6%), fatigue (44.7%), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) increased (42.6%), and vomiting (38.3%). The most common grade 3/4 drug-related AE was AST increased (21.3%). Five patients had drug-related AEs leading to treatment discontinuation. In the as-treated population, there was one complete response (0.5 mg/kg; breast cancer), and two partial responses (0.6 and 0.75 mg/kg; breast cancer)-all had prior trastuzumab, pertuzumab, and ado-trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1). MEDI4276 has demonstrable clinical activity but displays intolerable toxicity at doses > 0.3 mg/kg.

passages.text: The failure of MEDI4276 underscores the critical challenge of balancing efficacy and toxicity in ADC development. The unfavorable therapeutic index was likely attributable to a combination of factors rather than a single flaw. The tetravalent, biparatopic design, while driving exceptional internalization, may have contributed to an 'antigen sink' and rapid clearance, undermining its pharmacokinetics. Furthermore, the payload (tubulysin variant AZ13599185) and the relatively high DAR of 4 might have played a significant role. Even with Fc engineering to reduce FcgammaR binding, the potent payload and efficient delivery system may have led to unacceptable on-target/off-tumor toxicity in tissues with basal HER2 expression. Therefore, the failure of MEDI4276 should not be viewed solely as a failure of the Bispecific strategy, but as a lesson in the intricate optimization of antibody format, payload, and DAR.

passages.text: JSKN003:

JSKN003 is a Bispecific HER2-targeting ADC that harnesses the dual epitope binding (domains II/IV) of KN026. The Fc glycan-directed conjugation platform allows for site-specific attachment of four DXd molecules per antibody, resulting in enhanced structural homogeneity compared to maleimide-based stochastic cysteine conjugation. This approach also improves hydrophilicity, reducing aggregation, and enhances serum stability, leading to prolonged payload retention. These properties contribute to a favorable pharmacokinetic profile and reduced off-target toxicities, which is anticipated to extend the therapeutic window. The improved structural homogeneity and stability may, in theory, contribute to a reduced risk of certain off-target toxicities. However, the comparative safety profile, particularly regarding critical adverse events like ILD, awaits direct clinical validation in ongoing and future studies. This stable architecture delivers the topoisomerase I inhibitor DXd. DXd is a highly potent derivative of exatecan, demonstrating IC50 values in the low nM range (e.g., 0.5-5.5 nM) in multiple cancer cell lines. Furthermore, DXd is designed to be membrane-permeable, which is a key factor underlying the robust bystander effect that has become a hallmark of DXd-based ADCs like trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd), allowing it to effectively target heterogeneous tumors. In addition to its enhanced structural stability, JSKN003 retains the superior HER2-binding and internalization properties of KN026, ensuring efficient payload delivery to trastuzumab-resistant tumor cells. This enables JSKN003 to potentially suppress the proliferation of trastuzumab-resistant tumors.

Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: JSKN003 entered a first-in-human, dose-escalation, multicenter, open-label, phase I study (NCT05494918).The phase 1 clinical trial of 32 patients against various solid tumors with different HER2 expression levels yielded promising results. Treatment was well-tolerated, with Grade 3 or higher TRAEs occurring in 6.3% of patients (2/32), manifested as anemia (hematologic) and fatigue (constitutional). The most common TRAEs of any grade were diarrhea (62.5%) and nausea (50.0%). Importantly, no dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) were observed, and the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) was not reached up to 8.4 mg/kg. Pharmacokinetic analysis revealed dose-proportional exposure and a half-life of approximately 5-6 days at doses of 6.3 mg/kg and above, with minimal accumulation, supporting a Q3W dosing schedule. These efficacy outcomes can be contextualized against historical data from the DESTINY-PanTumor02 trial, where DS-8201a (T-DXd) reported an ORR of 37.1% across all HER2-expressing solid tumors and 61.3% in the IHC 3 + subgroup. While direct cross-trial comparisons have inherent limitations, the notably higher DCR observed with JSKN003 (90.6%) may indicate a potential for sustained disease control. Based on these encouraging preliminary efficacy and safety signals, JSKN003 entered phase 3 trials in December 2023 (NCT06079983).
